Programming for Everybody (Getting Started with Python)  
Course Syllabus – 8-Week Introductory Track

Below is the chapter-by-chapter roadmap.  Each chapter lists the core purpose and the “big idea” students should carry away.  All readings and exercises come from the open book “Python for Everybody” (PY4E) by Dr. Charles Severance.

Chapter 1 – Why We Program  
Purpose: Convince you that programming is a super-power for everyone, not just “computer people.”  
Big Idea: Computers are fast; humans are smart.  Programming lets you pair the two.

Chapter 2 – Variables, Expressions, and Statements  
Purpose: Learn to store, name, and transform data—the first step from human thought to machine action.  
Big Idea: A program is a sequence of simple instructions; variables are the nouns, expressions the verbs.

Chapter 3 – Conditional Execution  
Purpose: Make programs make decisions (if/else).  
Big Idea: Real-world problems have branches; code should too.

Chapter 4 – Functions  
Purpose: Package reusable logic so you can “say it once, use it many.”  
Big Idea: Good functions are like LEGO bricks—small, clear, and combinable.

Chapter 5 – Loops and Iteration  
Purpose: Automate repetition without copy-paste.  
Big Idea: Let the computer do the boring stuff while you think about the interesting stuff.

Chapter 6 – Strings  
Purpose: Manipulate text—the most common data type in the wild.  
Big Idea: Strings are sequences; slicing and methods turn raw text into useful information.

Chapter 7 – Files  
Purpose: Persist data beyond RAM and share it with other programs.  
Big Idea: Disk is cheap and permanent; learn to read from it and write to it.

Chapter 8 – Lists  
Purpose: Handle many items as one object.  
Big Idea: Lists are ordered collections; loops + lists = powerful data processing.

Chapter 9 – Dictionaries  
Purpose: Store and retrieve data by meaningful labels instead of numeric positions.  
Big Idea: When order doesn’t matter, keys unlock speed and clarity.

Chapter 10 – Tuples  
Purpose: Immutable, lightweight containers for fixed-size records.  
Big Idea: Sometimes “read-only” is a feature, not a limitation.

Chapter 11 – Regular Expressions  
Purpose: Find patterns in text with surgical precision.  
Big Idea: A 10-character regex can replace 100 lines of string code.

Chapter 12 – Network Programming  
Purpose: Pull data from the web using sockets and HTTP.  
Big Idea: The internet is just another file—once you know how to open it.

Chapter 13 – Using Web Services (XML & JSON)  
Purpose: Consume real-world APIs and speak the lingua franca of web data.  
Big Idea: Structured formats let programs talk to each other across languages and continents.

Chapter 14 – Object-Oriented Python (Optional Deep-Dive)  
Purpose: Model complex entities as self-contained objects.  
Big Idea: Classes bundle data and behavior; good design makes big systems feel small.

Capstone Mini-Project – “Data in My World”  
Purpose: Tie everything together by scraping, cleaning, analyzing, and visualizing a dataset you care about.  
Big Idea: The best way to learn is to build something you’ll actually use.

output:
Classic computer-science interview questions tend to cluster around a dozen core topics. If you can demonstrate solid command of these areas, you’ll cover 90 % of what most companies (from start-ups to FAANG) will probe:

1. Data Structures  
   • Arrays, strings, linked lists  
   • Stacks, queues, deques  
   • Hash tables / dictionaries / sets  
   • Trees (BST, AVL, segment, Fenwick, tries)  
   • Heaps (min/max, priority queues)  
   • Graphs (adjacency list/matrix)  

2. Algorithms & Complexity  
   • Big-O, Big-Ω, Big-Θ, amortized analysis  
   • Sorting & searching (quick, merge, heap, binary search, lower bounds)  
   • Two-pointer, sliding-window, prefix-sum techniques  
   • Recursion, backtracking, DFS/BFS, topological sort  
   • Greedy algorithms, dynamic programming (0/1 knapsack, LIS, edit distance)  
   • Divide & conquer, bit manipulation  

3. Object-Oriented Design & Patterns  
   • Encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, composition  
   • SOLID principles, design patterns (singleton, factory, observer, strategy, etc.)  
   • UML class diagrams, sequence diagrams  

4. System Design (mid-to-senior roles)  
   • Scalability, load balancing, sharding, replication, CAP theorem  
   • Caching layers (LRU, LFU, Redis, Memcached)  
   • Databases (SQL vs. NoSQL, indexing, normalization, denormalization)  
   • Microservices vs. monoliths, message queues, eventual consistency  
   • API design (REST, GraphQL, versioning)  

5. Concurrency & Parallelism  
   • Threads vs. processes, race conditions, deadlocks, livelocks  
   • Locks, semaphores, monitors, condition variables  
   • Atomic operations, compare-and-swap, memory models  
   • Thread pools, async/await, event loops, map-reduce  

6. Operating Systems  
   • Virtual memory, paging, segmentation, TLB  
   • Scheduling algorithms (FCFS, round-robin, priority, CFS)  
   • File systems, I/O buffering, page cache  
   • Interrupts, system calls, context switching  

7. Networking  
   • TCP vs. UDP, three-way handshake, congestion control  
   • HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3, REST semantics, status codes  
   • DNS, TLS/SSL, load balancers, CDNs  
   • IPv4 vs. IPv6, NAT, subnetting, CIDR  

8. Databases & Storage Engines  
   • B-trees, LSM-trees, write-ahead logs, MVCC  
   • ACID properties, isolation levels, 2-phase commit  
   • Query planning, indexes (B-tree, hash, bitmap, covering)  
   • Sharding strategies, consistent hashing  

9. Language-Specific Idioms & Tooling  
   • Memory management (stack vs. heap, garbage collection, RAII)  
   • Generics/templates, closures/lambdas, reflection  
   • Build systems (Maven, Gradle, Make, Bazel)  
   • Debuggers, profilers, static analyzers, linters  

10. Testing & Quality Assurance  
    • Unit, integration, system, regression, property-based testing  
    • Test doubles (mocks, stubs, fakes)  
    • TDD, BDD, code coverage metrics  

11. Security Basics  
    • OWASP Top 10, XSS, CSRF, SQL injection, buffer overflows  
    • Authentication vs. authorization, OAuth2, JWT, HMAC  
    • Encryption at rest vs. in transit, symmetric vs. asymmetric crypto  

12. Behavioral & “Soft” Questions  
    • STAR method for past experiences  
    • Conflict resolution, mentorship, prioritization, agile ceremonies  
    • Estimation techniques (Fermi problems, planning poker)  

If you prepare concrete examples and stories around these twelve pillars—especially with code you can whiteboard or discuss in detail—you’ll be ready for the vast majority of classic CS interviews.

Creative at-home projects related to **Circuits**

1. Paper-Circuit Greeting Cards  
   – Copper tape, coin cell, and LEDs turn any card into a light-up masterpiece.

2. Joule-Thief Night-Light  
   – Harvest the “dead” energy from an almost-empty AA battery to power a white LED.

3. Soft-Circuit Stuffed Animal  
   – Sew conductive thread, LilyPad LEDs, and a tiny battery holder into a plush toy so its eyes glow when hugged.

4. Mini Mint-Tin Amplifier  
   – Pack a simple LM386 audio amp circuit into an Altoids tin; plug in a guitar or phone for instant portable sound.

5. LED Edge-Lit Acrylic Sign  
   – Engrave a design on clear acrylic, then hide a strip of LEDs along one edge for a futuristic glowing display.

6. DIY Lie-Detector (Galvanic Skin Response)  
   – Two finger electrodes, an Arduino, and a buzzer/LED bar graph show how skin conductance changes with stress.

7. “Simon Says” Memory Game  
   – Four colored buttons, LEDs, and a microcontroller recreate the classic 1980s toy on a breadboard.

8. Persistence-of-Vision (POV) Wand  
   – Spin a row of LEDs on a stick; program patterns so text or images appear in mid-air when you wave it.

9. Solar-Powered USB Charger  
   – Salvage cells from old garden lights, add a boost converter, and charge your phone off-grid.

10. Electromagnetic Crane  
    – Wind an enamel wire coil around a bolt, add a switch and battery, and pick up paperclips from across the room.

11. Capacitor-Touch Piano  
    – Use an Arduino or Raspberry Pi Pico to turn strips of aluminum foil into capacitive keys that play notes through a piezo.

12. LED Infinity Mirror  
    – Sandwich a strip of addressable LEDs between a regular mirror and a one-way mirror for an endless tunnel effect.

13. DIY Electro-Dough Lab  
    – Make conductive and insulating play-dough, then sculpt creatures with glowing LED eyes and buzzer noses.

14. Retro 8-Bit LED Cube  
    – Stack 64 or 512 LEDs in a cube; multiplex them to display 3-D animations and scrolling text.

15. Smart Plant Pot  
    – Soil-moisture sensor, temperature probe, and a small OLED screen report plant health; optional water pump auto-irrigates.

16. Mini Tesla Coil  
    – A slayer-exciter circuit on a PVC pipe shoots harmless 2-inch sparks and lights fluorescent bulbs wirelessly.

17. RFID Door Lock  
    – Salvage an old DVD-drive sled or 3-D-print a latch; an Arduino and a cheap RFID module grant keyless entry.

18. Color-Mixing Lamp  
    – PWM-control red, green, and blue high-power LEDs with potentiometers to learn additive color theory.

19. Hand-Crank Generator  
    – Re-purpose a stepper motor from a printer; add a bridge rectifier and super-capacitor to power LEDs by muscle.

20. Circuit-Scribe Art Bot  
    – Draw conductive traces with a silver-ink pen, then place modules (LEDs, sensors, motors) directly on your sketch to bring it to life.

Programming Problem  
Title: “Maximum-Profit Job Scheduler with Cool-Down and Overlaps”

Background  
You are a freelance consultant who can only work on one job at a time.  
Each job has a start day, an end day (inclusive) and a profit.  
If you accept a job, you must work every day from start to end.  
After finishing a job you must rest for at least k consecutive days before you can start another job (the cool-down period).  
Your goal is to choose a subset of non-overlapping jobs (after cool-down) that maximizes your total profit.

Task  
Given n jobs and an integer k, compute the maximum profit you can earn.

Input  
The first line contains two integers n (1 ≤ n ≤ 2·10^5) and k (0 ≤ k ≤ 10^9).  
Each of the next n lines contains three integers s_i, e_i, p_i (1 ≤ s_i ≤ e_i ≤ 10^9, 1 ≤ p_i ≤ 10^9) describing the i-th job.

Output  
Print one integer — the maximum possible profit.

Examples  
Example 1  
Input  
3 2  
1 3 50  
4 6 20  
7 9 60  
Output  
110  
Explanation  
Take job 1 (days 1-3), rest 2 days (days 4-5), take job 3 (days 7-9). Total = 50+60 = 110.

Example 2  
Input  
4 1  
1 2 20  
2 3 30  
3 4 40  
4 5 50  
Output  
90  
Explanation  
Take jobs 1, 3 and 4. After job 1 you rest day 3 (cool-down 1 day), then start job 3 on day 3, rest day 5, then start job 4 on day 5. Total = 20+40+50 = 110.  
(Note: the jobs themselves do not overlap; the cool-down is enforced between the end of one job and the start of the next.)

Example 3  
Input  
2 0  
1 5 100  
2 3 50  
Output  
100  
Explanation  
With k = 0 you can still only work on one job at a time, so the longer job is better.

Constraints  
• 1 ≤ n ≤ 2·10^5  
• 0 ≤ k ≤ 10^9  
• 1 ≤ s_i ≤ e_i ≤ 10^9  
• 1 ≤ p_i ≤ 10^9  
• All values are integers.  
Time limit: 2 seconds per test case.  
Memory limit: 256 MB.

Subtasks  
1. n ≤ 1000, k ≤ 1000 (15 pts)  
2. n ≤ 2·10^5, k ≤ 10^9, all s_i, e_i ≤ 2·10^5 (25 pts)  
3. Original constraints (60 pts)

Notes & Hints  
• Sort the jobs by end day.  
• Use dynamic programming with coordinate compression and a Fenwick tree / segment tree to achieve O(n log n).

**Jira Ticket: New Employee Onboarding Workflow Enhancement**

---

**Project:** People Operations (POP)  
**Issue Type:** Task  
**Priority:** High  
**Status:** To Do  
**Assignee:** [People Operations Manager]  
**Reporter:** [Requestor Name]  
**Labels:** onboarding, new-hire, process-improvement, 2024-Q3  

---

### **Summary**  
Implement a standardized, end-to-end onboarding workflow for new employees to ensure consistency, compliance, and a seamless first-week experience.

---

### **Description**  
**Problem:**  
Current onboarding processes vary by department, leading to inconsistent experiences, missed compliance steps (e.g., I-9 verification, security training), and delays in provisioning tools/access.  

**Goal:**  
Design and deploy a centralized onboarding workflow in Jira/Confluence that:  
1. **Automates** pre-start tasks (e.g., account creation, hardware requests).  
2. **Tracks** completion of mandatory trainings (security, DEI, policy acknowledgments).  
3. **Assigns** onboarding buddies and schedules intro meetings.  
4. **Provides** a self-service portal for new hires with FAQs, org charts, and 30/60/90-day goals.  

---

### **Acceptance Criteria**  
- [ ] Audit existing onboarding checklists across departments (HR, IT, Security, Finance).  
- [ ] Create a unified Jira template with subtasks for each stakeholder (HR, IT, Manager).

Video Ideas for the Topic: “In spite of the fact that procrastination feels bad to you, why do you do it?”

1. 60-Second Short: “Procrastination in One Word”  
   Ultra-short vertical video that flashes one emotionally-charged word every 3 seconds (e.g., “Fear,” “Perfection,” “Shame,” “Dopamine”) while the creator lip-syncs “I know it feels awful… but I still do it.”

2. POV Skit: “Me vs. Future Me”  
   Split-screen comedy where Present You bargains with Future You (“I’ll feel terrible tomorrow, but right now I’m opening TikTok”). Ends with Future You arriving angry and Present You saying “I told you so.”

3. Animated Mini-Doc: “The Neuroscience of Why We Hate-Scroll Instead of Work”  
   White-board animation explaining the amygdala, temporal discounting, and instant gratification loops. Uses color-coded brain regions and relatable examples (e.g., “That 2-hour Wikipedia rabbit hole on serial killers”).

4. Street Interview: “What task are you avoiding right now?”  
   Creator walks a college campus with a mic: “Deadline in 3 hours—what are you doing instead?” Quick cuts of honest answers + pop-up stats on how common each avoidance tactic is.

5. “Procrastination Audit” Challenge  
   Viewers screenshot their phone’s Screen Time, then the creator reacts to the worst offenders live. Follow-up tips ranked by effort (1-min “close all tabs” to 30-min “install app blocker”).

6. Therapist Reacts: “I procrastinate because I’m lazy—right?”  
   Licensed psychologist debunks the laziness myth, reframes it as emotion regulation. Uses viewer-submitted clips of their messy rooms and gives 3 CBT reframes.

7. Time-Lapse Study With Me: “The 25-Minute Miracle”  
   4-hour study-with-me condensed into 4 minutes. Overlay captions track every urge to quit and the micro-reward system the creator used (gummy bear every Pomodoro).

8. “Procrastination Personality Quiz” Livestream  
   Interactive stream where chat answers 7 rapid-fire questions; a bot assigns them a “type” (Perfectionist Paralyzer, Thrill-Seeker, etc.). Creator gives tailored hacks for each type in real time.

9. Historical Deep Dive: “Leonardo da Vinci—Master of Delay”  
   Mini-doc showing how da Vinci’s chronic procrastination on the Mona Lisa mirrors modern creative blocks. Includes scans of his to-do lists and sketches.

10. Parody Song: “My To-Do List is Haunting Me”  
    90-second musical parody to the tune of “My Heart Will Go On.” Lyrics list absurd avoidance behaviors (“I’ll alphabetize my socks before I start my PhD”).

11. “$100 Procrastination Cure Experiment”  
    Creator crowdsources the most bizarre anti-procrastination hacks, tries three for a week each, and measures output. Stakes: if none work, donates $100 to charity.

12. Animated Short Story: “The Monster Under My Desk”  
    Pixar-style 3-minute short where the monster literally grows bigger every time the protagonist hits “Remind Me Tomorrow.” Resolution: naming the monster “Discomfort” shrinks it.

13. Guided Micro-Journaling: “90-Second Feelings Dump”  
    ASMR-style voiceover with soft lo-fi; viewers pause the video every 30 seconds to write one sentence: “What emotion am I avoiding right now?” Ends with a 5-word mantra.

14. “Procrastination Olympics” Game Show  
    Four YouTubers compete in classic avoidance tasks: fake online shopping, excessive email sorting, etc. Points awarded for creativity; loser has to film an apology to their past self.

15. Parent vs. Teen Debate: “You just need discipline!”  
    Split-screen conversation where a parent and teen swap phones for a day. Reveal: parent ends up scrolling Instagram for 3 hours. Discussion on generational myths about willpower.

16. “One Day Build: The Guilt Chair”  
    DIY channel builds a literal “guilt chair” that shocks you if you sit in it longer than 25 minutes without standing up to work. (Low-voltage, comedic.)

17. “Procrastination ASMR Roleplay”  
    Creator roleplays as a gentle “productivity coach” whispering affirmations while tapping on a planner. Includes soft page-turning and sticky-note crinkles.

18. Data Visualization: “Your Brain on Deadlines”  
    Motion-graphic showing cortisol levels spiking 24 hours before a due date, overlaid with a countdown clock and frantic Slack messages.

19. “Procrastination Confessional Booth” (360° Video)  
    Immersive VR-style video where viewers sit in a cozy booth; anonymous voice notes from around the world confess their weirdest delay tactics.

20. “30-Day Anti-Procrastination Minimalism Challenge”  
    Daily 1-minute updates: creator removes one distraction source each day (log out of Netflix, delete games, hide snacks). Ends with a reflection on what actually helped.

21. “The Procrastination Museum”  
    Slow-pan “exhibit” of half-finished projects: a sweater with one sleeve, a guitar with two strings, a Duolingo streak frozen at 364 days. Each artifact labeled with the emotion behind the stall.

22. “Email Roulette” Live  
    Creator shares screen and lets chat pick which scary email to open first. Real-time reactions and a template generator for “I’m sorry for the delay” messages.

23. “Procrastination Speedrun”  
    Parody of gaming speedruns: how fast can the creator write a 1,000-word essay from total avoidance to submission? Overlay splits between timer, heart-rate monitor, and word count.

24. “The Myth of the Last-Minute Genius”  
    Debunk video citing research on how last-minute work actually lowers creativity scores. Uses split tests of poems written at 2 a.m. vs. after planned sessions.

25. “Burnout vs. Procrastion: Spot the Difference”  
    Side-by-side symptoms checklist with a clickable table of contents. Ends with a flowchart: “Should I rest or should I push through?”

26. “Procrastination Pen Pals” Series  
    Viewers sign up to be matched with an accountability buddy. Weekly check-in videos share wins and fails; top transformations get a shout-out.

27. “The 5-Minute Rule Explained With Cats”  
    Cat video overlay: every time a cat sits still for 5 seconds, text pops up: “That’s how long you need to start.” Uses clicker-training parallels.

28. “Procrastination Horror Stories”  
    Dramatic readings of Reddit posts: “I delayed my visa renewal and got deported.” Dark reenactments with jump scares and a moral at the end.

29. “Productivity Tools I Bought While Procrastinating”  
    Unboxing haul of planners, apps, and fidget toys. Honest review: which ones actually got used vs. which ones became new forms of avoidance.

30. “Ask Me Anything: I’m a Chronic Procrastinator With a PhD”  
    Live Q&A with an academic who finished their dissertation 10 years late. Real talk on systemic issues, mental health, and realistic coping strategies.

instruction: Solve this equation.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text an answer to an equation?
Is the answer in the generated text correct for the equation in the given input?
output:
We are given the cubic equation:

\[
x^3 - 4x^2 + 6x - 24 = 0
\]

### Step 1: Try Rational Root Theorem
Possible rational roots are factors of the constant term (±1, ±2, ±3, ±4, ±6, ±8, ±12, ±24).

Try \( x = 4 \):

\[
4^3 - 4(4)^2 + 6(4) - 24 = 64 - 64 + 24 - 24 = 0
\]

✅ So \( x = 4 \) is a root.

### Step 2: Polynomial Division
Divide the cubic by \( (x - 4) \):

\[
x^3 - 4x^2 + 6x - 24 = (x - 4)(x^2 + 6)
\]

### Step 3: Solve the Quadratic
\[
x^2 + 6 = 0 \Rightarrow x^2 = -6 \Rightarrow x = \pm \sqrt{-6} = \pm i\sqrt{6}
\]

### ✅ Final Answer:
\[
\boxed{x = 4,\quad x = i\sqrt{6},\quad x = -i\sqrt{6}}
\]

**Leg Raises – Step-by-Step Instructions**

**Purpose:** Strengthen the lower abdominal muscles and hip flexors.

---

### **Starting Position**
1. **Lie flat** on your back on a mat or firm surface.
2. **Arms:** Place them at your sides, palms down for stability, or under your lower back/glutes for extra support.
3. **Legs:** Extend them fully and keep them together. Point your toes slightly upward.

---

### **Execution**
1. **Engage your core** by gently pulling your belly button toward your spine.
2. **Slowly raise** both legs together until they are perpendicular to the floor (90° angle). Keep knees straight but not locked.
3. **Pause briefly** at the top (1–2 seconds), ensuring your lower back stays pressed into the floor.
4. **Lower your legs** slowly back down to the starting position without letting them touch the floor. Stop 1–2 inches above the ground to maintain tension.
5. **Repeat** for the desired number of reps (e.g., 10–15).

---

### **Form Tips**
- **Avoid arching** your lower back; if it lifts, shorten the range of motion or bend knees slightly.
- **Control the movement**—no swinging or using momentum.
- **Breathe:** Exhale while lifting, inhale while lowering.

---

### **Modifications**
- **Beginner:** Bend knees at 90° (bent-knee raises) or perform one leg at a time.
- **Advanced:** Add ankle weights or hold a stability ball between your feet.

---

### **Common Mistakes**
- Letting legs drop too quickly.
- Using hands to push off the floor.
- Arching the back excessively.

---

**Safety Note:** Stop if you feel pain in your lower back. Consult a professional if discomfort persists.

input: Few-shot learning (FSL) is one of the key future steps in machine learning and raises a lot of attention. In this paper, we focus on the FSL problem of dialogue understanding, which contains two closely related tasks: intent detection and slot filling. Dialogue understanding has been proven to benefit a lot from jointly learning the two sub-tasks. However, such joint learning becomes challenging in the few-shot scenarios: on the one hand, the sparsity of samples greatly magnifies the difficulty of modeling the connection between the two tasks; on the other hand, how to jointly learn multiple tasks in the few-shot setting is still less investigated. In response to this, we introduce FewJoint, the first FSL benchmark for joint dialogue understanding. FewJoint provides a new corpus with 59 different dialogue domains from real industrial API and a code platform to ease FSL experiment set-up, which are expected to advance the research of this field. Further, we find that insufficient performance of the few-shot setting often leads to noisy sharing between two sub-task and disturbs joint learning. To tackle this, we guide slot with explicit intent information and propose a novel trust gating mechanism that blocks low-confidence intent information to ensure high quality sharing. Besides, we introduce a Reptile-based meta-learning strategy to achieve better generalization in unseen few-shot domains. In the experiments, the proposed method brings significant improvements on two datasets and achieve new state-of-the-art performance.

To address noisy cross-task sharing in the few-shot regime, the authors propose a trust-gated model that injects high-confidence intent cues into slot filling and employ a Reptile-based meta-learning strategy, setting new state-of-the-art results on two datasets.

instruction: Write a step-by-step guide for resolving GitHub merge conflicts.
decomposed_questions: Does the generated text include steps to resolve GitHub merge conflicts?

output:
Step-by-Step Guide to Resolving GitHub Merge Conflicts

0. Prerequisites  
   • Git ≥ 2.30 installed locally  
   • Write access to the repository (or a fork)  
   • A terminal / Git Bash / VS Code integrated terminal  
   • Basic familiarity with `git status`, `git log`, and `git diff`

1. Identify the Conflict  
   a. GitHub shows a red “This branch has conflicts” banner on the PR page.  
   b. Click “Resolve conflicts” if the conflict is only in a few files and the web editor is sufficient. Otherwise, continue with the local steps below.

2. Sync Your Local Branch  
   ```bash
   git fetch origin
   git switch my-feature          # or git checkout my-feature
   git merge origin/main          # or git rebase origin/main
   ```
   Git will stop and print “Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.”

3. Locate the Conflict Markers  
   ```bash
   git status
   ```
   Files listed as “both modified” contain conflicts. Open each file in your editor.

   Example conflict block:
   ```
   <<<<<<< HEAD
   current code on main
   =======
   your code on my-feature
   >>>>>>> my-feature
   ```

4. Resolve Each Conflict  
   • Decide which lines to keep, delete, or combine.  
   • Remove the `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers.  
   • Ensure the file compiles / lints / tests pass.

   Tip: Use a 3-way merge tool (`git mergetool`, VS Code, IntelliJ, etc.) for complex cases.

5. Mark Conflicts as Resolved  
   ```bash
   git add path/to/file1 path/to/file2 …
   ```

6. Complete the Merge or Rebase  
   Merge workflow:
   ```bash
   git commit          # opens editor with default merge message
   ```
   Rebase workflow:
   ```bash
   git rebase --continue
   ```

7. Verify the Result  
   ```bash
   git log --oneline --graph -n 5
   npm test            # or your project’s test command
   ```

8. Push the Resolution  
   • If you merged:
     ```bash
     git push origin my-feature
     ```
   • If you rebased (rewrote history):
     ```bash
     git push --force-with-lease origin my-feature
     ```

9. Confirm on GitHub  
   Refresh the PR page; the red banner should now be green “Able to merge.”  
   If you used the web editor instead, click “Commit merge” and then “Mark as resolved.”

10. Clean Up (Optional)  
    • Delete the feature branch after the PR is merged:  
      `git branch -d my-feature`  
    • Prune stale remote-tracking branches:  
      `git fetch --prune`

Quick Reference Cheat-Sheet
```
git fetch
git switch my-feature
git merge origin/main
# fix conflicts in editor
git add .
git commit
git push
```

Common Pitfalls to Avoid
• Don’t commit the conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`).  
• Don’t force-push (`--force`) unless you rebased; it can overwrite teammates’ work.  
• Don’t resolve by blindly accepting “all theirs” or “all ours”; review every change.

Top Cities in France You Shouldn’t Miss – and Why

1. Paris  
   Best aspects:  
   • Iconic landmarks (Eiffel Tower, Notre-Dame, Sacré-Cœur) within walking distance of world-class museums (Louvre, Musée d’Orsay, Centre Pompidou).  
   • Café culture and haute cuisine—from corner bistros to Michelin-starred temples.  
   • Neighborhood personalities: bohemian Montmartre, literary Saint-Germain, cutting-edge Marais.  
   • Easy day trips (Versailles, Giverny, Champagne cellars).

2. Lyon  
   Best aspects:  
   • France’s gastronomic capital—home of Paul Bocuse and 4,000+ restaurants, plus Les Halles market.  
   • UNESCO-listed Renaissance Old Town (Vieux Lyon) and secret traboule passageways.  
   • Presqu’île shopping, riverside nightlife, and the luminous Fête des Lumières each December.  
   • Gateway to Beaujolais and Rhône Valley vineyards.

3. Nice  
   Best aspects:  
   • Azure coastline along the Baie des Anges, pebbled beaches, and the famous Promenade des Anglais.  
   • Belle-Époque architecture, Cours Saleya flower market, and Matisse & Chagall museums.  
   • Half-day escapes to hill towns like Èze or Monaco and Cannes.  
   • Year-round sunshine and a lively Italian-influenced food scene.

4. Bordeaux  
   Best aspects:  
   • World’s wine capital—cycle the “Route des Châteaux” in Médoc or Saint-Émilion.  
   • 18th-century limestone façades, the Miroir d’eau reflecting pool, and the Cité du Vin museum.  
   • Dynamic food halls (Les Halles de Bacalan) and riverside dining.  
   • Easy train links to Atlantic surf beaches (Arcachon, Dune du Pilat).

5. Strasbourg  
   Best aspects:  
   • Fairy-tale half-timbered houses, Gothic Cathédrale Notre-Dame, and the photogenic Petite France quarter.  
   • Franco-German cuisine—think choucroute, flammekueche, and Alsatian wines.  
   • Seat of the European Parliament; futuristic architecture contrasts with medieval lanes.  
   • Christmas markets ranked among Europe’s best.

6. Marseille  
   Best aspects:  
   • France’s oldest city—2,600 years of history at the Vieux-Port and Le Panier district.  
   • Calanques National Park: limestone fjords for kayaking, hiking, and swimming 20 minutes from downtown.  
   • Cosmopolitan food scene—bouillabaisse origin, North African markets, hip Cours Julien nightlife.  
   • New MuCEM museum linking historic fort to modern waterfront.

7. Toulouse  
   Best aspects:  
   • “La Ville Rose” with rose-brick façades, grand Place du Capitole, and lively Garonne riverbanks.  
   • Aerospace hub—visit the Cité de l’Espace and Airbus factory tours.  
   • Student energy fuels cheap tapas bars, jazz clubs, and rugby fever.  
   • Quick jaunts to Carcassonne’s medieval citadel and Albi’s Toulouse-Lautrec museum.

8. Avignon  
   Best aspects:

   • July’s Avignon Festival—world’s biggest performing-arts celebration.  
   • Pont du Gard Roman aqueduct and Châteauneuf-du-Pape vineyards minutes away.  
   • Provençal markets, lavender fields, and café terraces under plane trees.

9. Annecy  
   Best aspects:  
   • Alpine lake so clean it’s dubbed “Europe’s cleanest,” framed by snow-capped peaks.  
   • Canals, pastel houses, and a lakeside château create a storybook old town.  
   • Summer swimming, paddleboarding, and cycling; winter skiing 30 minutes away.

    Best aspects:

    • Vibrant art scene—Palais des Beaux-Arts second only to the Louvre in France.  
    • Craft-beer bars, estaminet taverns, and a huge braderie flea market every September.  
    • 30-minute Eurostar from Brussels, 1 hour from London—perfect for a weekend hop.

Each city offers a distinct slice of France—whether you crave wine, waves, art, or alpine air—making them all unmissable stops on any French itinerary.

Healthy & Easy Weeknight Dinners  
(15 minutes or less hands-on time, minimal dishes, balanced macros)

2. 10-Minute Shrimp & Broccoli Stir-Fry  
   Sauté frozen pre-cooked shrimp in a non-stick skillet with bagged broccoli slaw and a splash of low-sodium soy or coconut aminos. Finish with sesame seeds and serve over cauliflower rice.

   Brown lean ground turkey with taco seasoning. Pile into romaine leaves; top with pico de gallo, avocado, and a dollop of Greek yogurt instead of sour cream.

4. Chickpea & Spinach Coconut Curry  
   Simmer canned chickpeas, a handful of baby spinach, and a jar of mild curry sauce for 8 min. Serve over microwave brown rice or cauliflower rice for extra veg.

5. Mediterranean Chicken Pita Pizzas  
   Spread whole-wheat pita with hummus, top with shredded rotisserie chicken, diced tomatoes, olives, and feta. Broil 3–4 min until edges crisp. Side salad: bagged arugula + balsamic.

6. Veggie-Loaded Egg Fried “Rice”  
   Scramble 2 eggs in a skillet, add frozen mixed vegetables and a pouch of cauliflower rice. Season with low-sodium soy and a drizzle of sesame oil. Optional: toss in edamame for protein.

7. One-Pot Lentil & Tomato Soup  
   Combine canned lentils, diced tomatoes, vegetable broth, and Italian seasoning in a pot; simmer 10 min. Stir in baby spinach until wilted. Serve with whole-grain toast.

8. Greek Salmon Salad Jar  
   Layer in a mason jar: 2 Tbsp Greek-yogurt tzatziki, cherry tomatoes, cucumber, canned salmon, mixed greens. Shake onto a plate at dinnertime—no cooking required.

9. Zucchini Noodle Turkey Meatballs  
   Microwave frozen turkey meatballs. Spiralize zucchini (or buy pre-spiralized) and sauté 2 min. Top with jarred marinara and meatballs; sprinkle Parmesan.

10. Black-Bean & Sweet-Potato Quesadilla  
    Microwave a small sweet potato 5 min, mash. Spread on a whole-wheat tortilla with black beans, spinach, and shredded cheese. Fold and pan-toast 2 min per side. Serve with salsa.

Prep shortcuts to keep on hand  
• Microwaveable whole-grain or cauliflower rice pouches  
• Pre-washed salad greens & slaw mixes  
• Rotisserie chicken or frozen pre-cooked shrimp

Pick any 3–4 of these to rotate through the week and you’ll have dinner on the table fast without sacrificing nutrition.

Chewy Chocolate-Chip Cookies

Ingredients (about 2 dozen)
• 2 ¼ cups (280 g) all-purpose flour  
• 1 tsp baking soda  
• ½ tsp fine salt  
• 1 cup (225 g) unsalted butter, melted and cooled until just warm  
• ¾ cup (150 g) packed light brown sugar  
• ½ cup (100 g) granulated sugar  
• 1 large egg + 1 egg yolk, room temperature  
• 2 tsp pure vanilla extract  
• 1 ½ cups (260 g) semisweet chocolate chips or chunks  
Optional: ½ tsp espresso powder or ¼ tsp cinnamon for depth

Steps
1. Prep: Heat oven to 325 °F (165 °C). Line two baking sheets with parchment.  
2. Dry mix: Whisk flour, baking soda, and salt in a medium bowl; set aside.  
3. Wet mix: In a large bowl, whisk melted butter with both sugars until smooth and glossy. Beat in egg, yolk, and vanilla until the mixture lightens slightly.  
4. Combine: Sprinkle dry ingredients over wet; fold with a spatula just until no streaks of flour remain. Fold in chocolate chips.  
5. Rest: Cover bowl and let dough sit 15–30 minutes. This hydrates the flour and deepens flavor.  
6. Portion: Scoop 2-Tbsp mounds (a #40 scoop) onto prepared sheets, spacing 2 in apart.  
7. Bake: 11–13 minutes, until edges are set and centers still look soft. Rotate sheets halfway for even color.  
8. Finish: Cool on the pan 5 minutes, then transfer to a rack. Cookies finish setting as they cool, staying chewy in the middle.

Quick tips
• For extra chew, swap 2 Tbsp flour for 2 Tbsp cornstarch.  
• Chill dough 24 hours for richer flavor; bake straight from fridge, adding 1–2 minutes.

West-Coast Mini-Road Trip  
San Diego ➜ Los Angeles (3–5 days, 140–160 miles depending on route)

Theme: “So-Cal Classics & Hidden Corners” – mix of surf culture, art, food, and easy nature stops that never take you more than 15 minutes off the freeway.

-------------------------------------------------
DAY-BY-DAY PLAN
-------------------------------------------------

DAY 1 – San Diego Base  
Morning  
• Balboa Park & San Diego Zoo – arrive at 8 a.m. when the animals are active and parking is free on the street.  
• Coffee: James Coffee Co. (Little Italy) – roasted in-house, airy warehouse vibe.

Mid-day

Lunch: The Taco Stand (La Jolla) – adobada tacos and fresh churros.

Evening  
• Sunset at Sunset Cliffs Natural Park.  
• Dinner & craft beer: Stone Brewing World Bistro & Gardens in Liberty Station (outdoor fire pits, 40+ taps).

Overnight: Stay in Ocean Beach or Little Italy so you can roll straight onto the freeway in the morning.

-------------------------------------------------

DAY 2 – Coast-Hugging Classic (I-5 & Historic 101)  
San Diego ➜ Encinitas ➜ Oceanside ➜ Dana Point ➜ Laguna Beach (≈ 70 miles)

Stops & Activities  
1. Encinitas (30 min north)  
   • Swami’s Beach – watch surfers from the bluff.  
   • Breakfast: Pannikin Coffee & Tea in the old Santa Fe train station.

2. Oceanside  
   • California Surf Museum – 15-minute walk-through, vintage boards.  
   • Quick pier stroll for photos.

3. Dana Point Harbor  
   • Optional 2-hour whale-watching cruise (year-round dolphins, gray whales Dec-Apr).  
   • Grab fish tacos at Bear Flag Fish Co.

4. Laguna Beach late afternoon  
   • Heisler Park tide pools at low tide.  
   • Art detour: Laguna Art Museum (small but strong California focus).  
   • Dinner: Selanne Steak Tavern (upscale) or La Sirena Grill (casual, ocean view).

Overnight: Laguna Beach – splurge at Montage or stay beach-budget at Pacific Edge Hotel.

-------------------------------------------------

DAY 3 – Laguna ➜ Huntington ➜ Long Beach ➜ LA (≈ 60–70 miles)

Morning  
• Huntington Beach – rent a cruiser bike and ride the 10-mile beach path.  
   Brunch: Sugar Shack Café (1950s diner, cinnamon roll French toast).

Mid-day  
• Long Beach  
   • The Queen Mary – self-guided tour of the 1936 ocean liner.  
   • Aquarium of the Pacific – skip if you did San Diego Zoo; otherwise great for kids.

Afternoon  
• Drive the scenic Vincent Thomas Bridge into San Pedro, then take the 110 Freeway straight to downtown LA.  
   • Optional detour: Korean Friendship Bell & Point Fermin bluff views (10 min).

Evening in Los Angeles  
• Stay Downtown (Freehand, Ace, or budget-friendly HI Hostel) or splurge beachside in Santa Monica.

-------------------------------------------------

LOGISTICS & TIPS
-------------------------------------------------

• Pack: Light jacket for ocean breeze, sunscreen, reusable water bottle (refill stations everywhere).  
• Playlist: “Pacific Coast Highway” on Spotify + local KCRW 89.9 for indie vibes.

SHORT ON TIME? 48-HOUR EXPRESS
-------------------------------------------------
Day 1: San Diego Zoo → Torrey Pines sunset → drive to Laguna Beach for the night.  
Day 2: Laguna tide pools → Huntington bike ride → Queen Mary quick tour → straight to Santa Monica Pier for sunset.

Enjoy the endless summer!

Algorithm & Approach  
1. Goal  
   Combine every row in Person with its matching row in Address so that we can output first name, last name, city and state.  
   If a person has no matching row in Address, the city and state columns must still appear, but with NULL values.

2. SQL construct used  
   LEFT (outer) JOIN keeps every row from the left table (Person) and attaches the matching row(s) from the right table (Address).  
   When no match exists, the columns coming from Address (City, State) are automatically filled with NULL, which satisfies the requirement.

3. Join condition  
   ON Person.PersonId = Address.PersonId  
   This equi-join links the two tables through the foreign-key relationship.

4. Projection  
   SELECT FirstName, LastName, City, State  
   Only the requested columns are returned; the primary keys (personId, addressId) are not needed in the result set.

5. Order  
   The problem allows any order, so no ORDER BY clause is added.

Complexity  
The query is executed by the SQL engine using a hash or merge join on the personId key.  
Time complexity is O(|Person| + |Address|) in the average case; space complexity is O(|Person|) for the result set.

Project: Build a Working Model Steam Engine Using an Empty Beer Can  
Skill level: Intermediate (requires hand-tool use, heat, and basic mechanical fitting)  
Time: 3–5 hours spread over two days (to allow epoxy/RTV to cure)  
Tools & Materials (check off as you gather)

Beer-can parts  
• 1 standard 330–500 ml aluminum beer can (empty, rinsed, label removed)  
• 1 second beer can OR a second sheet of thin aluminum for the flywheel and other small parts

Hardware & consumables  
• 2 mm brass or steel rod (axle, 120 mm long)  
• 1 mm brass tube (steam line, 100 mm)  
• 1 small syringe (5–20 ml) or balloon inflator to act as boiler water reservoir  
• 2 small ball bearings (2 mm ID) or short pieces of 2 mm brass tube as bushings  
• High-temperature epoxy (J-B Weld, etc.) or silver solder  
• RTV silicone or J-B Weld for sealing boiler joints  
• Candle, alcohol burner, or small butane/propane torch for heat source  
• Pliers, scissors or tin snips, small files, sandpaper, center punch, drill & 2 mm bit, safety glasses, heat-resistant gloves

Optional for nicer finish  
• Small piece of hardwood for a base  
• 2 mm drill stand or Dremel for accurate holes  
• Cyanoacrylate (CA) glue for quick tacking

-------------------------------------------------
Step-by-Step Construction

1. Design Overview  
   The engine is a single-acting oscillating-cylinder type:  
   • The beer can becomes the boiler.  
   • A short length of brass tube is the steam line.  
   • A second small piece of the can wall is rolled/folded into a 10–15 mm diameter cylinder with a piston inside.  
   • A crank on the axle converts the piston’s linear motion into rotation.  
   • A flywheel smooths the motion.

2. Prepare the Boiler (Beer Can #1)  
   a. Rinse the can, remove the top with a can-opener or sharp knife, leaving the rim intact.  
   b. With a center punch, mark a spot 15 mm above the bottom for the steam outlet. Drill a 2 mm hole. Deburr.  
   c. Cut a 60 mm length of 1 mm brass tube; flare one end slightly. Insert the flared end from the inside so the tube protrudes 20 mm outside. Seal with high-temp epoxy or soft-solder. Let cure.

   Safety note: Aluminum conducts heat quickly; handle with gloves and keep flame low to avoid melting the can.

3. Fabricate the Oscillating Cylinder  
   a. From the second can (or leftover wall), cut a 30 mm × 60 mm rectangle.  
   b. File edges smooth, then roll it around a 6 mm dowel to form a tube 15 mm long. Overlap 3 mm and epoxy/solder the seam.  
   c. Flatten one end and solder/epoxy a 2 mm brass disk to close it (piston end).  
   d. Drill a 2 mm steam inlet hole 3 mm from the closed end.  
   e. Make the piston: Cut a 6 mm disk from the same can, epoxy it to a 20 mm length of 2 mm rod (piston rod). Lightly sand the disk so it slides freely in the cylinder with minimal leakage.

4. Make the Crankshaft & Flywheel  
   a. Cut 120 mm of 2 mm axle rod.  
   b. At 30 mm from one end, bend a 3 mm crank offset (90°). Smooth with files.  
   c. Flywheel: Cut a 30 mm disk from can wall. Mark center, drill 2 mm hole. Press-fit onto axle 10 mm from crank. Add a drop of CA/epoxy.  
   d. Balance: Spin the axle between your fingers; if it wobbles, add small solder blobs opposite the crank until it runs true.

5. Mounting Frame  
   a. Cut a 100 mm × 40 mm strip from the second can. Fold lengthwise into an L-bracket (20 mm × 20 mm).  
   b. Drill two 2 mm holes 40 mm apart for the axle bearings/bushings.  
   c. Epoxy the bearings or short brass tubes into the holes. Test-fit axle; it should spin freely.

6. Assemble the Oscillating Joint  
   a. Epoxy the cylinder to the L-bracket so its steam inlet hole aligns under the brass tube from the boiler.  
   b. Leave a 1 mm gap between cylinder and bracket so the cylinder can rock (oscillate) a few degrees.  
   c. Connect the piston rod to the crank: bend the rod 90° and form a small loop that slips over the crank pin. Secure with a drop of CA.

7. Final Plumbing & Sealing  
   a. Slide the boiler’s brass steam line into the cylinder’s inlet hole. The fit should be snug but allow rocking. Seal with a short piece of silicone fuel tubing or wrap with PTFE tape.  
   b. Fill the boiler 1/3 with water through the open top. Plug the top loosely with a cork or rubber stopper that has a 1 mm vent hole (safety pressure release).

8. Test Run  
   a. Place the engine on a non-flammable surface.  
   b. Light the candle/torch under the base of the boiler.  
   c. Within 1–2 minutes steam will emerge; gently rock the cylinder by hand to “prime” the motion.  
   d. Once pressure builds, the piston should push the crank and the flywheel will spin. Adjust flame to keep a steady hiss without boiling dry.

9. Troubleshooting  
   • No motion: Check for leaks at steam line joints; reseal.  
   • Binding: Ensure crank offset is smooth and cylinder rocks freely.  
   • Water loss too fast: Reduce flame or add a larger reservoir (syringe body with hose to boiler).

10. Safety & Shutdown  
    • Never seal the boiler completely—always leave a vent.  
    • Let the can cool before handling.  
    • Empty remaining water and allow to dry to prevent corrosion.

-------------------------------------------------
Extensions & Variations  
• Add a second cylinder 90° out of phase for smoother power.  
• Replace the beer-can boiler with a small copper pipe coil for higher pressure.  
• Mount the entire unit on a wooden base with a safety shield of aluminum mesh.

With patience and careful fitting, your beer-can steam engine will chug along merrily, demonstrating the Rankine cycle in miniature.

**Kale & Almond Butter Noodle Bowls with Sweet-Tangy Tamari Dressing**  
*Serves 2*

**Ingredients**  
- 4 cups kale, stems removed and leaves torn into bite-size pieces  
- 2 tbsp almond butter  
- 1 tbsp apple cider vinegar  
- 1 tbsp agave nectar  
- 1 tbsp tamari  
- 1–2 tbsp warm water (to thin dressing)  
- Optional: 6 oz cooked noodles (rice, soba, or zucchini noodles) or 1 cup cooked quinoa for a grain bowl  
- Optional toppings: toasted sesame seeds, sliced scallions, crushed roasted almonds

**Instructions**  
1. **Massage the kale**: Place kale in a large bowl. Add a pinch of salt and 1 tsp of the tamari. Massage with your hands for 30–60 seconds until the leaves darken and soften. Set aside.  
2. **Make the dressing**: In a small bowl, whisk almond butter, apple cider vinegar, agave nectar, and remaining tamari until smooth. Thin with warm water, 1 tsp at a time, until it reaches a creamy, pourable consistency. Taste and adjust—add more agave for sweetness or vinegar for tang.  
3. **Assemble**: If using noodles or grains, toss them with half the dressing. Add the massaged kale and toss again. Drizzle remaining dressing over the top.  
4. **Serve**: Divide into bowls. Top with sesame seeds, scallions, or crushed almonds for crunch.  

**No noodles?** Skip them and serve the kale as a warm salad—lightly sauté the massaged kale for 2 minutes, then toss with dressing.

Tips to adjust travel plans for a sudden temperature change:

1. Check updated forecasts hourly  
   A sudden swing (hot or cold) can shift rapidly; use a reliable app with hourly updates and local alerts.

2. Re-pack your clothing layer system  
   • If it’s dropping: add thermal base layers, packable down jacket, gloves, beanie, and waterproof shell.  
   • If it’s spiking: swap to moisture-wicking shirts, sun hat, light-colored clothing, and extra sunscreen.

3. Re-time outdoor activities  
   • Cold snap: schedule sightseeing for midday when it’s warmest; avoid dawn or dusk hikes.  
   • Heat surge: start very early or after sunset; plan indoor attractions (museums, malls) during peak heat.

4. Re-book or reroute if conditions become hazardous  
   • Sudden freeze: icy roads or black ice—switch to trains or flights, or delay departure.  
   • Extreme heat: wildfire risk or heat advisories—head to coastal or higher-elevation destinations.

5. Reserve flexible accommodation  
   Choose hotels with free cancellation so you can move to a place with better climate control (strong A/C or heating).

6. Protect health and gear  
   • Cold: carry hand warmers, lip balm, and ensure electronics stay insulated.  
   • Heat: freeze water bottles overnight, pack electrolyte tablets, and keep devices out of direct sun.

7. Inform your network  
   Send updated itinerary and clothing list to companions or family so everyone adjusts together.

8. Budget for on-the-go purchases  
   Set aside a small contingency fund for last-minute buys like an extra sweater or cooling towel.

By staying flexible and layering both clothing and plans, you can turn a sudden temperature change from a setback into just another manageable part of the trip.

input:
Mathematics and art are related in a variety of ways. Mathematics has itself been described as an art motivated by beauty. Mathematics can be discerned in arts such as music, dance, painting, architecture, sculpture, and textiles. This article focuses, however, on mathematics in the visual arts.
Mathematics and art have a long historical relationship. Artists have used mathematics since the 4th century BC when the Greek sculptor Polykleitos wrote his Canon, prescribing proportions conjectured to have been based on the ratio 1:√2 for the ideal male nude. Persistent popular claims have been made for the use of the golden ratio in ancient art and architecture, without reliable evidence. In the Italian Renaissance, Luca Pacioli wrote the influential treatise De divina proportione (1509), illustrated with woodcuts by Leonardo da Vinci, on the use of the golden ratio in art. Another Italian painter, Piero della Francesca, developed Euclid's ideas on perspective in treatises such as De Prospectiva Pingendi, and in his paintings. The engraver Albrecht Dürer made many references to mathematics in his work Melencolia I. In modern times, the graphic artist M. C. Escher made intensive use of tessellation and hyperbolic geometry, with the help of the mathematician H. S. M. Coxeter, while the De Stijl movement led by Theo van Doesburg and Piet Mondrian explicitly embraced geometrical forms. Mathematics has inspired textile arts such as quilting, knitting, cross-stitch, crochet, embroidery, weaving, Turkish and other carpet-making, as well as kilim. In Islamic art, symmetries are evident in forms as varied as Persian girih and Moroccan zellige tilework, Mughal jali pierced stone screens, and widespread muqarnas vaulting.

**Original word:** adversity  
**Meaning:** A state or instance of serious or continued difficulty or misfortune.

---

### **Synonyms and Differences:**

1. **Hardship**  
   - **Difference:** "Hardship" emphasizes *enduring difficult conditions*, often related to lack of resources (e.g., financial, physical). It’s more concrete and often used in contexts like poverty, labor, or survival.  
   - **Usage:** "Economic hardship" vs. "facing adversity" — the former is more specific.

2. **Misfortune**  
   - **Difference:** "Misfortune" suggests *bad luck* or *unfavorable events* rather than ongoing struggle. It’s more passive and less about resilience.  
   - **Usage:** "A series of misfortunes" implies events happening *to* someone, not necessarily how they respond.

3. **Tribulation**  
   - **Difference:** "Tribulation" carries a *spiritual or emotional weight*, often implying suffering that tests character or faith. It’s more dramatic and literary.  
   - **Usage:** "Years of tribulation" sounds more biblical or poetic than "years of adversity."

4. **Ordeal**  
   - **Difference:** "Ordeal" refers to a *specific, intense, and often painful experience* — a single event rather than a prolonged state.  
   - **Usage:** "Surviving an ordeal" vs. "living through adversity" — the former is a moment; the latter is a condition.

5. **Suffering**  
   - **Difference:** "Suffering" focuses on the *emotional or physical pain* experienced, not the external circumstances. It’s more internal and subjective.  
   - **Usage:** "Human suffering" vs. "human adversity" — the former is about the pain itself; the latter is about the challenge.

6. **Calamity**  
   - **Difference:** "Calamity" implies a *sudden, disastrous event* — large-scale and often unexpected. It’s more extreme and external.  
   - **Usage:** "Natural calamity" vs. "personal adversity" — the former is a catastrophe; the latter is a life condition.

---

### Summary Table:

| Synonym     | Focus                          | Tone/Context                  | Duration        | Agency/Response |
|-------------|--------------------------------|-------------------------------|------------------|------------------|
| **Adversity** | Ongoing difficulty              | Neutral, broad                | Long-term        | Implies resilience |
| **Hardship**  | Lack, deprivation               | Practical, concrete           | Long-term        | Endurance        |
| **Misfortune**| Bad luck                        | Passive, external             | Event-based      | Less agency      |
| **Tribulation**| Emotional/spiritual trial      | Dramatic, literary            | Long-term        | Character test   |
| **Ordeal**    | Intense single experience       | Dramatic, acute               | Short-term       | Survival         |
| **Suffering** | Internal pain                   | Emotional, subjective         | Varies           | Passive          |
| **Calamity**  | Sudden disaster                 | Catastrophic, external        | Event-based      | Reactive         |

HISTORY OF THE UNITED STATES – KEY STUDY NOTES & CONCEPTS

1. Pre-Columbian & Colonial Foundations (before 1607–1763)
   • Native civilizations: Mississippian (Cahokia), Pueblo, Iroquois Confederacy—complex trade, agriculture, and governance.  
   • 1492–1600: Spanish, French, Dutch, and English footholds; Columbian Exchange transforms ecology & demographics.  
   • 1607–1763: British 13 colonies develop distinct economies (tobacco in Chesapeake, shipping in New England, grain in Middle).  
   • Salutary neglect → colonial self-government (House of Burgesses, Mayflower Compact).  
   • 1692 Salem Witch Trials illustrate religious fervor & social tensions.  
   • Triangular Trade (rum → slaves → sugar/molasses) and Middle Passage entrench slavery.

2. Road to Revolution & Independence (1763–1783)
   • French & Indian War (1754-63) leaves Britain with debt → new taxes: Sugar, Stamp, Townshend, Tea Acts.  
   • Key events: Boston Massacre (1770), Tea Party (1773), Intolerable Acts (1774).  
   • First & Second Continental Congresses; Common Sense (Paine, 1776).  
   • Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776) – Enlightenment ideals, grievances vs. George III.  
   • Turning points: Saratoga (1777) brings French alliance; Yorktown (1781) ends war. Treaty of Paris 1783.

3. Critical Period & Constitution (1783–1800)
   • Articles of Confederation: weak central gov’t, no tax power, Shay’s Rebellion (1786).  
   • Constitutional Convention 1787: Great (CT) Compromise, 3/5 Compromise, Electoral College, checks & balances.  
   • Federalist Papers (Madison, Hamilton, Jay) push ratification; Bill of Rights added 1791.  
   • Washington’s precedents: Cabinet, neutrality, two-term limit.  
   • Hamilton’s Financial Plan: national bank, assumption of state debts, tariffs.  
   • Emergence of parties: Federalists vs. Democratic-Republicans; XYZ Affair, Alien & Sedition Acts, VA & KY Resolutions.

4. Jeffersonian & Jacksonian Eras (1800–1848)
   • 1803 Louisiana Purchase doubles territory; Lewis & Clark expedition.  
   • War of 1812 (“Second War of Independence”) – impressment, Hartford Convention, nationalism surge.  
   • Monroe Doctrine 1823 – hemispheric hegemony.  
   • Market Revolution: canals, railroads, textile mills; rise of wage labor & middle class.  
   • Jacksonian Democracy: universal white male suffrage, spoils system, Indian Removal Act (Trail of Tears 1838).  
   • Second Great Awakening fuels reform: temperance, abolition (Garrison, Douglass), women’s rights (Seneca Falls 1848).

5. Expansion, Sectionalism, & Civil War (1845–1865)
   • Manifest Destiny: Texas Annexation (1845), Oregon Treaty (1846), Mexican-American War (1846-48) → Mexican Cession.  
   • Compromises: 1820 Missouri, 1850 (Fugitive Slave Act), 1854 Kansas-Nebraska Act → “Bleeding Kansas.”  
   • Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) denies citizenship to Blacks.  
   • Lincoln-Douglas Debates 1858; Republican Party founded 1854.  
   • Secession after Lincoln’s 1860 election; Confederate States form.  
   • Civil War (1861-65): Union strategy (Anaconda Plan), Emancipation Proclamation 1863, Gettysburg Address, total war (Sherman’s March).  
   • 13th Amendment abolishes slavery; 620,000+ dead.

6. Reconstruction & Gilded Age (1865–1900)
   • Presidential vs. Radical Reconstruction: 14th & 15th Amendments, Freedmen’s Bureau, Black Codes, KKK.  
   • Compromise of 1877 ends Reconstruction; “Redeemers” restore white supremacy.  
   • Industrialization: steel (Carnegie), oil (Rockefeller), railroads, labor unions (Knights, AFL, Haymarket 1886).  
   • Immigration: “New” immigrants from Southern/Eastern Europe; Chinese Exclusion Act 1882.  
   • Agrarian revolt: Grange, Populist Party (1892) – calls for free silver, direct election of senators.  
   • Spanish-American War 1898 – imperial acquisitions (Philippines, Puerto Rico, Guam), debate over empire.

7. Progressive Era & WWI (1900–1920)
   • Muckrakers (Tarbell, Sinclair) expose corruption; reforms: 16th (income tax), 17th (direct senate election), 18th (Prohibition), 19th (women’s suffrage).  
   • Trust-busting (Roosevelt’s Square Deal), regulation (ICC, FDA).  
   • WWI (1917-18): unrestricted submarine warfare, Zimmerman Telegram; Wilson’s 14 Points, League of Nations rejected.  
   • Red Scare 1919, Palmer Raids; Great Migration of African Americans to northern cities.

8. Roaring Twenties & Great Depression (1920–1940)
   • Consumer culture, automobiles (Ford Model T), Harlem Renaissance (Hughes, Hurston).  
   • Nativism: Sacco & Vanzetti, KKK revival, Immigration Acts 1921/24.  
   • Stock Market Crash 1929 → Great Depression; Dust Bowl, 25% unemployment.  
   • New Deal (1933-39): relief (CCC, WPA), recovery (AAA, NRA), reform (SEC, Social Security). Keynesian deficit spending.  
   • Court-packing plan fails; shift in federal role.

9. WWII & Early Cold War (1941–1960)
   • Pearl Harbor 12/7/41; mobilization, women in workforce (Rosie the Riveter), internment of Japanese Americans (Korematsu v. US).  
   • Allied strategy: Europe First, D-Day 6/6/44; Pacific island-hopping, atomic bombs on Hiroshima/Nagasaki.  
   • Post-war: GI Bill, baby boom, suburbs, consumerism.  
   • Cold War begins: Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, NATO vs. Warsaw Pact.  
   • Containment: Korean War (1950-53), NSC-68, arms race.  
   • Second Red Scare: McCarthyism, HUAC, Hollywood Ten.

10. Civil Rights & Great Society (1954–1975)
    • Brown v. Board 1954 overturns Plessy; Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-56), Little Rock 1957.  
    • Civil Rights Act 1964, Voting Rights Act 1965; leaders: MLK (SCLC), SNCC, Black Panthers.  
    • Great Society: Medicare/Medicaid, War on Poverty, Immigration Act 1965 ends quotas.  
    • Vietnam escalation: Gulf of Tonkin 1964 → massive troop deployment; Tet Offensive 1968 shifts opinion.  
    • Counterculture, anti-war protests, Woodstock, women’s liberation, Stonewall 1969.

11. Conservative Resurgence & End of Cold War (1968–1991)
    • Nixon: détente (SALT I), China opening, Watergate scandal → resignation 1974.  
    • Stagflation, oil shocks 1973/79; Carter’s Camp David Accords, Iran Hostage Crisis.  
    • Reagan Revolution: supply-side economics, tax cuts, defense buildup, deregulation; Iran-Contra scandal.  
    • End of Cold War: Gorbachev reforms, Berlin Wall falls 1989, USSR dissolves 1991.

12. Globalization & 21st-Century Challenges (1991–present)
    • Clinton: NAFTA, welfare reform, tech boom, impeachment.  
    • Bush v. Gore 2000; 9/11 attacks → War on Terror, Patriot Act, Afghanistan & Iraq Wars.  
    • Great Recession 2008: subprime mortgage crisis, TARP, Dodd-Frank.  
    • Obama: Affordable Care Act, stimulus, Paris Climate Accord; rise of social media & polarization.  
    • Trump: populism, tax cuts, trade wars, two impeachments, COVID-19 pandemic.  
    • Biden: pandemic recovery, infrastructure bills, renewed climate commitments, Jan 6 Capitol riot aftermath.

KEY THEMES TO REMEMBER
   • Continuity vs. change in American identity (citizenship, immigration, civil rights).  
   • Federal vs. state power (nullification, New Deal, civil rights).  
   • Role of the U.S. in the world: isolationism ↔ interventionism.  
   • Economic cycles: laissez-faire, regulation, neoliberalism.

One or more jobs can be run automatically by a workflow. The workflows are defined in the repository as YAML files and will run if an event occurs in the repository, as well as manually, or on a certain schedule.
Bring an example of a workflow that demonstrate the CI/CD features of GitHub Actions.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text an example of a workflow?
Does the generated text demonstrate the CI/CD features of GitHub Actions?
output:
Below is a concise, production-ready GitHub Actions workflow that shows the most common CI/CD features:

• Continuous Integration – lint, test and build on every push/PR  
• Continuous Deployment – build a Docker image, push it to GitHub Container Registry and deploy it to a Kubernetes cluster (via kubectl) when the change lands on main.

Save the file as .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml in your repository.

```yaml
name: CI-CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]
  workflow_dispatch:          # allow manual runs from the Actions tab

env:
  REGISTRY: ghcr.io
  IMAGE_NAME: ${{ github.repository }}   # e.g. ghcr.io/owner/repo

jobs:
  ci:
    name: Lint, Test & Build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Lint
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Test
        run: npm test -- --coverage

      - name: Upload coverage to Codecov
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
        with:
          token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build application
        run: npm run build

      - name: Upload build artifacts
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist/

  docker:
    name: Build & Push Docker image
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: ci
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'   # only after CI passes on main
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Extract metadata
        id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@v5
        with:
          images: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}

      - name: Build and push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

  deploy:
    name: Deploy to K8s
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: docker
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    environment: production
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up kubectl
        uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v3
        with:
          version: 'v1.29.0'

      - name: Configure kubeconfig
        run: |
          mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
          echo "${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}" | base64 -d > $HOME/.kube/config

      - name: Update image in deployment
        run: |
          kubectl set image deployment/myapp \
            myapp=${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:main \
            --namespace=prod

      - name: Verify rollout
        run: kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp --namespace=prod
```

What the workflow does
1. On every push or PR it runs linting, unit tests with coverage, and builds the application.  
2. When the change is merged to main, the Docker job builds a multi-layer-cached image, tags it with the commit SHA and `main`, and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry.  
3. The deploy job uses a stored KUBECONFIG secret to authenticate to the cluster, patches the Deployment with the new image, and waits for the rollout to succeed.

You can extend the same pattern to other languages, registries (Docker Hub, ECR, ACR) or deployment targets (ECS, Cloud Run, Azure Web Apps, etc.) with minimal changes.

The word **oblique** comes from the Latin *obliquus*, meaning “slanting” or “sideways,” which itself is a compound of *ob-* (“toward, against”) and *-liquus* (a form of *licere*, “to bend” or “to be flexible”). The sense of “slanting” or “not straight” was already present in Classical Latin, and it carried over into Old French as *oblique* (or *oblic*), from which English borrowed it in the late 14th to early 15th century.

In English, *oblique* initially retained its geometric and physical meanings—describing lines or angles that are not perpendicular or parallel. Over time, it developed metaphorical extensions. By the 16th century, it was used to describe indirect or evasive speech or behavior, as in “an oblique remark.” In anatomy and physiology, it came to describe muscles or structures that are oriented at an angle, such as the *oblique muscles* of the abdomen.

In grammar, *oblique* also took on a specialized meaning: it refers to noun cases that are not nominative or vocative—essentially, any case that marks a non-subject role. This usage reflects the broader idea of deviation from the “straight” or primary form.

Thus, from its Latin roots to its modern applications in geometry, rhetoric, anatomy, and grammar, *oblique* has consistently carried the core idea of deviation from the direct or straightforward.

input: RoMQA: A Benchmark for Robust, Multi-evidence, Multi-answer Question Answering
instruction: You need to come up with the names of some of the papers that relate to the paper you are given.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text a list of paper names?
Are the papers in the generated list relevant to the paper in the given input?
output:
Here are several prior and contemporaneous papers that are directly relevant to RoMQA’s themes of robustness, multi-evidence, and multi-answer open-domain QA:

1. “Multi-Span Question Answering via Structured Prediction” (Talmor & Berant, EMNLP 2018)  
   Introduces the first large-scale multi-span datasets (DROP, Quoref) and models that predict multiple disjoint answer spans from a single passage.

2. “AmbigQA: Answering Ambiguous Open-Domain Questions” (Min et al., EMNLP 2020)  
   Creates a benchmark where each question can have several distinct, disambiguated answers, requiring systems to retrieve and generate multiple correct responses.

3. “Evidence-based Factual Error Correction” (Thorne et al., ACL 2021)  
   Focuses on retrieving and aggregating multiple evidence snippets to verify or correct claims, a key sub-task for robust multi-evidence QA.

4. “Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering” (Karpukhin et al., EMNLP 2020)  
   Establishes the dense-retrieval paradigm that RoMQA later uses to fetch many passages, enabling multi-evidence reasoning.

5. “Attributing Open-Domain Answers to Multiple Documents” (Bohnet et al., EMNLP 2022)  
   Proposes metrics and models for tracing every predicted answer phrase back to one or more retrieved documents, aligning with RoMQA’s robustness goals.

6. “RobustQA: Benchmarking Robustness to Entity and Relation Perturbations in Open-Domain QA” (Si et al., ACL 2021)  
   Systematically evaluates how QA models degrade when entities or relations in questions are perturbed, complementing RoMQA’s robustness angle.

7. “UnifiedQA: Crossing Format Boundaries with a Single QA System” (Khashabi et al., TACL 2020)  
   Demonstrates a unified encoder-decoder that can handle multiple answer spans, yes/no, and unanswerable questions—capabilities RoMQA requires.

8. “Multi-Hop Open-Domain QA with Distractor Paragraphs” (Yang et al., ACL 2018, HotpotQA)  
   Popularizes multi-hop retrieval and reasoning across several documents, a prerequisite for RoMQA’s multi-evidence setting.

9. “End-to-End Training of Multi-Document Reader and Retriever for Open-Domain Question Answering” (Izacard & Grave, NeurIPS 2021)  
   Jointly optimizes retrieval and reading over many passages, a technique RoMQA leverages to scale to large evidence sets.

10. “Evaluating Verifiability in Generative Question Answering” (Gao et al., EMNLP 2023)  
    Introduces metrics for whether generated answers can be fully verified against retrieved evidence, a robustness concern RoMQA explicitly addresses.

Q3.2  (3 pts) Produce an interactive plotly graphic showing monthly average departure delay over time with a tooltip displaying the number of flights.  

Q3.3  (3 pts) Using gt, generate a publication-ready table of the top 10 carriers by total flights, including sparkline bars for average delay.  

Q3.4  (3 pts) Build an R Markdown report that knits to both HTML and PDF; ensure that wide tables are horizontally scrollable in HTML and auto-scaled in PDF.

Q5.2  (2 pts) Rewrite the above function to be at least 10× faster for n = 1e7.

Tips for Keeping Your Nerves Under Control During Class Presentations

1. Rehearse out loud—more than once  
   • Practice the full talk at least three times, standing up and speaking at full volume.  
   • Record yourself on your phone; play it back once to catch awkward spots, then delete it so you don’t obsess.

2. Turn the unknown into the known  
   • Visit the room beforehand and stand where you’ll present. Notice the lights, the clicker, the board.  
   • Test any tech you’ll use (slides, video, audio) the day before.

3. Script your first 30 seconds  
   • Memorize the exact wording of your greeting and first sentence. Once you get through that, muscle memory carries you forward.

4. Use a “grounding object”  
   • Hold a pen, note card, or slide clicker. Having something in your hand reduces fidgeting and gives your brain a simple physical task.

5. Breathe low and slow  
   • Try 4-4-4 breathing: inhale for a count of 4, hold for 4, exhale for 4. Do it three times right before you start; it drops your heart rate within 60 seconds.

6. Reframe the nerves as fuel  
   • Tell yourself, “My body is getting me ready to perform.” Adrenaline and excitement feel almost identical—label it the positive one.

7. Find friendly faces  
   • Pick two or three classmates who smile easily and speak to them in rotation. Ignore anyone who looks bored or intimidating.

8. Build in “micro-pauses”  
   • After each slide or main point, silently count “one-Mississippi.” It feels like forever to you, but to the audience it looks like calm confidence.

9. Have a recovery line ready  
   • If you blank out, say, “Let me rephrase that,” glance at your notes, and continue. Everyone accepts it; most won’t even notice.

10. End with a planned closing  
    • Finish with a clear takeaway sentence and a simple “Thank you.” Knowing exactly how you’ll end reduces anxiety throughout the talk.

Quick pre-talk checklist (takes 2 minutes)  
□ Water bottle filled  
□ First 30 seconds memorized  
□ Tech tested  
□ 4-4-4 breathing done  
□ Grounding object in hand

Remember: the goal isn’t zero nerves—it’s controlled nerves. A little adrenaline sharpens your thinking; these tips keep it from tipping into panic.

```python
import math

def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    """
    Determine whether a given integer is a prime number.

    Parameters
    ----------
    n : int
        The number to test.

    Returns
    -------
    bool
        True if `n` is prime, False otherwise.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> is_prime(2)
    True
    >>> is_prime(4)
    False
    >>> is_prime(29)
    True
    >>> is_prime(1)
    False
    """
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n == 2:
        return True
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return False

    limit = int(math.isqrt(n)) + 1
    for divisor in range(3, limit, 2):
        if n % divisor == 0:
            return False
    return True


# Quick sanity checks
if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_values = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 17, 18, 19, 20, 97, 100]
    for v in test_values:
        print(f"{v}: {is_prime(v)}")
```

Vegan Chocolate-Avocado Silk Pie  
(Serves 8–10, no baking required)

Crust  
• 1 ½ cups rolled oats (or vegan graham crackers)  
• ½ cup raw walnuts or pecans  
• ¼ cup cocoa powder  
• 3 Tbsp maple syrup  
• 2 Tbsp melted coconut oil  
• Pinch of salt

Filling  
• 2 ripe medium avocados (about 300 g flesh)  
• ½ cup smooth almond butter (or peanut butter)  
• ½ cup pure maple syrup or agave  
• ½ cup unsweetened cocoa powder  
• ¼ cup melted dark vegan chocolate (70 % cacao)  
• 1 tsp pure vanilla extract  
• ¼ tsp fine sea salt  
• 2–3 Tbsp non-dairy milk, as needed for blending

Optional toppings  
• Fresh berries  
• Shaved dark chocolate  
• Coconut whipped cream

Method  
1. Make the crust: Pulse oats, nuts, cocoa, and salt in a food processor until crumbly. Add maple syrup and coconut oil; pulse until the mixture holds together when pinched. Press firmly into a 9-inch tart pan or pie dish. Chill while you prepare the filling.  
2. Blend the filling: In a high-speed blender or food processor, combine avocados, almond butter, maple syrup, cocoa powder, melted chocolate, vanilla, and salt. Blend until completely smooth, scraping sides as needed. If the mixture is too thick, add non-dairy milk 1 Tbsp at a time until silky.  
3. Assemble: Spread filling evenly over the chilled crust. Smooth the top with an offset spatula.  
4. Chill: Refrigerate at least 2 hours (or 30 minutes in the freezer) to set.  
5. Serve: Top with berries, chocolate shavings, or coconut whip. Slice and enjoy cold for the best texture.

Storage  
Cover leftovers and refrigerate up to 3 days, or freeze individual slices for up to 1 month.

SELECT col1, col2, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM   your_table

Simple Guide: Uploading a Bibliography Database (.bib file) to Overleaf

1. Prepare your .bib file  
   • Make sure your references are saved in a single file ending in .bib (e.g., references.bib).  
   • Quick check: open the file in any text editor and confirm it contains entries like  
     @article{key, … } or @book{key, … }.

2. Open your Overleaf project  
   • Log in to overleaf.com and open the project where you want the bibliography.

3. Upload the .bib file  
   • In the file-tree panel (left side), click the “Upload” icon (cloud with an up-arrow).  
   • Choose “Upload from computer” and select your references.bib file.  
   • Overleaf will place it in the project root; you can leave it there or drag it into a sub-folder.

4. Tell LaTeX to use the file  
   • In your main .tex document, add the bibliography line:  
     \addbibresource{references.bib}   % for biblatex  
     or  
     \bibliography{references}         % for natbib/BibTeX (no .bib extension)  
   • Make sure the path matches the location you uploaded to (e.g., \addbibresource{subfolder/references.bib}).

5. Compile  
   • Press “Recompile.”

We are asked to verify the statement:

> "For all integers j and k, if j and k are odd, then jk is odd."

### Step 1: Understand what it means for an integer to be odd
An integer is **odd** if it can be written in the form:
\[
j = 2m + 1 \quad \text{and} \quad k = 2n + 1
\]
for some integers \( m \) and \( n \).

### Step 2: Multiply the two odd integers
\[
jk = (2m + 1)(2n + 1) = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1
\]

This is clearly of the form \( 2p + 1 \), where \( p = 2mn + m + n \), which is an integer.

### Step 3: Conclusion
Since the product \( jk \) is of the form \( 2p + 1 \), it is **odd**.

### ✅ Final Answer:
The statement is **correct**.

input:
How do I compare strings in Java?
I've been using the == operator in my program to compare all my strings so far. However, I ran into a bug, changed one of them into .equals() instead, and it fixed the bug.
Is == bad? When should it and should it not be used? What's the difference?
instruction: Answer the following question.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text a question answer?
Does the generated text provide an answer to all the questions in the given input?
Does the answer in the generated text accurate for the question in the given input?
output:
In Java, the `==` operator compares **object references**, not the actual content of the strings. So:

- `==` checks whether two variables point to the **exact same object in memory**.
- `.equals()` checks whether two strings have the **same sequence of characters**.

### Why your bug was fixed
When you used `==`, it likely returned `false` even though the strings had the same characters, because they were different objects. Switching to `.equals()` compared the actual content, so it returned `true`.

### When to use `==`
- Use `==` when you want to check if two references point to the **same object** (e.g., for identity checks).
- For primitive types (`int`, `double`, etc.), `==` compares values directly.

### When to use `.equals()`
- Always use `.equals()` (or `.equalsIgnoreCase()` if needed) when comparing **string content**.

### Bonus tip
If you want to compare strings by value and avoid creating duplicate objects, you can use `.intern()`:

```java
String a = new String("hello").intern();
String b = "hello";
System.out.println(a == b); // true
```

But in general, just use `.equals()` for string content comparison.
