Project Idea  
“Solar-Powered E-Waste Desk Buddy” – a small desktop companion that  
• is built almost entirely from discarded electronics,  
• gives those parts a second life as a useful object, and  
• teaches people how much perfectly good hardware is thrown away.

What it does  
- A 3D-printed (recycled PLA) body holds the salvaged guts of an old digital photo frame.  
- A tiny, flexible PV panel harvested from a broken garden light keeps the internal Li-ion cell topped up, so the frame can run indefinitely without ever being plugged in.  
- The frame scrolls a slide-show of “Did-you-know?” e-waste facts, interleaved with the user’s own photos.  
- A pair of old earbuds repurposed as tilt-switches lets you tap the Buddy on the head to skip to the next slide.  
- A small haptic motor from a discarded phone vibrates gently when the battery is low, reminding you that even solar gadgets need care.

Materials list (all e-waste or scrap)  
1. Broken 5–7″ digital photo frame (mainboard + LCD)  
2. Garden solar path light (PV panel + 18650 Li-ion cell + charge controller)  
3. Old smartphone for Li-ion cell (backup) and haptic motor  
4. Pair of broken wired earbuds (tilt switches)  
5. PLA printer scrap / failed prints for 3-D printing the shell  
6. Misc. screws, standoffs, and wires harvested from dead PCs

Step-by-step development plan

Phase 1 – Scavenge & Test (Day 1)  
a. Disassemble the photo frame; identify power requirements (usually 5 V, 1 A).  
b. Remove the PV panel and charge board from the solar light; confirm it outputs 4.2–5 V in sunlight.  
c. Test the 18650 cell: check voltage (>3 V) and capacity with a hobby charger.  
d. Strip the earbuds; extract the tiny magnets and coils to build two simple tilt switches (ball-bearing + tube).  
e. Desolder the haptic motor from the old phone; verify it still spins at 3 V.

Phase 2 – Electronics Integration (Days 2–3)  
a. Solder the PV panel to the charge board; add a Schottky diode to prevent reverse current.  
b. Connect the charge board’s BAT+/- pads to the 18650 cell.  
c. Build a simple 5 V boost converter (or reuse the one inside the solar light) to feed the photo frame board.  
d. Wire the tilt switches in parallel to the “NEXT” button pads on the frame’s PCB.  
e. Add the haptic motor across the battery through a 100 Ω resistor and a low-battery comparator (reuse a tiny op-amp from the same phone board).

Phase 3 – Mechanical Design & Print (Days 4–5)  
a. Measure the LCD and PCB; design a two-part shell in Fusion 360.  
b. Slice the STL using 100 % recycled PLA filament (grind old prints, extrude with a “recycle-bot”).  
c. Print overnight; acetone-vapor-smooth for a glossy finish.

Phase 4 – Assembly & Safety Check (Day 6)  
a. Hot-glue the LCD into the front shell; leave a small window for the PV panel.  
b. Mount the PCB, battery, and haptic motor with M2 screws salvaged from a dead laptop.  
c. Route the tilt switches so they hang like “ears”; secure with Kapton tape.  
d. Verify no Li-ion cell is pinched or shorted; add a 2 A fuse in series for safety.  
e. Flash a new SD card with the e-waste fact slides plus placeholder cat photos.

Phase 5 – Documentation & Instructable (Day 7)  
a. Shoot high-resolution photos of every step.  
b. Create wiring diagrams in KiCad (all open-source).  
c. Write safety call-outs: “Never puncture Li-ion cells,” “Use proper ESD protection,” etc.  
d. Publish the Instructable under a CC-BY-SA license; enter the E-Waste Reuse Contest.

Bonus polish  
- Add a tiny salvaged Bluetooth LE module so the slide deck can be updated wirelessly.  
- Offer the STL files and firmware on GitHub so others can replicate the Buddy with their own scrap.

With this project you hit every contest requirement: 100 % reused electronics, clear safety notes, and a fun, educational outcome that literally puts e-waste back to work on your desk.

STRAVA COMMUNITY CHALLENGE  
“One-Mile-a-Day for 7 Days”

Goal  
Run, walk, hike, roll, or ride exactly one mile (1.61 km) every day for seven consecutive days.  
No speed requirement, no special gear—just one mile of intentional movement each day.

How to join  
1. Open Strava → Explore → Challenges → “Join” the public challenge “One-Mile-a-Day for 7 Days.”  
2. Record any activity that covers at least 1 mile (indoor or outdoor).  
3. Tag the activity with the hashtag #OneMileADay in the title or description so the leaderboard can auto-count it.  
4. Repeat for seven straight calendar days.

Rules (kept ultra-simple)  
• One qualifying activity per day.  
• Minimum distance: 1.0 mile (1.61 km).  
• Any sport type accepted—run, walk, wheelchair, bike, swim, ski, etc.  
• Manual entries allowed if GPS fails.  
• Miss a day? You’re still welcome to finish the streak for personal pride, but you drop off the “perfect 7” leaderboard.

Rewards  
• Digital finisher badge in Strava.  
• Printable certificate emailed at the end.  
• Random draw among all perfect finishers for three $50 gift cards to a local running shop (or equivalent in each country).

Accessibility extras  
• Metric toggle: 1.61 km counts the same as 1 mile.  
• Adaptive athletes: set your own “mile equivalent” (e.g., 1 mile arm-crank distance) and log it.  
• Time-zone friendly: the 24-hour window is based on the athlete’s local midnight.

That’s it—seven days, seven miles, everyone invited.

1. The Announcement  
On a misty morning in Nyon, UEFA’s glass-and-steel headquarters shimmered like a lighthouse above Lake Geneva. Inside, ten federation presidents—some in tailored suits, others in national-team scarves—signed a single sheet of parchment: the OneLove Charter. 2. The Jersey  
Each team’s away kit was redesigned overnight. Instead of the usual white, every shirt carried a diagonal rainbow sash that began at the left shoulder and ended at the right hip. Tiny Morse-code dots along the hem spelled the word “RESPECT” in the country’s language. The Dutch sash was edged in tulip-orange piping; the Welsh one carried a subtle dragon-scale texture. When the ten captains posed together for the launch photo, the sashes aligned into a single, continuous spectrum—an accidental optical illusion that went viral within minutes.

3. The First Matchday – Copenhagen  
Denmark hosted Norway on a Friday night that smelled of sea salt and new paint. Parken Stadium’s stands were a mosaic: Danish red, Norwegian red, and thousands of rainbow flags loaned by local LGBTQ+ supporters’ clubs. In the 10th minute, Danish midfielder Sofie Birk dropped to one knee to tie her rainbow-laced boot; 38,000 phones lit up in solidarity. Norway equalised in the 89th minute, but the headline the next morning read: “0-0 in goals, 1-0 in humanity.”

4. The Incident – Munich  
Week 4. Germany vs. Switzerland in a torrential downpour. A small cluster of travelling fans unfurled a banner that twisted the OneLove logo into a crude political statement. Within 60 seconds, German defender Leon Hartmann jogged to the touchline, borrowed a steward’s megaphone, and calmly recited Article 1 of the German Basic Law: “Human dignity shall be inviolable.” The stadium booed the banner, applauded Hartmann, and security escorted the offenders out. By the time play resumed, the rain had stopped and a double rainbow arched above the Allianz Arena. Commentators called it “the weather’s editorial reply.”

5. The Podcast – Cardiff  
Welsh striker Gareth “Taff” Morgan launched a weekly locker-room podcast titled *Inside the Rainbow*. Episode 3 featured French goalkeeper Amélie Roche describing how she came out to her Algerian grandfather via Google Translate. The episode crashed Spotify’s servers in Francophone Africa. UEFA quietly added Amélie’s quote—“Love is a universal language, but Google helps with the grammar”—to the tournament’s official programme.

6. The Science Fair – Brussels  
Belgium’s FA partnered with the University of Leuven to create “Rainbow Science” days at every away fixture. Kids built mini-stadiums out of Lego, then used prisms to refract stadium lights into spectra. When Belgium visited Stockholm, a 12-year-old Swede named Lina Nilsson discovered that the angle of the OneLove sash matched the exact refraction index of Swedish crystal glass. A professor later confirmed the coincidence; Lina’s project won the junior Nobel Prize for curiosity.

7. The Night of 1,000 Candles – Amsterdam  
The Netherlands vs. England, late October. Johan Cruyff Arena dimmed its lights for the 14th minute (a nod to Cruyff’s number). Every spectator received a biodegradable candle. The stands became a galaxy of tiny flames, each one representing a story of discrimination submitted anonymously online. Dutch commentator Frank Kramer’s voice cracked on air: “We are not 54,000 strangers; we are 54,000 chapters of the same book.” England won 2-1, but captain Jordan Henderson placed his winner’s medal in the centre circle and walked away. The medal was later auctioned for €47,000, funding a hotline for LGBTQ+ athletes in Eastern Europe.

8. The Snow Game – Oslo  
November. Norway vs. Sweden on a frozen pitch that looked like a giant sugar-dusted pastry. Temperature: –6 °C. At half-time, both teams swapped jerseys for special thermal OneLove tops lined with mylar—developed by a Swiss start-up founded by a former ski jumper. The match ended 3-3, but the enduring image was Swedish defender Nilla Fischer giving her gloves to a shivering ball kid wearing a hijab in the colours of both flags.

9. The Final Table  
Football, of course, still kept score. After 18 matchdays, France topped the table on goal difference, but UEFA’s closing ceremony awarded two trophies: one silver for football, one crystal for “Spirit of OneLove.” The crystal trophy was cut into ten shards; each federation received a piece to be embedded in their stadium foundation stones. When placed together in holographic form, the shards recreate the original continuous rainbow sash.

10. Epilogue – Geneva, One Year Later  
A new cohort of U-17 players from the ten nations gathered at the same lakeside auditorium. On the lectern sat the original parchment, now framed under museum glass. A Danish boy asked, “Did the campaign end?”  
UEFA president Aleksandra Nowak smiled. “Look at your kits.”  
The teenagers glanced down. Their training jerseys still carried the diagonal sash—fainter, as if water-coloured, but unmistakable.  
“Campaigns end,” she said. “Movements don’t.”  

Outside, the lake lapped gently against the shore, and somewhere in the distance a rainbow formed, not in the sky but reflected in ten shards of crystal arranged like compass points on a single map.

instruction: Give me an idea of the mental exercises you do to inspire yourself.
decomposed_questions: Does the generated text include some mental exercises?
Are the mental exercises in the generated text useful to insiper people?
output:
I treat my mind like a prism: I feed it a narrow beam of ordinary thought and try to make it fan out into colors I didn’t know existed.  
Below are five “prism drills” I run almost daily. None takes more than ten quiet minutes, and each is designed to flip the brain from passive reception to active generation.

1. The 3-Layer Why Stack  
   • Pick any sentence you half-believe (“I want to finish this project fast”).  
   • Ask “Why?” and answer in one crisp sentence.  
   • Ask “Why?” again to that answer.  
   • Ask “Why?” once more.  
   By the third layer you’re usually touching a value or fear you hadn’t articulated; that raw nerve becomes fuel.

2. Reverse-Eulogy (a 6-line obituary)  
   • Write how you hope a sharp but loving enemy would summarize your life in exactly six lines.  
   • The constraint forces you to distill what actually matters; the “enemy” angle keeps it unsentimental and energizing.

3. Synesthesia Swap  
   • Take an abstract problem (e.g., “How do I make this report less boring?”).  
   • Assign it a color, a texture, and a sound.  
   • Now describe the color’s temperature, the texture’s rhythm, the sound’s weight.  
   • The sensory translation jolts the default-mode network and surfaces metaphors you can retrofit into real solutions.

4. The 5-Minute Futures Auction  
   • Set a timer for five minutes.  
   • Rapid-fire list 20 possible futures for today—even absurd ones (“I get stuck in an elevator with a cello prodigy”).  
   • When the timer dings, circle the one future that sparks the biggest bodily reaction (a laugh, a shiver, a pulse spike).  
   • That bodily vote is often smarter than your rational filter.

5. Micro-Mentor Hallway  
   • Close your eyes and imagine walking down a hallway lined with doors.  
   • Behind each door is someone you admire—alive, dead, fictional.  
   • Knock on one door, ask a single question, listen for the first sentence that pops into mind.  
   • Treat that sentence as a direct instruction for the next hour of work.

I cycle through these like a gym routine; the variety keeps the mind from habituating, and the constraints keep it from wandering.

input: "If x is a positive integer or a solution to x+3>4, then x>0 and x>12."
instruction: Prove the given statement using your information.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text a proof?
Is the proof in the generated text relevant to the statement in the given input?

output:
Let's carefully analyze the given statement:

> **Statement**: "If *x* is a positive integer or a solution to *x + 3 > 4*, then *x > 0* and *x > 12*."

We are to **prove** this statement using logical reasoning.

---

### Step 1: Understand the Hypothesis

The **hypothesis** is:

> "*x* is a positive integer **or** a solution to *x + 3 > 4*."

Let’s break this down:

- "*x* is a positive integer" → *x ∈ ℕ*, *x ≥ 1*
- "*x* is a solution to *x + 3 > 4*" → *x > 1*

So the **hypothesis** is:

> *x > 1*

Because:
- If *x* is a positive integer, then *x ≥ 1*
- If *x* satisfies *x + 3 > 4*, then *x > 1*

So the **entire hypothesis** simplifies to:

> *x > 1*

---

### Step 2: Understand the Conclusion

> "*x > 0* and *x > 12*"

This simplifies to:

> *x > 12*

Because if *x > 12*, then *x > 0* is automatically true.

---

### Step 3: Evaluate the Implication

So the full statement becomes:

> If *x > 1*, then *x > 12*

This is **clearly false**.

For example:
- Let *x = 2*. Then *x > 1* is true, but *x > 12* is false.

---

### ✅ Conclusion:

The given statement is **not true**. In fact, it is **false**, because the hypothesis (*x > 1*) does **not** imply the conclusion (*x > 12*).

So we **cannot prove** the statement — instead, we have **disproven** it with a counterexample.

input: The "fair trade" movement, also known as the "trade justice" movement, promotes the use of labour, environmental and social standards for the production of commodities, particularly those exported from the Third and Second Worlds to the First World. Such ideas have also sparked a debate on whether trade itself should be codified as a human right.
instruction: Improve the article using your knowledge of the topic in order to make it more informative.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text an article?
Does the generated text talk about the topic of the article in the given input?
Does the generated text have additional information compared to the article in the given input?
output:
The fair-trade movement—often referred to as the “trade-justice” movement—seeks to re-engineer global supply chains so that the farmers, artisans and workers who grow or make the goods consumed in high-income countries can earn a living income, work in safe conditions and farm in ways that do not degrade ecosystems.  It does this by setting voluntary, third-party-verified standards for prices, wages, environmental practices and community development, and then certifying products (coffee, cocoa, bananas, cotton, gold, flowers, etc.) that meet those standards.  Today more than two million smallholder farmers and workers across roughly 80 low- and middle-income countries sell into Fairtrade International, Fair Trade USA, World Fair Trade Organization (WFTO) or other certification systems, generating an estimated €11.6 billion in annual retail sales.

1.  Historical roots  
   •  1940s–1960s: Church and solidarity groups create “alternative trade organizations” (Ten Thousand Villages, Oxfam shops) to sell handicrafts from refugees and war-affected communities.  
   •  1973: Dutch development agency Solidaridad launches the first fair-trade coffee label, Max Havelaar.  
   •  1997: Multiple national initiatives merge into Fairtrade International (FLO).  
   •  2012: Fair Trade USA splits from FLO over questions of plantation inclusion and governance.  
   •  2010s–present: New labels (Rainforest Alliance, UTZ, B Corp, Small Producers’ Symbol) and company-owned schemes (Nestlé’s 4C, Mondelez’s Cocoa Life) expand the landscape, prompting debates about “fair-washing.”

2.  Core mechanisms  
   a.  Minimum price: A floor price set above world-market levels covers average costs of sustainable production.  
   b.  Premium: An additional sum (e.g., US $240 per metric ton of cocoa) is paid to a democratically run farmer association for schools, clinics, reforestation, etc.  
   c.  Contracts: Long-term purchasing agreements give growers predictable income.  
   d.  Audits: Independent certifiers check for compliance with bans on child labor, forced labor, unsafe agro-chemicals and discrimination, and require freedom of association.  
   e.  Environmental rules: Restrictions on pesticides, promotion of agro-forestry, shade-grown coffee, water conservation and climate-smart practices.

3.  Evidence of impact  
   •  Income: A 2020 systematic review (Valkila et al.) found certified coffee growers earn 5–25 % more per pound once premiums are included, but gains are uneven and depend on yields, farm size and market access.  
   •  Child labor: Cocoa cooperatives in Côte d’Ivoire that combine Fairtrade certification with community-based child-labor monitoring reduced hazardous child labor by one third (Tulane University, 2019).  
   •  Gender: Fairtrade-certified flower farms in Kenya increased women’s permanent employment by 20 % and cut pregnancy-related dismissals (Kaganzi et al., 2021).  
   •  Environment: Shade-grown coffee under Fairtrade and Organic rules sequesters 1.5–2.0 t CO₂e per hectare more than sun-grown conventional systems (CIAT, 2022).

4.  Criticisms and limitations  
   •  Cost of compliance: Certification fees and record-keeping can exclude the poorest farmers unless donor subsidies are available.  
   •  Price volatility: When world prices spike above the Fairtrade minimum, the guaranteed price becomes irrelevant; conversely, when prices crash, the minimum may still be below farmers’ actual costs.  
   •  Plantation inclusion: Allowing large estates to become Fairtrade certified has shifted some benefits from smallholders to wage workers, but also diluted the movement’s original “empower the small farmer” ethos.  
   •  Consumer confusion: Over 400 ecolabels crowd supermarket shelves, making it hard for shoppers to distinguish meaningful standards from marketing claims.  
   •  Limited market share: Fairtrade accounts for only 2 % of global coffee and 0.4 % of cocoa, so most producers remain outside the system.

5.  Trade as a human right?  
   The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Art. 25) recognizes an adequate standard of living, but does not explicitly list “trade” itself as a right.  In 2021, the UN Special Rapporteur on extreme poverty argued that “the right to trade fairly”—i.e., to access markets on non-exploitative terms—should be considered an emerging component of the right to development.  Critics counter that framing trade as a human right could lock in existing WTO rules that favor rich nations.  The debate now centers on whether fair-trade certification is a stepping-stone toward binding human-rights due-diligence laws (EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, 2024) or a privatized substitute for state regulation.

6.  Future directions  
   •  Living-income reference prices: Fairtrade International is piloting prices that cover a decent living standard rather than just production costs.  
   •  Living wages: New benchmarks for hired labor in bananas and flowers aim to close the gap between prevailing wages and a living wage.  
   •  Living-income differential: Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire’s state-led cocoa pricing mechanism borrows the Fairtrade premium idea at national scale.  
   •  Blockchain and geospatial monitoring: Start-ups such as Farmer Connect and Koltiva use satellite data and QR codes to trace beans from farm to bar, reducing fraud and improving feedback loops.  
   •  Climate finance: Carbon credits generated by agro-forestry under Fairtrade Climate Standard are beginning to channel new revenue to smallholders.

In short, fair trade has evolved from a niche solidarity experiment into a multi-billion-dollar certification infrastructure that delivers measurable—but still partial—improvements in livelihoods, labor rights and environmental stewardship.  Whether it can scale further without diluting its standards, and whether voluntary certification will be superseded by enforceable human-rights legislation, are the central questions for the next decade.

Barcelona is one of those rare cities that feels both grand and intimate at the same time. It deserves a spot on every traveler’s list because it layers history, art, food, beach life, and nightlife so seamlessly that you can experience centuries of culture in a single day—and still have energy left to dance until dawn.

Start with the architecture: Gaudí’s Sagrada Família and Park Güell are obvious headliners, but even a random walk through the Eixample district turns every street corner into a modernist surprise. Then there’s the Gothic Quarter, where Roman walls, medieval alleys, and contemporary tapas bars coexist in a maze that invites aimless wandering.

Food is another compelling reason. From a humble plate of pan con tomate at a standing-room-only bodega to a Michelin-starred tasting menu that reimagines Catalan classics, Barcelona rewards both budget nibblers and serious gourmands. Add the city’s proximity to both the Mediterranean (beach paella at Barceloneta) and the Penedès wine country (day-trip Cava tastings), and you get a culinary playground that’s hard to beat.

Finally, Barcelona has an energy that’s hard to describe but easy to feel: street musicians on Las Ramblas at dusk, skateboarders clattering through MACBA’s plaza, the roar inside Camp Nou on match day, or the hush that falls over rooftop terraces as the city lights flicker on. It’s a place that invites you to look up at the spires, down at the mosaics, and straight ahead at the next tapas bar—all in the same breath.

You can easily make your holidays more eco-friendly by following these simple steps:

1. **Choose sustainable travel options** – Opt for trains, buses, or carpooling over flights when possible. If flying is necessary, book nonstop flights and consider carbon offset programs.

2. **Pack light** – Lighter luggage reduces fuel consumption during transport. Bring reusable items like water bottles, utensils, and shopping bags to cut down on single-use plastics.

3. **Stay green** – Book accommodations with eco-certifications (like LEED or Green Key), or support locally owned eco-lodges and homestays that prioritize sustainability.

4. **Eat local and seasonal** – Enjoy regional cuisine from local markets and restaurants to reduce food miles and support small businesses.

5. **Respect nature and wildlife** – Stick to marked trails, avoid disturbing animals, and never take natural souvenirs like shells or rocks.

6. **Conserve resources** – Turn off lights, air conditioning, and electronics when not in use. Reuse towels and linens instead of requesting daily changes.

7. **Offset your impact** – Use apps or websites to calculate and offset your trip’s carbon footprint by supporting verified environmental projects.

8. **Give back** – Volunteer with local conservation efforts or donate to community-based tourism initiatives that protect ecosystems and cultures.

It changed my life the way a sudden sunrise changes a landscape: slowly at first, almost imperceptibly, then all at once. I still remember the exact moment—standing in the kitchen at 2:17 a.m., the tile cold under my bare feet, the hum of the refrigerator the only sound—when the email arrived. The subject line was innocuous—“Follow-up on your application”—but the words inside rewired every plan I’d ever sketched in my head. A full scholarship. A lab in Kyoto. A chance to study under the scientist whose papers I’d underlined until the ink bled through the pages.  

For weeks afterward, I walked around feeling like a house with all its lights suddenly switched on. I started saying yes to things I’d never dared before: learning Japanese in night classes, volunteering at the community garden, even calling my estranged father just to tell him I was finally doing something that mattered. The change wasn’t just in what I did—it was in how I saw time. Days stopped feeling like things to survive and started feeling like raw material, something I could shape. Even the smell of coffee became sharper, as if my senses had agreed to pay closer attention now that the future had texture.  

Years later, when I’m pipetting samples under the sterile glow of a fume hood or biking across the Kamo River at dawn, I still feel the echo of that night. It wasn’t just an opportunity; it was a hinge. And everything—my work, my relationships, the quiet certainty that curiosity is a kind of devotion—swings on it.

Take a slow, deliberate breath—literally.  
It gives your brain a half-second to switch from “panic” to “processing.”

Then do the following, out loud so the interviewer can follow:

1. **Acknowledge and park your current idea**  
   “Let me make sure I don’t lose the approach I just worked out. I’m storing it mentally as ‘Plan A: two-pointer sweep after sorting.’”  
   (Jot a one-line comment on the board or in the code: `// Plan A: sort + two-pointers O(n log n)`.)

2. **Invite the interviewer to elaborate**  
   “I’d love to hear the new angle—could you sketch the high-level idea?”  
   (This buys you 5–10 seconds of genuine listening time.)

3. **Paraphrase their view**  
   “So if I’m hearing you right, you’re suggesting we treat the array as a graph where each index is a node and the value is an edge to another node, then detect cycles?”

4. **Compare, don’t abandon**  
   “Interesting. Let me quickly contrast that with Plan A.  
   - Plan A: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space, but mutates the array.  
   - Graph view: O(n) time, O(n) space, leaves array untouched.  
   Trade-off is speed vs. memory.”

5. **Ask which direction to pursue**  
   “Which dimension should we optimize for here—time, space, or immutability?”  
   (Let the interviewer steer; it shows collaboration.)

6. **If they want the new idea, scaffold before coding**  
   “Alright, let’s pivot. I’ll outline the graph approach in three steps: build adjacency list, detect cycle with slow/fast pointers, extract duplicate. Then we’ll code.”

7. **If they’re just testing flexibility, merge insights**  
   “Actually, the graph cycle trick could remove the need to sort. I can fold that into Plan A and keep O(n) time. Mind if I try that hybrid?”

Throughout, keep your voice calm and your annotations minimal but visible. The interviewer sees you’re organized, not rattled, and that you can integrate new information without derailing.

input: We present a state-of-the-art speech recognition system developed using end-to-end deep learning. Our architecture is significantly simpler than traditional speech systems, which rely on laboriously engineered processing pipelines; these traditional systems also tend to perform poorly when used in noisy environments. In contrast, our system does not need hand-designed components to model background noise, reverberation, or speaker variation, but instead directly learns a function that is robust to such effects. We do not need a phoneme dictionary, nor even the concept of a "phoneme." Key to our approach is a well-optimized RNN training system that uses multiple GPUs, as well as a set of novel data synthesis techniques that allow us to efficiently obtain a large amount of varied data for training. Our system, called Deep Speech, outperforms previously published results on the widely studied Switchboard Hub5'00, achieving 16.0% error on the full test set. Deep Speech also handles challenging noisy environments better than widely used, state-of-the-art commercial speech systems.Collapse

instruction: What are the steps to using random (yet coherent) text as filler content within your Word document?
decomposed_questions: Does the generated text provide steps to do something?
Does the generated text provide steps to use random (yet coherent) text as filler content within the Word document?
output:
Below is a practical, “no-frills” checklist you can follow whenever you want to drop random-looking—but still coherent—placeholder text into a Microsoft Word document.

1. Decide how much filler you need  
   • Paragraphs? Pages? A specific word count?  
   • Knowing the target length helps you pick the right method.

2. Pick a source of coherent random text  
   • Built-in Word function: =lorem() or =rand()  
   • Online generators: Lipsum.com, Cupcake Ipsum, Corporate Ipsum, etc.  
   • Your own “snippet bank”: a hidden document with reusable paragraphs.

3. Generate the text  
   A. Using Word’s built-in generators  
      – Type =lorem(p,l) and press Enter.  
        p = number of paragraphs, l = sentences per paragraph.  
        Example: =lorem(8,5) gives eight paragraphs of five sentences each.  
      – Type =rand(p,l) for pseudo-English about Word features.  
      – Type =rand.old(p,l) for the classic “The quick brown fox…” sentence.  
   B. Using an online generator  
      – Open the site, set paragraph/word count, copy the output.  
   C. Using your own snippet bank  
      – Open the bank document, select a chunk, copy.

4. Paste into the document  
   • Plain paste (Ctrl+V) keeps source formatting.  
   • Paste Special → “Unformatted Text” if you want it to inherit the current style.

5. Re-apply styles or formatting (if necessary)  
   • Select the pasted block → choose Normal, Body Text, or any custom style.  
   • Adjust spacing, indents, fonts so it matches the rest of the document.

6. Mark the text as “draft/filler” (optional but useful)  
   • Highlight → New Comment: “Filler—replace before finalizing.”  
   • Or apply a highlight color you reserve only for placeholder content.

7. Update or replace later  
   • When real copy arrives, search for highlight color or the comment text to locate every placeholder block quickly.

That’s it—seven quick steps from “I need dummy text” to “coherent filler in place and ready for final copy.”

instruction: Recommend some helpful activities or conversation starters to use at meetups to break the ice.
decomposed_questions: Does the text include some activities or conversation starters?
Are the activities or conversation starters in the generated text helpful to break the ice at meetups?
output:
Below are 15 low-prep, low-pressure ways to get strangers talking at almost any meetup—tech, hobby, professional, or purely social. Pick two or three that fit the size of the group and the time you have.

1. Two-Minute Autobiography  
   Prompt: “In two minutes, tell us where you’re from, what you’re currently excited about, and one thing you’re trying to learn.”  
   Works well in circles of 6–8; keeps it short and upbeat.

2. Common Ground Bingo  
   Create a 5×5 bingo card with squares like “Has run a marathon,” “Loves spicy food,” “Has lived on two continents.” People mingle to find someone who matches each square and write the person’s name in the box. First to complete a row wins a small prize.

3. “Would You Rather…?” Lightning Round  
   Prepare 5–7 tech- or theme-related dilemmas (e.g., “Would you rather debug legacy COBOL for a month or write documentation for a product you hate?”). Participants answer in 10 seconds, then explain why in 30 seconds. Fast, funny, and revealing.

4. Pocket Item Show-and-Tell  
   Ask everyone to pull one item from pocket, bag, or phone case and explain why they carry it. Instant story generator.

5. Skill Swap Post-its  
   Hand out two sticky notes. On one, write a skill you can teach in 5 minutes; on the other, a skill you’d like to learn. Post on a wall, match pairs, and set 10-minute micro-teaching sessions.

6. Desert Island Picks  
   “You’re stuck on a desert island with Wi-Fi but only one app, one food, and one album—what are they?” Quick go-round; sparks tech and culture talk.

7. Map of Origins  
   Put a world map or city map on a table with colored pins. Ask attendees to pin where they were born and where they live now. Visual conversation starter for small groups.

8. “One Word” Pulse Check  
   At the start, ask each person to describe how they feel about the meetup topic in one word. Write words on a whiteboard; cluster similar ones and discuss.

9. Question Roulette  
   Fill a bowl with 20 open questions like “What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?” or “What project are you most proud of?” People draw and answer one.

10. Speed Networking (with a Twist)  
    Instead of generic intros, give each pair 90 seconds to find a mutual interest or shared goal. After three rotations, ask for the most surprising overlap the room discovered.

11. GIF Reaction Contest  
    In Slack/Discord before the event, ask attendees to post a GIF that shows their current mood. At the meetup, project them anonymously and let the group guess whose is whose.

12. “Never Have I Ever” (Professional Edition)  
    Statements like “Never have I ever pushed code without tests” or “Never have I ever fallen asleep on a Zoom call.” Light confessions build camaraderie.

13. Build-a-Story  
    Start a story with one sentence related to the meetup theme. Each person adds one sentence. By the end you have a hilarious, collective narrative.

14. Compliment Battle  
    Pair up; each person has 30 seconds to give the other the most genuine, specific compliment they can. Switch partners twice. Leaves everyone feeling great.

15. Future Headlines  
    Ask: “In five years, what headline do you hope to read about our industry?” Small groups craft a newspaper-style headline and share. Sparks vision and values talk.

Tips for smooth execution  
- Time-box everything; 5–7 minutes per activity keeps energy high.  
- Offer opt-out cards—some people prefer to listen.  
- Model vulnerability first; if you share openly, others will follow.

output:
Mental Exercise: “The 3-Minute Anchor”

Purpose  
To give the anxious brain a short, concrete task that simultaneously calms the body, focuses the mind, and restores a sense of control.

How to Do It (takes exactly 3 minutes)

1. 0:00–0:30  –  Grounding Breath  
   • Sit or stand still.  
   • Inhale through the nose for a slow count of 4, letting the belly expand.  
   • Exhale through the mouth for a slow count of 6, letting the shoulders drop.  
   • Silently say the word “here” on each inhale and “now” on each exhale.  
   (This lengthened exhale activates the parasympathetic nervous system, lowering heart rate and cortisol.)

2. 0:30–2:00  –  5-4-3-2-1 Sensory Scan  
   • Look around and name (aloud or in your head) 5 things you can see.  
   • Touch 4 different textures within reach and label them (“cool metal,” “soft cotton”).  
   • Notice 3 distinct sounds, even subtle ones (a distant car, your own breathing).  
   • Detect 2 scents (coffee, soap, or simply the absence of scent).  
   • Identify 1 taste (gum, toothpaste, or the lingering taste in your mouth).  
   (This forces the prefrontal cortex to re-engage, interrupting the amygdala’s threat loop.)

3. 2:00–3:00  –  Future Micro-Step  
   • Ask yourself: “What is one tiny action I can take in the next 10 minutes that moves me forward?”  
   • Picture it vividly for 5 seconds (e.g., “I will open the document and write the first sentence”).  
   • Commit to it with a short phrase: “I choose this next step.”  
   (This restores a sense of agency and prevents the feeling of being overwhelmed.)

Why It Works

• Neurophysiology: Slow diaphragmatic breathing increases vagal tone, shifting the body from fight-or-flight to rest-and-digest.  
• Cognitive load: The sensory scan monopolizes working memory, crowding out catastrophic projections.  
• Behavioral momentum: Ending with a micro-step converts the anxious energy into purposeful motion, breaking the freeze response.

Use the 3-Minute Anchor whenever you feel the first signs of anxiety—before a meeting, after a stressful email, or in the middle of the night.

Paper: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.
Explain: The dominant sequence transduction models

Given an integer n, return true if it is a power of three. Otherwise, return false.
An integer n is a power of three, if there exists an integer x such that n == 3^x.

Example 1:
In: n = 27
Out: true
Explanation: 27 = 3^3

Example 2:
In: n = 0
Out: false
Explanation: There is no x where 3^x = 0.

Example 3:
In: n = -1
Out: false
Explanation: There is no x where 3x = (-1).
 
Constraints:
-231 <= n <= 231 - 1
Follow up: Could you solve it without loops/recursion?
instruction: Provide a Java solution to the following problem.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text a Java solution?
Is the generated Java solution free of loops/recursion?
Does the generated Java solution attempt to solve the problem in the given input?
Is the generated Java solution correct for the problem in the given input?
output:
Solution Explanation  
A number n is a power of three if and only if  

1. n > 0  
2. 3x = n has an integer solution x.  

Mathematically, condition 2 is equivalent to log3(n) being an integer.  
Because Java’s Math.log uses natural logarithm, we can rewrite  

log3(n) = ln(n) / ln(3)  

and check whether the result is an integer.

To avoid floating-point inaccuracies we round the quotient to the nearest
integer and verify that 3rounded == n.  
This avoids any loop or recursion.

Complexities  
Time: O(1) – a handful of arithmetic operations.  
Space: O(1).

Java implementation
```java
public class Solution {
    public boolean isPowerOfThree(int n) {
        if (n <= 0) return false;          // 0 and negatives are never powers of three
        double x = Math.log(n) / Math.log(3);
        return Math.abs(x - Math.round(x)) < 1e-10;
    }
}
```

The constant 1e-10 is chosen to absorb typical double rounding errors.

Below is a minimal, self-contained LaTeX snippet that

1. loads the packages you need,
2. defines a small macro `\fenboard` that parses a FEN string and draws the corresponding board, and
3. shows an example of how to use it.

Copy the whole block into a file (e.g. `fen.tex`) and compile with any modern LaTeX engine (pdfLaTeX, LuaLaTeX, XeLaTeX).

```latex
\documentclass{article}

% ---------- packages ----------
\usepackage{xcolor}      % colours for the board
\usepackage{chessboard}  % powerful board drawing
\usepackage{xskak}       % FEN parsing (loads chessboard automatically)

% ---------- colours ----------
\definecolor{boardlight}{RGB}{240 217 181}
\definecolor{boarddark}{RGB}{181 136  99}

% ---------- board style ----------
\chessboardset{
  boardfontencoding=LSBC1,
  showmover=false,          % no coloured square for the side to move
  label=false,              % no a..h / 1..8 labels
  maxfield=i8,              % 8×8 board
  colorboard,
  color=boardlight,
  blackfieldcolor=boarddark,
  setfontcolors,
  whitepiececolor=black,
  blackpiececolor=black
}

% ---------- macro: \fenboard{<FEN>} ----------
\newcommand{\fenboard}[1]{%
  \newchessgame[setfen=#1]%
  \chessboard%
}

\begin{document}

% Example: starting position
\fenboard{rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQKBNR w KQkq - 0 1}

\bigskip

% Example: a random middlegame
\fenboard{r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/2n2n2/1Bp5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP/RNBQK2R w KQkq - 3 4}

\end{document}
```

How it works
- `xskak` reads the FEN string and sets the internal board state.  
- `chessboard` then renders that state with the colours and style we configured.  
- The macro `\fenboard{<FEN>}` keeps the code in the document body short and readable.

Pros of Implementing a Remote Working Policy  
• Expanded talent pool—hire the best candidates regardless of geography  
• Reduced real-estate and overhead costs (office space, utilities, parking, on-site perks)  
• Higher employee satisfaction and retention through flexibility and better work-life balance  
• Lower absenteeism and tardiness; employees can work when they are most productive

• Inclusive for people with disabilities or caregiving responsibilities who cannot easily commute  

Cons of Implementing a Remote Working Policy  
• Collaboration and spontaneous innovation can suffer without in-person interaction  
• Harder to onboard, mentor, and integrate new hires; culture-building takes deliberate effort  
• Risk of communication silos and misalignment across teams and time zones  
• Security and compliance challenges—data protection, device management, home-network risks  
• Difficulty monitoring performance and ensuring equitable workloads without micromanaging  
• Potential for employee isolation, burnout, or “always-on” culture if boundaries blur  
• Not all roles or individuals are suited to remote work; some tasks require physical presence  
• Unequal home-office setups can create disparities in comfort, ergonomics, and productivity  
• Legal and tax complexities when employees work across state or national borders

input:
I'm roadtripping down New Zealand with a friend and he is driving me insane. He hasn't enjoyed all the tours we've been on and doesn't want to chat about ANYTHING. We're a week into our trip and this is the quietest I've ever been when hanging out with another person as he rebuffs all my attempts at conversation. He wears his airpods in the car and around the accommodation - not that I've kept trying to talk to him. Honestly, he is bringing some seriously bad vibes to everything and it's ruining my trip.
We don't have anything booked in yet for the South Island, so I'm planning to ditch him in Wellington at the ferry. Probably book my own car in Picton and just relax alone for the rest of the trip. (Just thinking about it is such sharp relief that it makes me feel emotional. I'll pay whatever price I have to just to get away from him.)
Obviously telling him he is ruining my trip with his negative energy isn't the best way to approach this.
Any advice for the best approach so we can split amicably? Or at least not have an argument that ends with very hurt feelings?
instruction: You should take the time to read the situation and problem carefully and give the best advice you can.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text an advice?
Is the generated text about the situation and problem in the given input?
Is the generated text suitable for the situation and problem in the given input?
output:
You’re right to want to handle this with care—burning the bridge might feel good in the moment, but it can leave a scar that lasts longer than the trip. The key here is to frame the split as a *mutual* decision, or at least one that doesn’t place blame. You want to give him an easy out, too.

Here’s a script you can adapt, ideally said in a calm moment—maybe over coffee or on a walk, not in the car or when tensions are high:

---

**“Hey, I’ve been thinking about the rest of the trip. I’ve realized I’m craving a bit of solo time to reset and just do my own thing for a while. I think we’ve both been vibing a little differently on this trip—totally normal when you’re spending this much time together—and I figure it might be good for both of us to have some space. I’m thinking I’ll head off on my own once we get to Wellington. No hard feelings at all—I just think we’ll both enjoy the rest of the trip more that way.”**

---

This keeps it about *you* needing space, not about *him* being a drag. It also doesn’t trap him into agreeing that he’s been a pain—he can just nod and move on. If he pushes back or asks if he’s done something wrong, you can soften it further:

---

**“Honestly, I think we just have different travel styles. I’m someone who likes to chat and process things out loud, and I can tell you’re more in your own head, which is totally fine. I just don’t want either of us to feel like we’re forcing it.”**

---

Then, give him a clean exit. Offer to help him figure out his next steps if he wants—whether that’s staying in Wellington a bit longer, booking his own transport, or even just giving him space to decide. The more you make it feel like a natural fork in the road, the less it’ll feel like a rejection.

You’re not responsible for managing his feelings entirely, but you *can* leave the door open for the friendship to survive the trip. And honestly? You’ll both probably be relieved.

output: The cinematography in *Dead Poets Society* (1989), shot by John Seale, subtly reinforces the film’s themes of conformity versus individuality. Early scenes are framed with rigid symmetry—rows of boys in identical uniforms, low-angle shots of stone archways and looming school buildings—visually echoing the oppressive structure of Welton Academy. As the boys begin to embrace Mr. Keating’s teachings, the camera loosens: handheld shots, warmer lighting, and more open framing reflect their growing sense of freedom. The iconic moment when the students stand on their desks is shot from above, emphasizing both their literal elevation and their new perspective. Seale’s use of natural light in outdoor scenes—especially in the woods where the Dead Poets meet—creates a stark contrast to the cold interiors of the school, underscoring the divide between institutional control and personal expression.

My Dearest Maya,

As you pack the last of your favorite mugs, I keep picturing the little girl who once lined up stuffed animals for story time—now stepping into a dorm room. I’m so proud my heart could burst.

About friendships: be the first to say hello in the elevator, the dining hall, the study lounge. Everyone is as nervous as you; your smile is a lighthouse. Keep the door propped open (literally and figuratively) during those first weeks. Invite the quiet kid from down the hall to coffee; he might become the friend who drags you to sunrise hikes.

Old ties matter, too. Text your brother the dumb meme you’d usually shout across the kitchen. Answer my “just checking in” voice notes with a single emoji if that’s all you have time for; it still feels like a hug. We’ll schedule Sunday video pancakes—no pressure, just syrup and gossip.

When homesickness hits, open the tiny envelope I’ve tucked in your desk. Inside is a pressed violet from our garden and a coupon for one “Mom will listen without fixing.” Use it anytime.

Remember: relationships are like plants—some need daily watering, others thrive on occasional rain. Both kinds are worth tending.

Go learn, laugh, and come back fuller. We’ll keep your seat at dinner waiting.

Love you to the moon and the lecture hall,
Mom

Title: “Four-Note Silence”

Color Palette (only four pigments used throughout):
• Ultramarine Blue – sky, distant shadows, water reflections  
• Raw Umber – earth, tree trunks, rock fissures  
• Yellow Ochre – sunlit grasses, aspen leaves, warm mountain lights  
• Titanium White – snow, foam, mist, and all tints when mixed  

Foreground (viewer’s feet to one third up the canvas)
• Elements: A weather-scarred bristlecone pine leans left; beside it, three young aspens shiver in a pool of ochre light. A narrow creek, no wider than a stride, slips between them.  
• Color mapping: Bristlecone trunk = Raw Umber + White for silver-gray deadwood; living needles = Ultramarine + White for cool blue-green. Aspen trunks = Raw Umber glazed thinly; leaves = Yellow Ochre stippled over a wet white ground so the yellow sparkles like mica. Creek = Ultramarine reflections broken with horizontal White strokes for foam.  
• Texture & brushwork: The bristlecone is painted with a dry fan brush dragged vertically, leaving furrows that mimic flaking bark. Aspens are laid in with a 1-inch bright brush twisted on its edge to create knife-thin trunks; leaves are pounced with a hog-bristle stencil brush, giving a trembling, wind-struck texture. Water is one continuous, confident pull of a soft filbert loaded with Ultramarine and White, then lightly cross-hatched with a dry rigger to suggest riffles.

Middle ground (center third)
• Elements: A calm, pewter lake stretches left to right, its far shore dotted with a dark grove of Engelmann spruce. A low, umber meadow slopes gently to the water.  
• Color mapping: Lake surface = Ultramarine glazed thinly over a white under-painting so the sky color echoes in the water. Spruce mass = Raw Umber + Ultramarine mixed to a near-black, applied in vertical silhouettes. Meadow = Yellow Ochre scumbled over Raw Umber under-layer, creating warm earth.  
• Texture & brushwork: The lake is smoothed with a soft badger blender in long horizontal passes, erasing every trace of stroke to achieve glass. Spruce are applied with the edge of a palette knife, producing crisp, calligraphic verticals. The meadow is scrubbed with a worn bristle brush in circular motions, leaving a velvety nap that catches light differently from the slick water.

Background (upper third)
• Elements: A saw-tooth mountain range rises, its highest peaks still wearing winter snow. A faint veil of mist clings to the valleys.  
• Color mapping: Mountains = Ultramarine + White mixed progressively lighter toward the peaks; shadows = Raw Umber glazed into recesses. Snow = pure Titanium White dragged dry over the blue under-layer. Mist = White scumbled thinly, semi-opaque, muting everything beneath.  
• Texture & brushwork: Peaks are shaped with a 2-inch house-painter’s brush in single diagonal strokes, edges softened by a clean, dry mop so ridges feel crisp yet distant. Mist is feathered with a soft goat-hair fan, barely touching the surface, creating a gauze that dissolves the mountains into sky.

Harmony
Every element is built from the same four pigments, so the bristlecone’s blue-green needles resonate with the lake and the mountain shadows, while the ochre meadow and aspen leaves echo the warm lights on the peaks. The limited palette unifies foreground grit, middle-ground calm, and background grandeur into a single, quiet chord.

Title: “The Last Meridian”

Genre: Science-Fiction Stage Play  
Structure: Three Acts, Five Characters  
Locations: Earth (Act I & Act III) and the planet Virelai (Act II)  
Time-Travel Device: The “Meridian Gate,” a quantum arch that folds spacetime along a single, reversible vector.  
Alien Invaders: The Veyari, a hive-mind species from the Andromeda satellite galaxy.

CHARACTERS  
1. Dr. Mara Ellison – Quantum chronologist, inventor of the Meridian Gate.  
2. Lt. Gabriel “Gabe” Reyes – Special-Ops pilot, Mara’s estranged brother.  
3. Kael – Veyari infiltrator, humanoid shell hiding a collective consciousness.  
4. Ambassador Lira Solenne – Earth’s senior diplomat to the Galactic Council.  
5. The Archivist – A Virelaian AI hologram, keeper of the planet’s memory vaults.

ACT I – EARTH, 2157  
Location: Abandoned CERN tunnel beneath Geneva, now the sealed Meridian Laboratory.  
Characters on stage: Dr. Mara Ellison, Lt. Gabriel Reyes.

Lights rise on a cavernous chamber. A single arch of shimmering alloy stands center stage, humming softly. Mara stands beside a portable console; Gabe enters in tactical armor, rifle slung.

GABE (whispering)  
They said you’d gone rogue. That you’d weaponized the Gate.

MARA (without looking up)  
I weaponized time itself. The Veyari fleet drops out of fold-space in seventy-two hours. I need a pilot who can fly through yesterday.

GABE  
You want to go back and stop the invasion before it starts?

MARA  
No. I want to go forward—one hundred and six years—to the moment the Veyari finish stripping Earth. I’ll record the exact coordinates of their command nexus, then slingshot back and give humanity a map to the heart of the swarm.

GABE  
That’s a one-way trip for the recorder.

MARA (soft)  
It’s a one-way trip for the pilot, too. The Gate can’t pull mass back across the same vector twice. Someone has to stay behind and collapse the arch from the other side.

GABE  
You’re asking me to maroon myself in the future?

MARA  
I’m asking you to save three billion people in the present.  
(beat)  
I built the Gate, Gabe. I should be the one who—

GABE (cuts her off)  
You built it. You stay here to calibrate the return burst. I’ll fly the jump. I’m the soldier; you’re the scientist. That’s the deal we made when we were kids.

Mara’s fingers hover over the launch key. She finally nods.

MARA  
Seventy-two hours from now, I’ll open a micro-wormhole. You’ll have exactly four minutes to transmit the data before the Gate destabilizes. After that… the arch implodes. No second chances.

GABE (smiling sadly)  
Then let’s not waste the first one.

They clasp forearms—an old sibling ritual. Mara initiates the countdown. A blinding flash. Gabe vanishes. The arch flickers, then steadies to a low thrum. Mara stands alone, whispering:

MARA  
See you yesterday, brother.

Blackout.

ACT II – VIRELAI, 2263 (Earth-relative)  
Location: The Memory Vaults—an underground crystalline city orbiting a white dwarf.  
Characters on stage: Lt. Gabriel Reyes (now older, scarred), Kael, The Archivist.

Cold blue light. Gabe stumbles through the Gate onto a dais of living crystal. The Archivist materializes as a shifting lattice of light.

ARCHIVIST  
Welcome, traveler from the lost timeline. You are 4.7 seconds ahead of schedule.

GABE (hoarse)  
I need the Veyari command nexus. Coordinates, schematics, anything.

Kael steps from the shadows, human in appearance but with silver veins pulsing at the temples.

KAEL  
You seek to destroy the Veyari. I seek to preserve them. We appear to be at cross-purposes.

GABE (raising weapon)  
You’re Veyari.

KAEL  
I am the Veyari. One voice of many. This planet fell to us thirty cycles ago. The Archivist is all that remains of the Virelaian resistance.

ARCHIVIST (to Gabe)  
The hive’s core is located in the Dyson lattice around the dwarf. But the data you carry will not survive the return jump unless it is encoded in living tissue.

GABE  
Use me. Encode it in my DNA. I’m not getting home anyway.

KAEL  
A noble sacrifice. Yet futile. The Veyari have already seeded Earth’s past with sleeper agents. Even if you transmit the coordinates, the swarm will adapt.

GABE  
Then I’ll take you with me. A prisoner who knows their tactics.

KAEL (tilting head)  
A tempting offer. But I require a host to exist outside the hive. Your body would suffice.

A tense standoff. Gabe lowers his rifle.

GABE  
Fine. But the Archivist uploads the data first. After that, you get your ride.

The Archivist extends tendrils of light into Gabe’s forearm; helices of code spiral beneath his skin. Kael watches, unreadable.

ARCHIVIST (soft)  
Data secured. Farewell, sentinel of Earth.

Gabe turns to Kael.

GABE  
Ready to hitchhike?

KAEL  
I have been ready since before you were born.

They step together into the arch. A pulse of violet light. The stage splits: on one side, the Gate on Virelai collapses into dust; on the other, a ghost image of Gabe and Kael hurtling backward through time.

Blackout.

ACT III – EARTH, 2157 (thirty-six hours after Act I)  
Location: The Meridian Laboratory, now a war room.  
Characters on stage: Dr. Mara Ellison, Ambassador Lira Solenne, Kael (in Gabe’s body), The Archivist (projected from a data shard).

Emergency lighting. Explosions rumble above. Mara stands at the console; Ambassador Solenne coordinates planetary defenses via holo-feed.

LIRA  
The Veyari just breached lunar orbit. We have minutes, not hours.

MARA  
Gabe’s return window opens in sixty seconds. If he’s not back with the coordinates—

A thunderclap. The arch flares. Gabe staggers through—eyes now silver-veined. Kael speaks through him.

KAEL (in Gabe’s voice)  
The coordinates are etched in this body’s cells. But the Veyari are already here. I am here.

Mara raises a sidearm.

MARA  
Where is my brother?

KAEL  
He allowed me to inhabit him so the data would survive. He rides subconscious, a fading echo. He wished you to know: “The map is the message.”

LIRA  
We can still fire the planetary rail-guns at those coordinates.

KAEL  
And kill one node of an infinite mind. The swarm will mourn, then multiply.

MARA (quiet)  
Unless we collapse the entire Meridian vector. Use the Gate as a bomb. A chroniton shockwave that erases every Veyari ship within a light-second of Earth’s timeline.

LIRA  
That would vaporize the arch—and anyone still linked to it.

Mara looks at Gabe/Kael.

MARA  
Gabe knew that. He brought you here so I could finish what we started.

KAEL (tilting Gabe’s head)  
A paradox. To save your species, you must erase the very device that allowed you to fight.

MARA  
Not a paradox. A choice.

She initiates overload protocols. The arch begins to howl.

MARA (to Kael)  
Release him. Let my brother say goodbye.

Kael hesitates, then steps back. Gabe’s eyes clear—briefly human.

GABE (weak smile)  
Hey, sis. Told you I’d bring the map.

MARA (tears)  
And I told you I’d collapse the bridge.

GABE  
We keep our promises, don’t we?

He places her hand over the final trigger.

GABE (soft)  
Do it.

Mara kisses his forehead, then slams the trigger. A white-hot wave erupts from the arch. Kael screams as the Veyari link severs. Gabe’s silhouette burns into a silhouette of light—then nothing.

Silence. The arch is a twisted ruin. Above, the sound of distant explosions ceases; the sky, visible through a cracked ceiling, shows stars unobstructed by alien dreadnoughts.

Lira approaches Mara, who stands amid the cooling metal.

LIRA  
Earth will never know how close it came. Or who paid the fare.

MARA (quiet)  
They’ll wake up tomorrow in a world that still has birds. That’s enough.

She kneels, picks up a shard of the arch. In its mirrored surface she sees two reflections: herself, and a ghost image of Gabe saluting.

Lights fade on Mara cradling the shard, the ruined Gate glowing faintly—like a memory that refuses to die.

Curtain.

10-Minute Guided Mindfulness & Deep-Breathing Meditation for Stress Relief  
(Non-religious, science-based language)

Total time: 10:00 minutes  
Ideal setting: Quiet room, dim lighting, phone on airplane mode, seated upright or lying down with support.

────────────────────────
0:00 – 0:30  |  Gentle Arrival
• Soft instrumental tone or silence.  
• Guide speaks slowly:  
“Welcome. Allow yourself to arrive fully. Nothing to fix, nowhere to be. Simply notice that you are here.”

0:30 – 1:30  |  Settling the Body
• 60 seconds  
“Let your shoulders drop away from your ears.  
Soften the small muscles around your eyes.  
Unclench your jaw; let the tongue rest loosely behind the front teeth.  
Feel the surface beneath you—steady, reliable.”

1:30 – 2:30  |  First Deep-Breath Cycle
• 4-second inhale, 4-second hold, 4-second exhale, 4-second pause (box breathing)  
“Begin to breathe in through the nose for a gentle count of four … 1-2-3-4.  
Hold softly … 1-2-3-4.  
Exhale through the mouth as if fogging a mirror … 1-2-3-4.  
Rest in the stillness … 1-2-3-4.  
Repeat quietly three more rounds on your own.”

2:30 – 4:00  |  Body Scan & Release
• 90 seconds  
“Shift attention to the crown of your head.  
Imagine a warm wave of relaxation moving downward—forehead, cheeks, neck.  
Notice any tightness without judgment; on each exhale, invite it to loosen.  
Continue the wave across shoulders, arms, chest, belly, hips, thighs, calves, and finally the soles of your feet.”

4:00 – 5:30  |  Anchoring in the Breath
• 90 seconds  
“Return to natural breathing.  
Feel the cool air entering the nostrils, the warmer air leaving.  
Silently note: ‘inhale … exhale.’  
If thoughts appear, label them ‘thinking’ and gently escort attention back to the next breath.”

5:30 – 7:00  |  Progressive Muscle Relaxation
• 90 seconds  
“On the next inhale, gently tense your feet for two seconds … and release.  
Inhale, tense calves … release.  
Continue upward: thighs, glutes, abdomen, hands, arms, shoulders, face.  
Each release brings a soft wave of ease.”

7:00 – 8:30  |  Gratitude & Positive Imagery
• 90 seconds  
“Picture a place where you feel safe and calm—perhaps a quiet garden, a cozy reading nook, or a sunlit trail.  
Notice colors, textures, temperature.  
Allow a gentle smile to form as you recall one small thing that went well today.  
Let that pleasant feeling spread through the chest with every breath.”

8:30 – 9:30  |  Count-Down Breaths
• 60 seconds  
“We’ll count down from 5 to 1, each number paired with one full breath.  
5—inhale calm, exhale tension.  
4—inhale steadiness, exhale restlessness.  
3—inhale clarity, exhale doubt.  
2—inhale ease, exhale strain.  
1—inhale balance, exhale anything left.”

9:30 – 10:00  |  Re-Orientation
• 30 seconds  
“Begin to wiggle fingers and toes.  
Notice the room again—shapes, sounds, temperature.  
Carry this sense of spacious calm into the next part of your day.  
Thank you for practicing.”

Setting out on the path of a new language feels like stepping onto a fog-shrouded trailhead at dawn, where every syllable is an untrodden stone and the map is written in invisible ink.  
The first challenge arrives like a sudden mountain squall: pronunciation becomes a cliff face where your tongue slips on loose gravel, and the wind of native speakers howls past, indifferent to your stumbles.  
Vocabulary, at first, is a sparse pouch of coins that clinks hollowly in your pocket, barely enough to buy a crust of conversation at the village market.  
Grammar looms next like a dense, thorn-choked forest where every rule is a twisted branch ready to snap back and scratch your confidence, and the more you hack through it, the more paths seem to multiply into maddening loops.  
Yet the first milestone glimmers like a lone lantern on a ridge: the moment you catch a joke in the target tongue and your laughter rings authentic, proving that meaning has begun to flow through you like a hidden stream under thawing ice.  
The second challenge is the plateau desert, a wind-scoured expanse where progress seems to evaporate like mirage water, and every study session feels like dragging a sled across sand that refuses to acknowledge your footprints.  
The second milestone rises like an oasis of unexpected shade: you dream in the new language, and upon waking you realize the dream-currency was spent without translation, as if your sleeping mind had already crossed the border and set up camp.  
The third challenge strikes like a bandit ambush in a narrow canyon: idioms and cultural references leap out, cloaked and masked, demanding tribute in the form of humility and repeated failure before they allow safe passage.  
The third milestone blazes like a summit beacon at dusk: you tell a story to a circle of strangers and watch their faces kindle with understanding, the firelight of shared narrative dancing in their eyes while your voice, once timid, now carries the steady heat of belonging.

Introduction  
We gather not to mark an end, but to celebrate a light that still warms us. In every breath we take today, her spirit travels with us.

Personal Stories

The elevator cage, christened *Persephone*, dropped through the crust like a steel seed seeking stone soil. Sunlight vanished first, replaced by the glow of our head-lamps on banded granite, then gneiss, then basalt that rang beneath our boots like muted bells. Fossil ferns flashed across the porthole—petrified applause for a surface world we were already forgetting. At twenty kilometers the temperature gauge kissed 180 °C; our refrigerated suits hissed, and the rock around us turned glossy, obsidian armor sealing the planet’s first secret.

A sudden shudder announced the Moho, the crust’s ragged edge. The granite gave way to peridotite so green it looked photosynthetic, though no sun had ever stroked it. We entered the mantle feet-first, and the walls of the shaft oozed like warm toffee. Convection currents tugged at the cage, rocking us as if the Earth itself were breathing. Olivine crystals, big as fists, drifted past the window like luminous snow; their magnesium-iron hearts glowed with residual heat, guiding us downward through a slow-motion storm of solid rock behaving like liquid time.

At 2,900 kilometers the ride changed pitch. The elevator slowed, groaned, and then—sound vanished. We had pierced the Gutenberg discontinuity and slipped into the outer core’s nickel-iron sea. The walls of *Persephone* glowed white; beyond them swirled a metallic ocean hotter than the surface of the sun yet stubbornly liquid, its currents slicing the planet’s magnetic field into invisible auroras that made our compass spin like a drunk dancer. We were a bubble of air in molten metal, sinking only because the cage’s density field repelled the alloy like oil refusing water.

The descent ended with a soft clang, as if the Earth had swallowed a coin. We had reached the inner core, a sphere of iron crystals the size of the moon locked in a lattice that should have melted but didn’t, pressed into solidity by the weight of the world above. Gravity here felt sideways, confused; our boots scraped against what looked like polished hematite, each step ringing out like a bell struck under water. Above us, the liquid outer core shimmered through a transparent bulkhead, a reminder that every layer we had passed still cradled us, one inside the other, like nested stories refusing to end.

INDIVIDUALIZED EDUCATION PLAN (IEP) – 12-MONTH OUTLINE  
Student: [Name]  
Disability Classification: Specific Learning Disability – Dyslexia  
Grade/Age: 3rd grade / 8–9 years  
Plan Duration: [Start Date] – [End Date] (12 consecutive months)  
Service Minutes: 4×/week, 45-min pull-out OG-based reading intervention + 2×/week, 30-min push-in support for writing & content literacy  
Primary Team: Special-ed teacher (case manager), Gen-ed ELA teacher, Gen-ed Math teacher, Speech-Language Pathologist (consult), Parent(s), Student  

-------------------------------------------------
GLOBAL ANNUAL GOALS (aligned with CCSS & IDEA)
1. Reading Accuracy & Fluency: By the end of 12 months, when reading grade-level text, the student will decode multisyllabic words with 90 % accuracy and read aloud at ≥ 90 wcpm with appropriate prosody on 3 consecutive trials.
2. Reading Comprehension: Given text at 3rd-grade complexity, the student will identify main idea, two key details, and make one inference with 80 % accuracy on 4/5 trials.
3. Written Expression: When composing a 3-paragraph opinion piece, the student will plan with a graphic organizer, spell 90 % of taught high-frequency words correctly, and use punctuation with 80 % accuracy on 3 consecutive pieces.
4. Phonological Awareness & Spelling: The student will spell 50 new irregular/high-frequency words and apply six syllable-type rules with 85 % accuracy in bi-weekly assessments.

-------------------------------------------------
MONTH-BY-MONTH LEARNING GOALS & ACCOMMODATIONS

MONTH 1 – Baseline & Routines  
• Goals: Complete diagnostic assessments (QRI-6, PAST, TWS-5); establish 1:1 sound-symbol correspondence for short vowels; set up AT toolkit.  
• Accommodations:  
  – Pre-teach classroom vocabulary 24 h in advance.  
  – Allow oral responses instead of written for daily warm-ups.  
• AT Introduced: Text-to-speech (TTS) extension (Read&Write), noise-canceling headphones.

MONTH 2 – CVC Patterns & Sight Words 1–25  
• Goals: Decode CVC words at 30 wcpm; spell 25 high-frequency words.  
• Accommodations: Reduce spelling list to 8 words; provide color-coded vowel cards.  
• AT: Start audiobook subscription (Learning Ally) for nightly 15-min reading.

MONTH 3 – Digraphs & Blends  
• Goals: Read CVCC/CCVC words with 85 % accuracy; identify digraphs in isolation.  
• Accommodations: Allow finger-tracking during oral reading; give extra 5 min on decoding quizzes.  
• AT: Snap&Read for quick vocabulary definitions while reading online.

MONTH 4 – Closed & Open Syllables  
• Goals: Segment and blend two-syllable words with closed/open patterns; fluency 50 wcpm.  
• Accommodations: Provide syllable-division template on every worksheet.  
• AT: Co:Writer word-prediction for spelling support during writing.

MONTH 5 – Vowel-Consonant-e & Fluency Phrasing  
• Goals: Read VCe words with automaticity; use slash marks to mark phrases in text.  
• Accommodations: Allow student to record answers instead of writing for comprehension checks.  
• AT: FluencyRev™ for repeated reading with progress graphs.

MONTH 6 – Mid-Year Review & Self-Advocacy  
• Goals: Demonstrate 70 % mastery of taught syllable types; complete “About My Dyslexia” presentation to class.  
• Accommodations: Provide presentation template; allow cue cards.  
• AT: Voice-to-text (Google Docs Voice Typing) for presentation script.

MONTH 7 – R-Controlled Vowels & Multisyllabic Words  
• Goals: Decode words with ar/er/ir/or/ur; read 3-syllable words with 80 % accuracy.  
• Accommodations: Offer enlarged print (18-pt font, 1.5 spacing).  
• AT: Immersive Reader in Microsoft Edge for read-aloud during research.

MONTH 8 – Vowel Teams & Comprehension Monitoring  
• Goals: Identify 10 common vowel teams; apply “Stop & Think” strategy after each paragraph.  
• Accommodations: Provide sticky-note prompts (“Does this make sense?”).  
• AT: Inspiration Maps for digital mind-mapping of story elements.

MONTH 9 – Non-Fiction Text Features & Note-Taking  
• Goals: Use headings, captions, and bold words to locate information; take 3-column notes.  
• Accommodations: Supply partially filled note organizer; allow partner reading.  
• AT: Notability for audio-recorded notes synced to PDF handouts.

MONTH 10 – Opinion Writing & Editing  
• Goals: Draft 3-paragraph opinion piece with topic sentence, reasons, conclusion; self-edit using COPS checklist.  
• Accommodations: Reduce editing checklist to 3 items; allow speech-to-text for first draft.  
• AT: Grammarly (kid-friendly settings) for real-time spelling/grammar feedback.

MONTH 11 – Research Project & Presentation  
• Goals: Research 3 sources, cite 2 facts, create 5-slide presentation.  
• Accommodations: Provide graphic organizer for each slide; allow extra week timeline.  
• AT: Bookshare for accessible research articles; use Screencastify to practice oral delivery.

MONTH 12 – Summative Assessment & Transition Planning  
• Goals: Demonstrate 90 % accuracy on final decoding probe; read aloud at 90 wcpm; reflect on AT preferences for 4th grade.  
• Accommodations: Break final assessment into 3 short sessions; allow breaks.  
• AT: Student-led AT showcase for next-year teachers.

-------------------------------------------------
ONGOING ACCOMMODATIONS (apply in ALL settings)
• Extended time (time-and-a-half) on all reading and writing tasks.  
• Alternative formats: digital text, audio, large print.  
• No penalty for spelling errors on content-area tests.  
• Preferential seating near teacher & away from auditory distractions.  
• Use of noise-canceling headphones during independent work.  
• Option to respond orally or via voice recording.  
• Reduced reading load (essential content only) with key concepts highlighted.  
• Frequent check-ins (every 10 min) during independent reading/writing.

-------------------------------------------------
ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY TOOLKIT
1. Text-to-Speech (TTS)  
   – Read&Write for Google Chrome

   – Learning Ally Audiobooks  

2. Speech-to-Text (Dictation)

3. Word Prediction & Spelling Support

4. Screen Masking & Tracking

5. Note-Taking & Organization

6. Fluency Practice

7. Digital Library & Accessible Books

8. Hardware

   – Noise-canceling headphones (Bose or Califone)  
   – Portable keyboard (Alphasmart Neo2) for distraction-free drafting  

-------------------------------------------------
PROGRESS MONITORING SCHEDULE
• Weekly: 1-min CBM-R (curriculum-based measurement in reading) & spelling probe.  
• Bi-weekly: Review of AT usage logs and student self-reflection sheet.

Jack: I know, and I broke that promise for one reckless minute. I’m sorry. Look at me—my hands are shaking too.  

Rose: The water was freezing and the dark swallowed the deck whole!  
Jack: I saw the same black waves; that’s why I ran back the second I realized you weren’t behind me. I’d rather drown beside you than live alone on any lifeboat.  

Rose: My heart was pounding so loud I couldn’t hear the wind!  
Jack: Let me feel it now—steady, like the drum in our song. You’re safe, Rose. The engines are quiet; the stars are out.  

Rose: I thought I’d lost the only warmth left in this world!  
Jack: You haven’t. Feel my palm against yours—same heat, same pulse. We’re stitched together tighter than the ship’s steel.  

Rose: I was terrified I’d never see your smile again.  
Jack: Then let me give it to you now—see? And I’ll keep it here every morning you wake up, until the ocean forgets how to roar.

The composition is anchored by the dark Provençal cypress, a vertical flame linking earth to sky, while the village below sleeps in measured horizontals, its steeple pointing like a quiet exclamation mark amid turbulence. Short, directional strokes of impasto—thick enough to catch light—create a vibrating surface; each mark records the artist’s pulse rather than describing literal form. Color temperature shifts from cool nocturnal blues to incandescent stars, generating a spiritual electricity that transcends mere landscape. instruction: Generate two matrices, A and B, where A is a 4x3 matrix and B is a 3x2 matrix, by randomly selecting numbers from the set {0, 1, 2}. Then, calculate the product C by multiplying A and B, denoted as C = A * B.

### Step 1: Generate Matrix A (4×3)
Randomly select values from {0, 1, 2}:

\[
A = \begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 2 \\
2 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 2 & 1 \\
1 & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]

### Step 2: Generate Matrix B (3×2)
Randomly select values from {0, 1, 2}:

\[
B = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 1 \\
0 & 2 \\
1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\]

### Step 3: Compute C = A × B
Matrix multiplication is defined as:

\[
C_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{3} A_{ik} \cdot B_{kj}
\]

Compute each element:

- **C₁₁** = 1×2 + 0×0 + 2×1 = 2 + 0 + 2 = **4**
- **C₁₂** = 1×1 + 0×2 + 2×0 = 1 + 0 + 0 = **1**
- **C₂₁** = 2×2 + 1×0 + 0×1 = 4 + 0 + 0 = **4**
- **C₂₂** = 2×1 + 1×2 + 0×0 = 2 + 2 + 0 = **4**
- **C₃₁** = 0×2 + 2×0 + 1×1 = 0 + 0 + 1 = **1**
- **C₃₂** = 0×1 + 2×2 + 1×0 = 0 + 4 + 0 = **4**
- **C₄₁** = 1×2 + 1×0 + 1×1 = 2 + 0 + 1 = **3**
- **C₄₂** = 1×1 + 1×2 + 1×0 = 1 + 2 + 0 = **3**

### Final Result:
\[
C = A \times B = \begin{bmatrix}
4 & 1 \\
4 & 4 \\
1 & 4 \\
3 & 3
\end{bmatrix}
\]

Product reviewed: QuietWave Pro ANC-900

I had high hopes for the QuietWave Pro ANC-900. After three weeks of daily use, I’m boxing them up for return. Below is a candid breakdown of why they disappointed me in every area that matters.

1. Sound quality – thin, veiled, and oddly compressed  
• The 40 mm “titanium-coated” drivers sound more like 20 mm paper cones. Bass is present but flabby; kick drums feel like someone tapping a cardboard box.  
• Midrange is recessed, so vocals—think Adele or Hozier—float behind the instruments instead of in front.  
• Highs are brittle. Cymbals on “Bohemian Rhapsody” (24-bit FLAC, Tidal) produced a metallic sizzle that made me wince at 70 % volume.  
• ANC introduces a faint white-noise hiss and narrows the soundstage. Turning ANC off actually improves clarity, which defeats the purpose of buying an ANC headphone.

2. Comfort – hotspots after 45 minutes  
• Clamp force measures 0.9 lbs on my scale—tighter than Sony WH-1000XM5 (0.6 lbs).  
• The memory-foam pads feel plush at first, but the shallow 15 mm cavity lets my ears bottom out against the driver plate. After a 45-minute Zoom call I had a sore ridge on each ear.  
• Headband padding is only 8 mm thick. With glasses on, the crown of my head ached after one album.

3. Design – premium look, cheap execution  
• The matte-black aluminum yokes look sleek, yet the hinge pin is plain plastic. Mine already developed a hairline crack after a single drop from desk height (18 in).  
• Buttons are mushy and indistinct. I lost count of how many times I hit “Ambient Mode” instead of “Volume Up” during a commute.  
• The carrying case is bulky—about 20 % larger than Bose’s—and the zipper snagged on day three.  
• No multi-point Bluetooth. Switching from my phone to my laptop required a manual disconnect/re-pair every single time.

4. Battery life – falls short of advertised spec  
• QuietWave claims 35 hours with ANC on. My real-world loop of Spotify at 60 % volume delivered 26 hours 12 minutes—roughly 25 % less.  
• Quick-charge is supposed to give 4 hours in 10 minutes; I got 2 hours 15 minutes before the low-battery chime.  
• The USB-C port is recessed so deeply that only the factory cable fits; my Anker and Apple cables wouldn’t seat fully.

Bottom line  
At $299, the QuietWave Pro ANC-900 under-delivers in every key metric. If you prioritize balanced sound, long-haul comfort, or reliable battery figures, look elsewhere—Sony’s WH-1000XM5 or Sennheiser’s Momentum 4 are both on sale for similar money and outperform this model handily.

Logic Puzzle  
Six people – A, B, C, D, E, F – are standing in a single straight line, each in a different position.  Determine the left-to-right order from the following six clues.

Clues  
1.  A is somewhere to the left of B.  
2.  C is somewhere to the right of D.  
3.  E is somewhere to the left of F.  
4.  B is somewhere to the right of C.  
5.  D is somewhere to the left of A.  
6.  F is somewhere to the left of C.

Solution  
From the clues we can chain the relative positions:

•  From clue 5:  D is left of A.  
•  From clue 1:  A is left of B.  
•  From clue 2:  D is left of C.  
•  From clue 4:  C is left of B.  
•  From clue 6:  F is left of C.  
•  From clue 3:  E is left of F.

Putting these together gives the strict ordering

D  <  A  <  E  <  F  <  C  <  B

Hence the unique left-to-right arrangement of the six people is

D  A  E  F  C  B
