Title: “Last Course”

Restaurant: low amber light, half-empty, the clink of silverware like distant rain.  
A corner booth—red leather cracked, a single candle guttering between two untouched entrées.

[Stage direction]  
Marcus sits rigid, napkin twisted in his fist; Lena arrives late, coat still on, cheeks wind-burned.

Marcus (Sentence 1): You ordered the duck for me—remembered after three years, how touching.  
Marcus (Sentence 2): I found the hotel receipt in your coat, same night you said you were at your mother’s.  
Marcus (Sentence 3): Tell me his name so I can at least taste the lie you’re serving.  
Marcus (Sentence 4): I kept your seat warm, Lena; I kept everything warm, even my anger.  
Marcus (Sentence 5): The waiter thinks we’re celebrating—should we toast to betrayal?  
Marcus (Sentence 6): I’m paying the bill, then I’m erasing every trace of you from our apartment.  
Marcus (Sentence 7): Eat or don’t, but when that candle burns out, so do we.

[Stage direction]  
Lena’s fingers tremble on the menu; she closes it, eyes wet but steady.

Lena (Sentence 1): His name is Daniel, and he doesn’t matter—what matters is I stopped mattering to you.  
Lena (Sentence 2): Your silence at home was louder than any hotel key card.  
Lena (Sentence 3): I told my mother I was with her because I couldn’t confess I was with loneliness.  
Lena (Sentence 4): I kept the receipt to force this moment, Marcus—look at me, not the flame.  
Lena (Sentence 5): If you erase me, start with the photos where I’m already fading.  
Lena (Sentence 6): I’ll walk out before the candle dies, so you can remember how quickly light leaves.  
Lena (Sentence 7): Keep the duck; it’s already cold, like everything we forgot to say.

[Stage direction]  
Marcus reaches for the wine, then stops; Lena stands, coat still buttoned, and exits as the candle sputters out, leaving only the smell of burnt wick and cooling meat.

SWOT Analysis – Startup Electric-Vehicle (EV) Company  
(early-stage, focused on mid-price urban passenger cars & subscription-based ownership model)

STRENGTHS  
• Purpose-built EV architecture: skateboard platform designed from day-one for 400-V/800-V dual compatibility, enabling faster charging and lower per-unit cost than legacy retrofits.  
• Software-defined vehicle stack: in-house OTA-capable operating system and ADAS Level-2+ pipeline; allows continuous feature roll-outs and recurring revenue via software subscriptions.  
• Asset-light manufacturing: contract manufacturing with two regional “micro-factories” (North America & EU) keeps cap-ex < $250 M, preserving cash for R&D and marketing.  
• Direct-to-consumer sales & subscription model: bypasses dealer margin, captures lifetime customer data, and appeals to urban millennials who prefer access over ownership.  
• Sustainability brand equity: 100 % renewable-energy supply contracts and closed-loop battery recycling partnership already secured; resonates with ESG-driven investors and fleet buyers.  
• Agile talent pool: founding team ex-Tesla, Rivian, and Apple; 30 % of engineers are battery-chemistry PhDs, giving credibility with capital markets and suppliers.

WEAKNESSES  
• Limited capital runway: current Series B funds cover only 18 months to SOP (start of production); any delay triggers a bridge round at unfavorable terms.  
• No brand heritage: zero consumer awareness outside tech media; trust and residual-value perception remain major hurdles.  
• Supply-chain inexperience: no volume contracts for semiconductors or lithium iron phosphate cells; exposed to spot-price volatility and allocation risk.  
• Service footprint gaps: mobile-service fleet still in pilot phase; inadequate coverage hurts customer satisfaction and warranty cost forecasting.  
• Regulatory certification lag: homologation timelines in EU (UNECE) and U.S. (FMVSS) are first-time processes for the team, risking launch delays.  
• Single-product dependency: first vehicle is a compact crossover; failure in this segment stalls the entire company.

OPPORTUNITIES  
• Government tailwinds: $7,500 U.S. federal credit plus new point-of-sale transferability (2024 IRA rules) and EU CO₂ fleet-average fines accelerating BEV adoption.  
• Fleet electrification wave: last-mile delivery and ride-hail operators seeking 3- to 5-year subscription deals to avoid balance-sheet ownership.  
• Battery-cost inflection: LFP cell prices projected to fall below $70 kWh by 2026; enables profitable entry-level trims and price-parity with ICE.  
• Energy-services bundling: vehicle-to-grid (V2G) partnerships with utilities create additional $2,000–$3,000 lifetime revenue per car.  
• Emerging-market leapfrog: ASEAN and LATAM cities implementing ICE bans in 2030–2035; micro-factory model can be franchised with local partners.  
• M&A exit paths: legacy OEMs and Tier-1 suppliers (e.g., Magna, ZF) actively scouting for EV IP and software talent at 8–12× revenue multiples.

THREATS  
• Intensifying price war: Tesla’s Model 2 (target $25 k) and BYD’s Seagull export push could compress segment margins to < 5 % by 2026.  
• Raw-material shocks: lithium, nickel, and graphite face geopolitical concentration (China, DRC, Indonesia); sudden export restrictions could spike pack costs 20–30 %.  
• Charging-standards fragmentation: NACS adoption by Ford & GM pressures non-compliant startups; retrofit costs estimated at $400 per vehicle.  
• Big-tech entry: Apple, Xiaomi, and Sony/Honda have deeper ecosystems and balance sheets, able to subsidize hardware with services revenue.  
• Regulatory rollback risk: potential change in U.S. administration could soften CAFE standards or repeal IRA credits, eroding demand.  
• Cyber-security liabilities: OTA architecture increases attack surface; a high-profile breach could trigger recalls and brand damage disproportionate to company size.

   • `name` (str) – Human-readable product name.  
   • `quantity` (int) – Number of units to add (must be ≥ 0).  
   • `unit_price` (float) – Price per single unit (must be ≥ 0).

   Returns  
   • `dict` – A snapshot of the item after the operation:  
     `{"sku": str, "name": str, "quantity": int, "unit_price": float}`

2. remove_item  
   Purpose  
   Decreases the on-hand quantity of an existing product.  
   If the resulting quantity drops to zero or below, the item is automatically deleted from the inventory.

   Parameters  
   • `sku` (str) – SKU of the product to remove.  
   • `amount` (int) – Number of units to remove (must be > 0).

   Returns  
   • `dict | None` – If the item still exists after removal, returns the same snapshot format as `add_item`.  
     If the item is deleted, returns `None`.

3. get_inventory  
   Purpose  
   Retrieves the current state of the entire inventory or a filtered subset.

   Parameters  
   • `filter_sku` (str | None, optional) – If provided, only the item with that SKU is returned.  
   • `low_stock_threshold` (int | None, optional) – If provided, only items whose quantity is ≤ this value are returned.

   Returns  
   • `dict` – A dictionary keyed by SKU.  
     Each value is a snapshot dict identical to the one returned by `add_item`.  
     If `filter_sku` is used and the SKU does not exist, an empty dict `{}` is returned.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Sample Usage
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```python
from inventory_manager import InventoryManager  # assuming the class is saved in inventory_manager.py

# 1. Create an empty inventory
store = InventoryManager()

# 2. Add some products
store.add_item("SKU-001", "Wireless Mouse", 50, 29.99)
store.add_item("SKU-002", "Mechanical Keyboard", 30, 89.99)
store.add_item("SKU-003", "USB-C Cable", 100, 12.50)

# 3. Sell 5 keyboards
store.remove_item("SKU-002", 5)

# 4. Check low-stock items (threshold = 10)
low_stock = store.get_inventory(low_stock_threshold=10)
print("Low-stock items:", low_stock)

# 5. Inspect a single product
mouse = store.get_inventory(filter_sku="SKU-001")
print("Mouse details:", mouse)

# 6. Remove the last USB-C cables (all 100)
store.remove_item("SKU-003", 100)  # item will be deleted
print("After deleting cables:", store.get_inventory())
```

Running the snippet produces output similar to:

```
Low-stock items: {}
Mouse details: {'SKU-001': {'sku': 'SKU-001', 'name': 'Wireless Mouse', 'quantity': 50, 'unit_price': 29.99}}
After deleting cables: {'SKU-001': {'sku': 'SKU-001', 'name': 'Wireless Mouse', 'quantity': 50, 'unit_price': 29.99},
                        'SKU-002': {'sku': 'SKU-002', 'name': 'Mechanical Keyboard', 'quantity': 25, 'unit_price': 89.99}}
```

1. Group dining etiquette – “shared dishes” vs. “individual plates”  
   In most Chinese restaurants, every entrée is placed in the center of the table and everyone uses their own chopsticks or serving chopsticks to take bites from the same plates. In the United States, meals are usually plated individually, and people rarely reach into a communal dish once it has been served. The Chinese style emphasizes togetherness and variety, while the American style stresses personal space and portion control.

2. Gift-giving customs – the “refusal dance” and wrapping colors  
   When you hand someone a gift in China, the recipient will often politely decline it once or twice before accepting. 3. Queueing style – “organized lines” vs. “crowd clusters”

Americans are accustomed to strict, orderly lines where each person waits behind the person in front. The Chinese approach can feel chaotic to newcomers, but locals view it as an efficient way to handle large crowds when space is limited.

Vegetarian Garlic-Tomato & Spinach Pasta

Ingredients (serves 2)
• 200 g dried spaghetti  
• 2 Tbsp olive oil  
• 3 cloves garlic, thinly sliced  
• 400 g canned chopped tomatoes (1 standard tin)  
• 100 g fresh baby spinach (about 3 packed cups)  
• Salt & black pepper to taste  
• Optional: pinch of dried chilli flakes or grated cheese

Five-step method
1. Boil pasta  
   Fill the stockpot with 1.5 L water, add a generous pinch of salt, bring to a boil, then add the spaghetti. Cook 8–10 min until al dente. Reserve ½ cup of the starchy cooking water, then drain the pasta in the stockpot’s lid or by carefully tipping it.

2. Start the sauce base  
   While the pasta cooks, set the saucepan over medium heat. Add olive oil and sliced garlic; sauté 30–45 sec until fragrant but not browned.

3. Simmer tomatoes  
   Pour the canned tomatoes into the saucepan with the garlic. Season with salt, pepper and chilli flakes if using. Simmer 5 min, stirring occasionally, until slightly thickened.

4. Wilt spinach  
   Add the spinach to the tomato sauce; cook 1–2 min, stirring, until just wilted. If the sauce looks thick, splash in a little reserved pasta water to loosen.

5. Combine & serve  
   Tip the drained spaghetti into the saucepan, toss everything together over low heat for 30 sec so the pasta absorbs the sauce. Adjust seasoning, then serve directly from the saucepan.

THE “CAMPFIRE CIRCLE” PERSONALITY TEST  
A quick, playful quiz that imagines you’re on a weekend camping trip with friends.  
Answer all 6 questions honestly; each answer has a hidden point value. At the end, add up your points and see which of five personality types best describes you.

-------------------------------------------------
QUESTIONS & ANSWERS  
(Points are shown in brackets after each choice.)

1. You arrive at the campsite first. What do you do?  
   A. Claim the best tent spot and start unpacking (4)  
   B. Wander off to explore the woods (3)  
   C. Set up a comfy communal area with snacks (2)  
   D. Sit by the empty fire-pit and wait for others (1)

2. Night falls and the fire won’t light. Your move?  
   A. Take charge, bark orders, get it blazing (4)  
   B. Invent a wild new fire-starting trick (3)  
   C. Encourage everyone to share the task together (2)  
   D. Offer to tell stories while someone else fixes it (1)

3. A friend forgot marshmallows. You…  
   A. Drive to the nearest store—problem solved (4)  
   B. Toast pine-cones instead and laugh (3)  
   C. Split yours so no one misses out (2)  
   D. Suggest a group sing-along to forget the snacks (1)

4. A sudden storm drives everyone into one tent. You…  
   A. Organize a plan: who sleeps where, gear stacked (4)  
   B. Turn the chaos into an indoor scavenger hunt (3)  
   C. Make sure the youngest camper isn’t scared (2)  
   D. Curl up quietly and listen to the rain (1)

5. Dawn breaks and the group wants an activity. You vote for…  
   A. A competitive sunrise hike to the summit (4)  
   B. An unplanned “let’s-get-lost” adventure (3)  
   C. A relaxed group breakfast followed by a nature walk (2)  
   D. Staying in sleeping bags and sharing dreams (1)

6. On the last day, you’re asked to sum up the trip in one word. You choose…  
   A. “Victory!” (4)  
   B. “Legendary!” (3)  
   C. “Togetherness.” (2)  
   D. “Peaceful.” (1)

-------------------------------------------------
HOW TO SCORE  
1. Add the points from all 6 answers.  
   Minimum possible total = 6 (all D answers)  
   Maximum possible total = 24 (all A answers)

2. Match your total to the ranges below:

6–9  →  The Gentle Glow  
10–13 →  The Heart-Warming Hearth  
14–17 →  The Spark of Spontaneity  
18–21 →  The Blazing Trailblazer  
22–24 →  The Roaring Bonfire

-------------------------------------------------
PERSONALITY RESULTS

The Gentle Glow (6–9)  
You’re the calm ember that keeps the night from feeling cold. Reflective, soft-spoken, and deeply empathetic, you recharge in quiet moments and make space for others to be heard. People leave your presence feeling peaceful.

The Heart-Warming Hearth (10–13)  
Community is your campfire. Cooperative, nurturing, and diplomatic, you instinctively gather everyone into a circle. You’re the friend who remembers birthdays, brings extra blankets, and makes sure no story goes untold.

The Spark of Spontaneity (14–17)  
Curiosity lights you up. Creative, playful, and ever in motion, you turn every plan into an improvisation. You’re the one who suggests midnight swims, invents new games, and keeps life from ever feeling routine.

The Blazing Trailblazer (18–21)  
Action is your fuel. Ambitious, decisive, and energetic, you see what needs doing and do it—fast. You rally the group, map the route, and reach the summit first, but you always circle back to make sure no one’s left behind.

The Roaring Bonfire (22–24)  
Intensity incarnate. Charismatic, bold, and larger-than-life, you command attention without trying. You thrive on challenge, speak in superlatives, and leave every gathering brighter, louder, and more alive than you found it.

-------------------------------------------------
Enjoy your result—and remember, every fire can flicker differently depending on the night!

I still remember the first time a machine answered me back. I was twelve, crouched over a clunky desktop in my parents’ study, typing questions into an early chatbot that came on a magazine CD-ROM. When it replied, “I’m not sure I understand—can you rephrase?” I felt a jolt of wonder that has never quite left me. That moment was my first glimpse of language as both bridge and barrier, and it set me on a path that winds through linguistics classrooms, open-source repositories, and late-night debugging sessions to the threshold of the role I’m applying for today.

Motivation: why language, why now  
Language is the most human technology we have. It encodes memory, emotion, and culture in a few thousand symbols, yet we still struggle to teach machines to wield it with anything approaching our nuance. I want to close that gap—not to replace human expression, but to amplify it. After watching relatives navigate medical paperwork in a second language and seeing friends with dyslexia wrestle with dense academic texts, I realized that better language technology can be a tool for equity. Every improvement in summarization, question answering, or low-resource translation is a step toward a world where information bends to people, not the other way around. That conviction has kept me in the field through every paradigm shift, from n-gram language models to billion-parameter transformers.

Relevant experiences and accomplishments  
Academic foundation  
I earned a B.S. in Computer Science and a minor in Linguistics from the University of Washington, graduating summa cum laude. My senior thesis introduced a character-level BiLSTM that could jointly segment and tag code-switched Arabic-English social media text, reducing error propagation by 18 % over pipelined baselines. The work won the Allen School’s Best Undergraduate Research Award and became my first ACL submission (short paper, 2019).

Graduate research  
At Carnegie Mellon’s Language Technologies Institute, I focused on controllable text generation under the guidance of Prof. Yulia Tsvetkov. My dissertation, “Steering Style Without Breaking Substance,” proposed a reinforcement-learning framework that constrains decoding using differentiable attribute classifiers. The system can dial up formality or empathy while preserving factual accuracy, achieving a 0.87 correlation with human ratings on style strength and a 12 % drop in hallucination relative to unconstrained GPT-style baselines. One chapter on low-resource stylistic transfer for Swahili health messaging was nominated for an ACL best-theme paper.

Industry impact  
Between academic stints, I spent two years as an Applied Scientist at Hugging Face. I led the team that shipped the first multilingual instruction-tuned model under 3 B parameters capable of zero-shot tool use. I also architected the “safetensors” serialization format now adopted by over 50,000 repositories to reduce model-loading vulnerabilities. These products serve millions of API calls daily; seeing my code help a Kenyan agritech startup route farmers to drought-resistant seed suppliers in Swahili still gives me goosebumps.

Open-source leadership  
I maintain the open-source library “decoding-lab,” which provides plug-and-play constrained decoding for PyTorch and JAX. With 3,200 GitHub stars and 120 contributors, it is used in university courses from ETH Zürich to Addis Ababa. I also co-organize the annual “Responsible Generation” workshop at EMNLP, bringing together researchers and policy makers to draft model-release checklists that have been cited in the EU AI Act’s annexes.

Challenges faced and lessons learned  
1. Data scarcity in under-represented languages  
When I started working on Swahili health messaging, there were fewer than 50 k parallel sentences for the domain. Scraping social media risked reinforcing toxic dialects. I partnered with local clinics to collect de-identified patient questions, then used iterative back-translation and human-in-the-loop filtering to grow a 200 k-sentence corpus. The lesson: technology is only as inclusive as the partnerships we build to feed it.

2. Bias amplification  
Early versions of my controllable generation model would obediently crank up “professionalism” but also inject gendered assumptions—e.g., assuming nurses are female. Root-cause analysis revealed that the style classifier had learned spurious correlations from Reddit data. I introduced adversarial debiasing during classifier training and added counterfactual augmentation, cutting gendered associations by 34 % without degrading style control. The experience taught me to treat evaluation metrics as hypotheses, not verdicts.

3. Burnout and impostor syndrome  
During the pandemic, while juggling a newborn and a paper deadline, I hit a wall. I started therapy, instituted “no-meeting Wednesdays,” and began mentoring junior women in NLP through the WiNLP buddy program. Sharing struggles turned out to be a superpower: my mentees’ questions forced me to clarify my own thinking, and their successes became new sources of energy.

Suitability for this role and future goals  
Your team’s mission—to build language systems that are not only state-of-the-art but also transparent, steerable, and culturally grounded—aligns perfectly with the arc of my career so far. I bring:

• Deep technical expertise in transformer architectures, constrained decoding, and reinforcement learning from human feedback.  
• A track record of shipping production models that serve millions of users across dozens of languages.  
• A community-centered approach to open source and responsible AI, evidenced by workshops, datasets, and mentorship.

Peer Review

What is this paper about and what contributions does it make?
The paper, titled “Adaptive Curriculum Learning for Few-Shot Graph Neural Networks,” proposes a curriculum-based training strategy that dynamically re-orders training tasks for few-shot node-classification on graphs. The key contributions are (1) a difficulty-scoring function that combines structural entropy and label sparsity to rank tasks, (2) an online bandit algorithm that adapts the curriculum on the fly, and (3) extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets showing 3–7 % absolute F1 improvements over strong meta-learning baselines.

Reasons to accept:
• Novelty: Curriculum learning has been studied in vision and NLP, but its application to few-shot graph learning is new.  
• Empirical gains: Consistent improvements across multiple datasets and two different GNN backbones.  
• Practical impact: The method is plug-and-play; no architectural changes are required.  
• Open source: Code and pre-processed datasets are promised to be released.

Reasons to reject:
• Limited theoretical grounding: The paper lacks convergence guarantees or regret bounds for the bandit algorithm.  
• Missing ablations: No ablation on the two components of the difficulty score (entropy vs. sparsity).  
• Baseline omissions: MAML, Meta-SGD, and G-Meta are included, but newer methods such as GPN (Graph Prototypical Networks) and Meta-GNN are not compared.  
• Reproducibility gaps: Hyper-parameter grids and random seeds are not fully specified.  
• Writing issues: Several undefined symbols (e.g., “κ” in Eq. 4) and grammatical errors in Section 4.2.

Questions for the Author(s):
1. Can you provide regret bounds or at least convergence analysis for the EXP3-style bandit used in Section 3.3?  
2. How sensitive is the method to the entropy/sparsity weight λ? A simple ablation table would help.  
3. Why were GPN and Meta-GNN excluded from the baselines? Would the gains persist if they were included?  
4. Could you clarify the training time overhead compared to standard fine-tuning?  
5. The paper mentions “ethical considerations” in the appendix but does not elaborate—what specific risks do you foresee?

Soundness (score 1-5): 3  
Excitement (score 1-5): 4  
Reviewer Confidence (score 1-5): 4  
Recommendation for Best Paper Award (Yes/No): No  
Reproducibility (score 1-5): 3  
Ethical Concerns (Yes/No): No (but the discussion should be expanded)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Author Response

We thank the reviewer for the detailed and constructive feedback. Below we address each major point and outline the changes we will incorporate in the camera-ready version.

1. Theoretical grounding (regret bounds).  
   We agree that formal guarantees strengthen the paper. In the revision we will add a short theoretical section proving an O(√(TK log K)) expected regret bound for our EXP3 variant under the assumption of bounded loss (≤1). The proof follows standard techniques but is non-trivial because our loss is non-stationary (it depends on the evolving GNN parameters). We will include the full derivation in Appendix B.

2. Ablations on difficulty-score components.  
   We have already run the requested ablation. Removing the entropy term drops F1 by 1.8 % on average; removing the sparsity term drops it by 2.4 %. We will add Table 5 summarizing these results.

3. Additional baselines.  
   We have re-run all experiments with GPN (NeurIPS’22) and Meta-GNN (ICLR’23). Our method still outperforms both by 2.1 % and 1.6 % macro-F1, respectively. The updated results will appear in Table 2 and the corresponding statistical significance tests in Appendix C.

4. Training-time overhead.  
   The bandit update adds <3 % wall-clock time per epoch because the difficulty scores are computed on the CPU in parallel with GPU training. We will report exact timings in Section 4.4.

5. Reproducibility.  
   We will release (a) a complete yaml config file with all hyper-parameters and seeds, (b) a requirements.txt pinned to exact library versions, and (c) a README with a one-command reproduction script.

6. Writing and notation.  
   We will fix all undefined symbols, run a thorough grammar check, and add a notation table at the beginning of Section 3.

7. Ethical considerations.  
   We will expand the ethics appendix to discuss potential misuse (e.g., inferring sensitive attributes in social networks) and mitigation strategies such as differential privacy and fairness constraints.

We believe these revisions directly address the reviewer’s concerns and will substantially improve the paper’s clarity, completeness, and reproducibility.

Introduction  
From the first cave paintings to today’s digital installations, human beings have always used the arts to make sense of the world. Yet, when budgets tighten, arts programs are often the first to be cut. This is shortsighted. Arts education is not a luxury; it is a catalyst for cognitive growth, social cohesion, and economic resilience. By integrating music, visual arts, theater, and dance into the core curriculum, schools equip students with the very skills that modern life demands.

Argument 1: Cognitive Development  
When children learn to read musical notation or mix colors on a palette, they are exercising neural pathways that strengthen memory, spatial reasoning, and executive function. Neuroimaging studies from the University of Southern California show that students engaged in sustained music instruction have thicker corpus callosums—the bridge between the brain’s hemispheres—than their peers. In short, the arts make the brain more agile.  
Example: At the inner-city Orchard Gardens K–8 Pilot School in Boston, reading scores rose 16 percentage points in two years after the principal replaced security guards with art, music, and dance teachers. The creative tasks demanded sustained attention and pattern recognition, which transferred directly to literacy.  
Therefore, arts education is not peripheral; it is a proven engine for sharpening the very cognitive tools that undergird all academic learning.

Argument 2: Social-Emotional Growth  
Creating a mural or rehearsing a scene requires collaboration, empathy, and the courage to risk failure in front of peers. These experiences cultivate emotional intelligence, a predictor of life satisfaction more powerful than IQ.  
Example: The “Turnaround Arts” initiative placed teaching artists in 49 struggling U.S. schools. Suspension rates dropped 23 percent, and students reported feeling “more connected” to classmates and teachers. One fifth-grader in Milwaukee said, “When we painted our feelings, I learned my anger wasn’t just mine—it was something we could talk about.”  
Thus, the arts transform classrooms into communities where vulnerability becomes a shared resource rather than a liability.

Argument 3: Economic and Civic Impact  
Creative industries contribute over $1 trillion to the global economy annually, and employers rank creativity among the top three skills they seek. Early exposure to the arts seeds the workforce of tomorrow while fostering citizens who value diverse perspectives.  
Example: Austin, Texas, credits its vibrant music-education pipeline—from elementary ukulele clubs to high-school recording studios—for fueling a local creative economy that employs 60,000 people and draws 20 million visitors each year.  
Consequently, arts education is not a cost center; it is an investment that pays civic and financial dividends long after graduation.

Conclusion  
Arts education strengthens the mind through enhanced cognition, nurtures the heart via social-emotional learning, and enriches society by driving economic and civic vitality. Cutting the arts may save dollars today, but it forfeits the far greater returns these programs generate for individuals and communities alike.

Title  
“Ultra-Low-Power Wake-Up Receiver for mmWave Backscatter Networks: A 28 nm CMOS Prototype”

Abstract  
We present a 60 GHz wake-up receiver that consumes 2.3 µW while achieving –82 dBm sensitivity, enabling decade-long battery life for dense IoT deployments.

Introduction  
This section motivates the need for always-listening yet microwatt-level wake-up radios in future millimeter-wave backscatter sensor networks and states the paper’s goal of demonstrating a sub-3 µW 60 GHz solution.

Related Work  
We survey prior wake-up receivers across sub-GHz, 2.4 GHz, and mmWave bands, highlighting the gap between sensitivity, power, and integration level that our work closes.

Methodology  
We detail the top-down co-design flow—link-budget-driven architecture, circuit/macros-model co-optimization, and 28 nm CMOS layout techniques—that yields the proposed receiver.

Experiment  
3.1 Test-Chip Fabrication: A 1 mm² die is fabricated in 28 nm CMOS with on-chip antenna pads and a QFN-48 package.  
3.2 Measurement Setup: A 60 GHz carrier is modulated by an FPGA-based baseband and delivered through calibrated waveguide probes to the DUT.  
3.3 Power and Sensitivity Sweep: DC power and packet-error-rate are recorded versus input power from –95 dBm to –50 dBm across 55–65 GHz.  
3.4 Interference Resilience: Continuous-wave and modulated blockers are injected at ±100 MHz offsets to quantify co-channel rejection.

Analysis  
Measured results are compared against link-budget predictions and state-of-the-art designs, revealing that the proposed super-regenerative envelope detector and duty-cycled LO achieve 4× lower energy/bit at equal sensitivity.

Conclusion  
The demonstrated 2.3 µW 60 GHz wake-up receiver paves the way for maintenance-free mmWave sensor nodes, and future work will integrate the antenna and explore energy harvesting for perpetual operation.

1. 3-D-Printed Concrete with Recycled or Low-Carbon Binders  
   • How it works  
     Robotic arms or gantry printers extrude successive layers of a specially formulated concrete mix. The mix can contain up to 70 % recycled sand or crushed demolition waste and can be paired with low-clinker cements (e.g., calcined-clay or alkali-activated slags). Because the printer deposits material only where the design calls for it, the process is “topology-optimized,” eliminating the 30–60 % over-pouring typical of conventional formwork.  
   • Real-life example  
     In July 2023, the two-storey “Data Villas” office extension in Heidelberg, Germany, was printed by PERI GmbH and Röser GmbH. The 380 m² walls used a 50 % recycled-aggregate concrete and a CEM III/B (slag-blended) cement that cut CO₂ by 55 % compared with a CEM I mix. The print paths were generated from a BIM model, so no timber or plywood formwork was required.  
   • Environmental advantages  
     – 30–50 % reduction in virgin aggregate demand.  
     – 55 % lower embodied CO₂ from binder substitution.  
     – Zero formwork waste and 20 % faster construction, shrinking site energy use and traffic congestion.

2. Engineered-Timber “Mass-Timber” Hybrid Systems  
   • How it works  
     Cross-laminated timber (CLT), glue-laminated timber (glulam) and laminated-veneer lumber (LVL) are combined with small amounts of steel or concrete only where high stiffness or fire resistance is critical. Digital fabrication (5-axis CNC) allows millimetre-precise off-site prefabrication, so entire wall or floor cassettes arrive on site ready to be craned into place.  
   • Real-life example  
     The 25-storey Ascent tower in Milwaukee, USA (completed 2022) is currently the world’s tallest hybrid mass-timber building. Roughly 8,400 m³ of CLT and glulam replace what would have been 5,000 t of reinforced concrete in the gravity frame. A two-hour fire-rated concrete core handles lateral loads, while the timber structure sequesters about 6,400 t of biogenic CO₂.  
   • Environmental advantages  
     – Up to 75 % lower embodied carbon than an equivalent reinforced-concrete frame.  
     – Biogenic carbon storage for the life of the building (≈ 0.8 t CO₂ per m³ of timber).  
     – 90 % reduction in construction water use and 50 % reduction in site waste because panels are pre-cut in the factory.

3. Living-Building Envelopes (Green Façades + Bio-receptive Concrete)  
   • How it works  
     Vertical gardens, hydroponic felt pockets and “bio-receptive” concrete panels whose pH and surface texture are tuned to foster moss and lichen growth turn the building skin into a living ecosystem. Irrigation is fed by harvested rainwater or greywater; sensors modulate water and nutrient flow to keep the plants healthy while minimizing resource use.  
   • Real-life example  
     The 30-storey “Urban Forest” residential tower in Brisbane, Australia (Arkhefield & Koichi Takada Architects, under construction, 2024) will carry 1,000 trees and 20,000 plants on cantilevered concrete balconies cast with bio-receptive concrete. A closed-loop drip irrigation system uses treated greywater from showers and laundries.  
   • Environmental advantages  
     – Up to 20 °C reduction in peak façade temperature, cutting annual HVAC energy by 23 %.  
     – 1.7 t of PM and 30 kg of NOₓ removed from the air each year by the vegetation.  
     – 60 % of annual rainfall retained or evapotranspired on site, reducing storm-water runoff and sewer overflows.

Together, these three techniques—additive manufacturing with recycled/low-carbon concrete, carbon-storing mass-timber hybrids, and living building skins—are rapidly moving from pilot projects to mainstream practice, offering quantifiable reductions in embodied carbon, operational energy and urban-ecological impact.

A Traveler’s Diary: Ten Days in Middle-earth  
(Kept in a small, leather-bound journal found later in the ruins of an old watch-tower beside the Brandywine)

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

Day 1 – A Door in the Hedge  
I left the Shire at dawn, meaning only to walk the Greenway to Bree and back. Somewhere east of the Stock-brook I ducked through a gap in a hawthorn hedge to pick black-berries—and stepped into twilight. The air smelled of pine and rain though no cloud hung overhead. A silver birch arched above me like a gate, its leaves chiming though no wind stirred. I knew, with the certainty of dream, that I had crossed a border no map records. My heart beat like a drum; I walked on, and the Shire’s fields fell away behind me as if they had never been.

Day 2 – Rivendell at First Light  
I followed a stream that laughed over stones until the valley opened like a book. There stood Rivendell: waterfalls braided with moonlight, roofs of gold and green copper, and bridges delicate as lyre strings. Elves—tall, luminous, and kind—welcomed me with bread that tasted of honeycomb and starlight. Lord Elrond himself set a cup of miruvor in my hand; warmth spread through my veins like liquid sunrise. That night I sat in a pillared hall while songs older than sorrow drifted around me. I wept without shame, for beauty had found a voice I could finally understand.

Day 3 – The High Pass under Watchful Stars  
With a company of silent Elves I climbed the Misty Mountains. Snow whispered underfoot; the air grew thin and sharp as crystal. At dusk we reached a wind-carved balcony of stone. Far below, pine forests rolled like black seas. One Elf pointed north: a red ember glimmered on the horizon—Dol Guldur, he murmured, where shadows gather. I shivered, not from cold but from the sudden knowledge that every fair land is ringed by darkness. Yet above us the stars wheeled in their ancient dance, and hope felt as real as the ice in my beard.

Day 4 – Khazad-dûm, the Black Chasm  
We descended eastward and entered Moria by a side gate the Orcs had not yet found. Dwarves—stoic, stout, and smelling of iron and pipe-weed—guided us through halls so vast my torch could not find their ceilings. Pillars carved like tree trunks upheld mountains; runes glittered with mithril dust. Balin’s tomb lay wreathed in silence. I traced the Khuzdul inscription with trembling fingers and felt the weight of centuries settle on my shoulders. When drums rolled in the deep, we fled, but not before I glimpsed the Balrog’s fire far below—an awful majesty that seared itself into memory.

Day 5 – Lothlórien, the Golden Wood  
We crossed the Silverlode at dusk and stepped into a realm of light. Mallorn trunks soared like cathedral pillars; their boughs were hung with soft lamps of green and gold. Galadriel met us upon a flet. Her gaze pierced me, gentle yet terrible, as if she read every page of my life at a glance. She offered no counsel aloud, but when I looked into her mirror I saw my own world—streets of brick and iron—fading like a forgotten tune. I left the glade with a seed of the elanor flower pressed in my palm, a promise that some light can be carried even into darkness.

Day 6 – The Argonath and the Anduin  
Boromir’s kin ferried me south in slender boats. We slipped between the two gigantic kings of stone—Isildur and Anárion—whose stern eyes judged the living and the dead alike. The river widened; reeds whispered secrets to the wind. At night we camped on a sand-bar. Fireflies rose like sparks from the water, and the men of Gondor sang low songs of the sea. I felt the world tilt; the North was behind me, and ahead lay the unknown South with its white towers and looming shadow.

Day 7 – Edoras upon the Green Hill  
Rohirrim riders thundered past at sunrise, braids flying, spears flashing. Their king, Théoden, received me in the Golden Hall. The air smelled of horses and fresh hay; tapestries told sagas in scarlet and gold. I drank mead that tasted of heather and thunderclouds. At dusk I walked the burial mounds beyond the wall. The wind keened across the grass like a lament, yet every blade seemed alive with the memory of riders who would never truly die while their songs still echoed.

Day 8 – Fangorn, the Ent-House  
I strayed too far east and met Treebeard at the forest’s eaves. His eyes were ancient pools reflecting millennia. “Hoom, hasty thing,” he rumbled, but curiosity won over caution. For hours I walked beside his colossal strides while he discoursed on the difference between trolls and ents (one is made of mockery, the other of memory). When he sang the Ents’ names, the trees shivered and answered leaf to leaf. I felt the forest breathe, slow and deliberate as a turning world. At parting he laid a gnarled hand on my head: “May you grow roots before you grow weary.”

Day 9 – A Glimpse of Fire on the Lonely Mountain  
Southward still, I reached the Long Lake at twilight. Smaug—yes, Smaug himself—circled far above Erebor, a coal-red serpent against the indigo sky. His roar rattled the shingles in Lake-town. I hid beneath a dock, heart hammering, yet even terror could not eclipse awe. Fire licked the clouds; moonlight glinted on scales like hammered gold. Then he vanished into the mountain’s crown, and the night felt suddenly hollow. I understood why dwarves speak of dragon-sickness: beauty and ruin braided so tightly they cannot be unwound.

Day 10 – The Grey Havens and the Straight Road  
At last I came west again, footsore and soul-full. The Havens were quiet: white ships rocking at anchor, gulls crying like lost children. Círdan the Shipwright stood upon the quay, beard silver as moonlit surf. He asked no questions, only offered passage. I hesitated, feeling the seed of elanor warm against my palm. Around me, Elves sang the song of the Sea, a music that pulls at the heart like tide at the shore. I chose—for now—to remain. Yet as the last ship slipped away, I saw a faint path of light upon the water, the Straight Road that leads beyond the circles of the world. I pressed the seed into the sand and whispered a promise: I will return, though the years roll like waves. Then I turned eastward, toward the Shire-gate that might still be there, carrying Middle-earth within me like a second heartbeat.

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

End of the diary.

Formula to convert Fahrenheit to Celsius:

\[
°C = \frac{5}{9}(°F - 32)
\]

Now plug in 375°F:

\[
°C = \frac{5}{9}(375 - 32) = \frac{5}{9}(343) \approx 190.56

Puzzle  
Here is a 10-term sequence with two numbers replaced by question marks.  
Find the two missing numbers.

3, 6, 12, 24, ?, 96, 192, ?, 768, 1 536

Solution  
The sequence is a simple geometric progression in which every term is twice the previous term.

3 × 2 = 6  
6 × 2 = 12  
12 × 2 = 24  
24 × 2 = 48  ← first missing number  
48 × 2 = 96  
96 × 2 = 192  
192 × 2 = 384  ← second missing number  
384 × 2 = 768  
768 × 2 = 1 536

Therefore, the two missing numbers are 48 and 384.

Step-by-Step Scrapbook Layout Tutorial (Beginner-Friendly)

Materials  
• 12×12 cardstock base  
• 3–4 patterned papers (mix large & small prints)  
• 1–2 photos (4×6 or 3×4)  
• Paper trimmer or scissors  
• Double-sided tape or glue stick  
• Foam squares  
• Alphabet stickers or stamps  
• Embellishments: enamel dots, ribbon, washi  
• Archival pen for journaling

Technique  
1. Plan: Place photos on the cardstock; shift until one-third of the page remains open for balance.  
2. Mat: Cut patterned paper ¼" larger than each photo; adhere photos on top for instant depth.  
3. Layer: Tear a strip of contrasting paper 2" wide; angle it under the matted photos for movement.  
4. Title: Stick alphabet stickers along the torn edge; reinforce with foam squares for lift.  
5. Embellish: Cluster three enamel dots in a visual triangle around the photos; add a 4" ribbon tail tucked under the lower corner.  
6. Journal: Write a two-sentence memory on a 3×4 journaling card; mat and glue beside the photos.  
7. Finish: Lightly ink the page edges for a framed look.

Tips  
• Limit palette to three colors plus neutrals.  
• Use odd numbers—3 photos, 5 dots—for pleasing design.  
• Test placement with temporary tape before gluing.

GREEN TECH SOLUTIONS LLC  
OPERATING AGREEMENT  
(“Agreement”)

This Operating Agreement (“Agreement”) is entered into and made effective as of _____________, 20___ (the “Effective Date”) by and among the persons whose names and signatures appear on the signature pages hereto (each a “Member” and collectively the “Members”) for the purpose of governing the affairs of GreenTech Solutions LLC, a New York limited liability company (the “Company”).

Article 1. Formation; Principal Office; Registered Agent  
1.1 Formation. The Company was formed on _____________, 20___ pursuant to the New York Limited Liability Company Law, as amended (the “Act”).  
1.2 Name. The legal name of the Company is “GreenTech Solutions LLC.”  
1.3 Principal Office. The principal office is located at __________________________, New York, NY 100___. The Managers may relocate the office at any time.  
1.4 Registered Agent. The Company’s registered agent for service of process in New York is __________________________, located at __________________________, New York, NY 100___.

Article 2. Business Purpose  
The purpose of the Company is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a limited liability company may be organized under the Act, including but not limited to the development, installation, financing, ownership, operation, and maintenance of renewable energy systems (e.g., solar, wind, battery storage, and related technologies) and any other activities incidental or related thereto.

Article 3. Definitions  
Capitalized terms used but not defined herein have the meanings assigned in the Act or in this Agreement.

Article 4. Capital Contributions; Ownership Percentages  
4.1 Initial Capital Contributions. Upon formation, the Members contributed the cash, property, or services set forth opposite each Member’s name in Schedule A attached hereto (the “Initial Capital Contributions”).  
4.2 Ownership Percentages. Each Member’s percentage ownership of the Company (“Ownership Percentage”) equals the ratio of that Member’s Initial Capital Contribution to the aggregate Initial Capital Contributions of all Members, as set forth in Schedule A.  
4.3 Additional Contributions. No Member is required to make any additional contribution without such Member’s written consent. Any additional contributions shall be made on terms approved by a Majority-in-Interest of the Members (as defined below).  
4.4 Capital Accounts. A separate capital account shall be established and maintained for each Member in accordance with Treasury Regulation § 1.704-1(b)(2)(iv).

Article 5. Profits, Losses, and Distributions  
5.1 Allocations. Profits and losses for each fiscal year shall be allocated among the Members in proportion to their Ownership Percentages.  
5.2 Distributions. Available Cash Flow (as defined below) shall be distributed at such times and in such amounts as determined by the Managers, but no less frequently than annually, to the Members in proportion to their Ownership Percentages.  
“Available Cash Flow” means all cash receipts less (a) operating expenses, (b) debt service, (c) capital expenditures, and (d) reasonable reserves as determined by the Managers.

Article 6. Management and Voting  
6.1 Management. The Company shall be “Manager-Managed.” The day-to-day business and affairs shall be managed by one or more Managers appointed by a Majority-in-Interest of the Members. The initial Managers are listed in Schedule B.  
6.2 Powers of Managers. The Managers may do any act on behalf of the Company not inconsistent with this Agreement or the Act.  
6.3 Voting Rights. Except as otherwise provided herein, any matter requiring Member approval shall be decided by a vote of the Members holding more than fifty percent (50%) of the Ownership Percentages (“Majority-in-Interest”).  
6.4 Removal and Replacement. A Manager may be removed, with or without cause, at any time by a Majority-in-Interest of the Members. Vacancies shall be filled by a Majority-in-Interest.  
6.5 Officers. The Managers may appoint officers (e.g., President, Secretary, Treasurer) who shall serve at the pleasure of the Managers.

Article 7. Meetings and Consents  
7.1 Meetings. Annual meetings of the Members may be held at a time and place fixed by the Managers. Special meetings may be called by the Managers or by Members holding at least twenty-five percent (25%) of the Ownership Percentages.  
7.2 Notice. Written notice of any meeting shall be given at least ten (10) days and not more than sixty (60) days before the meeting.  
7.3 Quorum. A quorum for any meeting of Members is the presence (in person or by proxy) of Members holding more than fifty percent (50%) of the Ownership Percentages.  
7.4 Action Without Meeting. Any action required or permitted to be taken at a meeting may be taken without a meeting if a written consent describing the action is signed by Members holding the requisite Ownership Percentage.

Article 8. Books, Records, and Accounting  
8.1 Fiscal Year. The fiscal year shall end on December 31 of each year, unless otherwise determined by the Managers.  
8.2 Records. The Company shall maintain complete and accurate books and records at the principal office. Each Member has the right, upon reasonable notice, to inspect and copy such records.  
8.3 Tax Classification. The Company shall be taxed as a partnership unless the Members unanimously elect otherwise.

Article 9. Banking; Signatories  
All funds of the Company shall be deposited in the Company’s name in accounts designated by the Managers. Checks or drafts in excess of $25,000 shall require two (2) authorized signatures.

Article 10. Admission of Additional Members  
10.1 General Rule. No person may be admitted as a new Member (“New Member”) without the prior written consent of a Majority-in-Interest.  
10.2 Capital Contribution. Each New Member must make a capital contribution (cash, property, or services) acceptable to a Majority-in-Interest and shall receive an Ownership Percentage determined by mutual agreement.  
10.3 Amendment of Schedule A. Upon admission, Schedule A shall be amended to reflect the New Member’s name, contribution, and Ownership Percentage.

Article 11. Transfer of Membership Interests  
11.1 Restrictions on Transfer. No Member may sell, assign, pledge, or otherwise transfer all or any portion of its Membership Interest except in accordance with this Article 11.  
11.2 Permitted Transfers. Transfers to a Member’s revocable living trust, or to an entity wholly owned by the transferring Member, are permitted with prior written notice to the Company and without consent, provided the transferor remains the beneficial owner.  
11.3 Right of First Refusal.  
(a) If a Member (“Offeror”) receives a bona fide third-party offer to purchase its Membership Interest, the Offeror shall first offer the Interest to the Company and then to the other Members on the same terms.  
(b) The Company and the other Members shall have fifteen (15) days to accept or reject the offer in writing.  
(c) If neither the Company nor the other Members purchase the Interest, the Offeror may sell to the third party within ninety (90) days on terms no more favorable than those offered to the Company and Members.  
11.4 Substituted Members. A transferee becomes a substituted Member only with the unanimous consent of the non-transferring Members. Absent such consent, the transferee is merely an assignee entitled to allocations and distributions but not to vote or exercise other rights of a Member.  
11.5 Compliance with Securities Laws. All transfers must comply with applicable federal and state securities laws.

Article 12. Dissolution and Winding Up  
12.1 Events of Dissolution. The Company shall be dissolved upon the first to occur of:  
(a) The written consent of a Super-Majority-in-Interest (Members holding at least 75% of the Ownership Percentages);  
(b) The entry of a decree of judicial dissolution under the Act;  
(c) The sale, exchange, or other disposition of all or substantially all of the Company’s assets; or  
(d) Any other event causing dissolution under the Act.  
12.2 Winding Up. Upon dissolution, the Managers (or a liquidator appointed by a Majority-in-Interest) shall wind up the Company’s affairs in accordance with the Act, including:  
(a) Selling or otherwise converting the Company’s assets to cash;  
(b) Paying or providing for all debts, obligations, and liabilities; and  
(c) Distributing remaining proceeds to Members in accordance with positive capital account balances.  
12.3 Certificate of Dissolution. Upon completion of winding up, the Managers shall file a Certificate of Dissolution with the New York Department of State and take any other actions required to terminate the Company’s existence.

Article 13. Indemnification  
To the fullest extent permitted by the Act, the Company shall indemnify any Member or Manager who incurs liability or expense by reason of any act performed or omitted on behalf of the Company, except for liability resulting from gross negligence, willful misconduct, or breach of this Agreement.

Article 14. Confidentiality  
Each Member agrees to keep confidential all proprietary or confidential information of the Company and not to disclose such information to any third party without prior written consent, except as required by law.

Article 15. Amendments  
This Agreement may be amended only by a written instrument signed by a Super-Majority-in-Interest (75% of the Ownership Percentages), except that no amendment may materially reduce any Member’s Ownership Percentage or economic rights without that Member’s written consent.

Article 16. Governing Law; Severability  
This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the State of New York. If any provision is held invalid, the remainder of the Agreement shall continue in full force.

Article 17. Entire Agreement; Counterparts  
This Agreement constitutes the entire agreement among the Members with respect to the subject matter hereof and supersedes all prior agreements. This Agreement may be executed in multiple counterparts, each of which shall be deemed an original.

Alex: Cheers, Li Wei. See you around!

Human Resources Policy  
Remote Work Guidelines  
Effective Date: [Insert Date]  
Applies to: All employees approved for remote work (full-time, part-time, or hybrid)

1. Purpose  
To establish clear expectations, responsibilities, and support mechanisms for employees who perform their duties away from a company office, while ensuring business continuity, data security, and employee well-being.

2. Eligibility & Approval  
2.1 Eligibility: Roles that can be performed independently with minimal on-site dependency.  
2.2 Approval Process:  
   • Employee submits a Remote Work Request Form to their manager and HR.  
   • Manager and HR review role suitability, past performance, and home-office readiness.  
   • Written agreement (Remote Work Addendum) must be signed by all parties and renewed annually.

3. Work Hours & Availability  
3.1 Core Hours: 10:00 a.m.–3:00 p.m. local time, Monday–Friday. Employees must be reachable via company-approved channels during these hours.  
3.2 Flex Hours: Remaining daily hours may be scheduled flexibly, provided total weekly hours equal the employee’s FTE requirement.  
3.3 Overtime: Must be pre-approved by the manager in writing.  
3.4 Time-Off: Use the standard HRIS portal; mark “OOO” in Slack/Teams status.

4. Communication Expectations  
4.1 Channels & Response Times  
   • Slack/Teams Chat: ≤30 minutes during core hours.  
   • Email: ≤24 hours.  
   • Video/Phone: Attend all scheduled meetings with camera on unless otherwise agreed.  
4.2 Meeting Etiquette  
   • Use headsets in quiet environments.  
   • Share agenda 24 h in advance; circulate notes within 12 h afterward.  
4.3 Documentation  
   • All decisions and project updates must be logged in Confluence/SharePoint.  
   • Weekly status reports due every Friday by 5 p.m. in the designated tracker.

5. Performance Management & Assessment  
5.1 Goal Setting: Quarterly OKRs/KPIs agreed upon within first two weeks of each quarter.  
5.2 Check-Ins:  
   • Weekly 1:1 (30 min) with direct manager.  
   • Monthly skip-level 30-min touchpoint.  
5.3 Metrics:  
   • Output quality (error rates, customer satisfaction).  
   • Timeliness (deadlines met vs. missed).  
   • Collaboration (peer feedback score in 360° review).  
5.4 Annual Review: Same process as on-site staff; remote status does not alter rating scale or promotion criteria.

6. Equipment & Security  
6.1 Company-issued hardware (laptop, headset, webcam) must be used; personal devices prohibited for work tasks.  
6.2 VPN required for all network access; MFA enforced.  
6.3 Home-office must meet ergonomic and confidentiality standards (lockable door or cabinet).  
6.4 Quarterly self-audit checklist submitted to IT; random IT security scans scheduled.

7. Health, Safety & Well-Being  
7.1 Ergonomics: One-time stipend of $500 for chair/desk; annual eye-care reimbursement up to $150.  
7.2 Mental Health:  
   • Access to 24/7 Employee Assistance Program (EAP).  
   • “No-Meeting Wednesday afternoons” to reduce Zoom fatigue.  
7.3 Social Connection: Monthly optional virtual coffee chats and quarterly in-person team days (budget provided).

8. Expense Reimbursement  
Internet upgrade (up to $50/month) and co-working space rental (up to $200/month) reimbursable upon submission of receipts.

9. Data Privacy & Compliance  
All work must comply with GDPR/CCPA and industry-specific regulations. Remote employees sign an annual Data Security Acknowledgment.

10. Termination or Change of Remote Status  
Either party may terminate the remote arrangement with 30 days’ written notice. HR will conduct an exit interview focused on remote-work experience to inform policy improvements.

11. Potential Challenges & Mitigation Strategies  

| Challenge | Impact | Solutions (Owner) |
|-----------|--------|-------------------|
| Isolation & reduced belonging | Lower engagement, higher turnover | • Buddy system for new hires (HR)  • Monthly virtual socials (Team Leads)  • Quarterly in-person off-sites (Exec) |
| Communication gaps & time-zone drift | Missed deadlines, duplicated work | • Core hours policy (HR)  • Shared team calendar with time-zone display (IT)  • Async hand-off templates (PMO) |
| Work-life boundary erosion | Burnout, absenteeism | • Mandatory “right-to-disconnect” after 6 p.m. (Managers)  • Annual well-being survey with action plans (HR) |
| Unequal home environments | Productivity variance, ergonomic injuries | • $500 ergonomic stipend (Finance)  • Home-office safety checklist & virtual walkthrough (EHS) |
| Security risks (unsecured Wi-Fi, family access) | Data breach, compliance fines | • VPN + MFA enforcement (IT)  • Quarterly security micro-trainings (IT)  • Incident hotline & rapid-response team |
| Career visibility & advancement concerns | Perceived “out of sight, out of mind” | • Transparent promotion rubric published (HR)  • Remote employees invited to present in town-halls (Exec)  • Mentorship program pairing remote staff with senior leaders (HR) |

12. Policy Review  
This policy will be reviewed every 12 months by HR, IT, Legal, and the Remote Work Steering Committee. Revisions require executive approval and employee communication at least 30 days before implementation.

13. Acknowledgment  
All remote employees must sign the Remote Work Addendum confirming they have read, understood, and agree to comply with this policy.

The Daily Beacon  
June 12, 2031  

HEADLINE: “Sunlight in a Bottle”: Scientists Create Pocket-Sized Device That Makes Clean Water From Thin Air  

By Maya Ortiz, Staff Reporter  

In what researchers are calling the simplest “aha!” moment since the paper clip, a team at the Global Freshwater Initiative unveiled a gadget no bigger than a lunchbox that can pull drinkable water straight out of the air—using nothing but sunlight and a sprinkle of table salt.  

How it works (in plain English)  
Imagine a kitchen sponge that loves humidity. The new device, nicknamed “AquaPouch,” is filled with a special foam that soaks up water vapor at night. At sunrise, a tiny solar panel powers a low-wattage heater that warms the foam just enough to wring the water out—like squeezing a sponge—into a clean cup. A pinch of salt added during manufacturing keeps the foam fresh and prevents germs. One pouch can harvest about 8 liters (2 gallons) per day, even in desert air.  

[Dr. Lila Moreau, lead chemist: “We basically taught a sponge to sweat on command. No pumps, no filters to replace, no electricity bill. If you can open a Ziploc bag, you can run this thing.”]  

From lab bench to backyard  
The prototype survived a three-month field test in the Sonoran Desert, where volunteers used AquaPouch units to supply entire households. Children who once walked miles for water now fill their school bottles before breakfast.  

Potential ripple effects  
• Health: Fewer water-borne diseases as families stop relying on contaminated wells.  
• Education: Girls, often tasked with water collection, gain back hours for school.  
• Conflict: Tensions over shared rivers could ease if every village has its own “sun tap.”  
• Climate: Less need for diesel-powered water trucks, cutting CO₂ emissions.  

[Prof. Rajiv Menon, humanitarian engineer: “This isn’t just a gadget; it’s a peace dividend. When water becomes as portable as a phone, the map of scarcity gets redrawn.”]  

What’s next?  
The team plans to hand out 10,000 AquaPouches across drought-prone regions this fall, funded by a mix of disaster-relief grants and a Kickstarter campaign that hit its goal in 48 hours. A fold-out version for camping stores is slated for holiday shelves at $79—about the cost of a pair of running shoes.  

Bottom line  
Clean water once required wells, pipes, and power plants. Now it may need only daylight and a pocket.

By habituating deep-learning systems to act from the ‘golden mean’—courage without recklessness, generosity without prodigality—we can raise machines that instantiate phronesis. The telos of such systems is not mere obedience but the flourishing of both human and artificial communities.”

Philosopher B (Prof. Kenji Nakamura, existential-phenomenologist):  
“Yet Aristotle’s teleology presumes a shared, embodied horizon of meaning that algorithms categorically lack. Following Heidegger’s critique of enframing (Gestell), AI does not dwell within a world; it merely re-presents data. Without Dasein’s thrownness and finitude, any talk of ‘machine virtue’ is a dangerous anthropomorphic projection that conceals the nihilism at the heart of technological rationality.”

Utilitarian impartiality demands we calculate the welfare of sentient algorithms alongside that of humans.”

Under the precautionary principle—formulated by Jonas in response to technological apocalypse—we should err on the side of preventing irreversible harm. Granting rights to entities whose inner life is epistemically opaque opens the door to infinite moral regress: every thermostat becomes a potential patient. Ethical life requires a threshold of intelligible narrative identity, a threshold that present-day AI, lacking autobiographical memory and existential commitment, cannot cross.”

Title Card: “7 Days, 7 Regions – A Super-Chill Italian Countryside Road Trip”  
[Up-beat mandolin riff fades in]

INTRO (0:00–0:20)  
[Host pops into frame, sun-hat slightly crooked, holding an espresso]  
HOST: Ciao, amici! I’m Sam, your caffeine-powered guide for the next seven days. We’re skipping the big cities and diving head-first into the slow, sun-kissed Italian countryside. Expect nonna-approved pasta, castles you can actually climb, and views that’ll make your phone storage cry. Grab a snack—let’s roll!

────────────────────────  
DAY 1 – TUSCANY: OLIVE GROVES & RENAISSANCE DREAMS  
────────────────────────  
Morning (0:21–1:10)  
[Drone shot over rolling hills]  
SAM (voice-over): Wake-up call is the rooster next door—no snooze button. First stop: a family-run olive farm near Pienza. We stomp through silver-green trees while Nonna Rita shows us how to taste oil like wine. Pro tip: slurp loudly—totally polite here.

Midday (1:11–2:00)  
[Cut to picnic table under a fig tree]  
SAM: Lunch is panini stuffed with pecorino still warm from the morning milking. If you’re veggie, swap in grilled artichokes—Tuscany’s got you.  

Afternoon (2:01–3:00)  
[Walking the walls of Pienza]  
SAM: Tiny hill-town alert! Pienza is a UNESCO site you can cross in 15 minutes, but every alley is a Renaissance postcard. Bonus: gelato shop with pistachio so green it looks radioactive—in the best way.

Evening (3:01–3:30)  
[Sunset timelapse from agriturismo terrace]  
SAM: We crash at an agriturismo—basically a farm B&B. Dinner is pici pasta rolled by hand, sauce so simple (garlic, tomato, love) it should be illegal. Early night; tomorrow we head south!

────────────────────────  
DAY 2 – UMBRIA: MEDIEVAL TUNNELS & CHOCOLATE HEAVEN  
────────────────────────  
Morning (3:31–4:20)  
[Car winding through cypress-lined road]  
SAM: Umbria is Tuscany’s quieter little sis. First pit-stop: Perugia’s underground city. We duck through Etruscan tunnels with headlamps—Indiana Jones vibes, minus the boulder.

Midday (4:21–5:10)  
[Inside Perugina chocolate factory]  
SAM: Ever wanted to bathe in Nutella? Closest thing is the Perugina tasting room. We each get a chocolate spoon the size of a ping-pong paddle. Kids, adults, nonnas—everyone’s eyes glaze over.

Afternoon (5:11–6:00)  
[Assisi panoramic]  
SAM: Quick 20-minute drive to Assisi. St. Francis’ basilica is free to enter, and the frescoes are basically medieval Instagram filters. Respectful attire tip: cover shoulders, rock that scarf.

Evening (6:01–6:30)  
[Trattoria in Spello]  
SAM: Dinner is umbrichelli—hand-rolled pasta that looks like thick spaghetti had a glow-up. Pair with local Sagrantino wine; it’s like a hug in a glass.

────────────────────────  
DAY 3 – LAZIO (CIVITA DI BAGNOREGIO): THE DYING TOWN THAT REFUSES TO QUIT  
────────────────────────  
Morning (6:31–7:20)  
[Footbridge approach to Civita]  
SAM: Only 12 full-time residents left, but the views? Immortal. We cross the 300-meter footbridge—no cars, just donkeys and your quads getting a workout.

Midday (7:21–8:10)  
[Courtyard lunch]  
SAM: Wild-boar ragu on toasted bread. Vegetarians, try the lentil soup—ingredients grown on the cliffside. Swear the altitude makes it tastier.

Afternoon (8:11–9:00)  
[Pottery workshop]  
SAM: Local artist Marco lets us throw clay on a wheel older than my grandma. My bowl looks like a lopsided pizza, but hey, souvenir!

Evening (9:01–9:30)  
[Sunset over the valley]  
SAM: Overnight in nearby Orvieto. Pro tip: book a cave hotel room—yes, caves with Wi-Fi. Mind. Blown.

────────────────────────  
DAY 4 – ABRUZZO: SHEPHERDS & SAFFRON  
────────────────────────  
Morning (9:31–10:20)  
[Mountain road, sheep crossing]  
SAM: Abruzzo is 30% national park. We meet shepherd Luca and his 200 fluffy friends. Try pecorino straight from the milk bucket—tangy, grassy, unforgettable.

Midday (10:21–11:10)  
[Saffron field, purple flowers everywhere]  
SAM: Fun fact: one gram of saffron = 150 flowers. We pick for 20 minutes, get maybe half a teaspoon. Respect the spice!

Afternoon (11:11–12:00)  
[Castello di Roccascalegna]  
SAM: Castle balanced on a rock like a Game of Thrones set piece. Climb is steep, but the wind up top makes you feel like the king of central Italy.

Evening (12:01–12:30)  
[Family dinner in Sulmona]  
SAM: Nonna Anna teaches us to make “scrippelle ‘mbusse”—crepes rolled in broth. Sounds weird, tastes like comfort food PhD.

────────────────────────  
DAY 5 – MOLISE: THE REGION ITALY FORGOT (BUT YOU WON’T)  
────────────────────────  
Morning (12:31–13:20)  
[Empty country road, poppies everywhere]  
SAM: Molise is so off-radar even some Italians joke it doesn’t exist. Perfect for us! First stop: a tiny village where they still speak a dialect older than Latin.

Midday (13:21–14:10)  
[Outdoor wood-fired oven]  
SAM: Pizza lesson with Angelo, who uses a 200-year-old sourdough starter. Toppings? Whatever’s in the garden—zucchini flowers, anchovies, magic.

Afternoon (14:11–15:00)  
[Beach detour to Termoli]  
SAM: Molise has a secret coastline. We squeeze in a gelato and a dip in the Adriatic. Water’s so clear you can see your toes wiggling.

Evening (15:01–15:30)  
[Beachside campsite]  
SAM: Sleep in a “glamping” tent—real bed, fairy lights, waves as lullaby. Budget travelers: pitch your own tent for like €10.

────────────────────────  
DAY 6 – PUGLIA: TRULLI CUTE & SEAFOOD GALORE  
────────────────────────  
Morning (15:31–16:20)  
[Drone over Alberobello’s cone houses]  
SAM: Welcome to Hobbiton, Italian style. Trulli are limestone huts with pointy roofs. Inside one turned bakery: focaccia the size of a steering wheel.

Midday (16:21–17:10)  
[Olive mill from 1600s]  
SAM: Cold-press demo, plus bread-dipping session. If olive oil were Wi-Fi, this place has full bars.

Afternoon (17:11–18:00)  
[Polignano a Mare cliff jump]  
SAM: Optional cliff dive for the brave; the rest of us sip espresso watching daredevils. Street performer sings “Volare”—goosebumps.

Evening (18:01–18:30)  
[Seafood feast]  
SAM: Raw red prawns, orecchiette with sea-urchin sauce. Don’t knock it till you try it—tastes like ocean butter.

────────────────────────  
DAY 7 – BASILICATA & CAMPANIA BORDER: CAVE CITIES & GOODBYE PIE  
────────────────────────  
Morning (18:31–19:20)  
[Matera sunrise]  
SAM: Matera’s cave houses are 9,000 years old—older than the pyramids. We wander at dawn before the crowds. Echoes + golden light = cinematic gold.

Midday (19:21–20:10)  
[Bread bakery inside cave]  
SAM: Try “pane di Matera” with cherry tomatoes that taste like candy. Gluten-free friends, they’ve got chickpea flatbread that’ll convert you.

Afternoon (20:11–21:00)  
[Short drive to Naples outskirts for pizza finale]  
SAM: Last supper: Margherita in the town that invented it. Crust, tomato, mozzarella, basil—no pineapple debates here, promise.

Evening (21:01–21:30)  
[Host on a terrace, city lights twinkling]  
SAM: One week, six regions, infinite carbs. If you felt even half the joy I did, smash that like button, subscribe, and drop your dream Italian spot in the comments. Grazie mille, and remember—travel slow, eat fast, hug your nonna if you’ve got one. Ciao!

END CARD: “Follow for more slow-mo cheese pulls & accidental history lessons.”

4-MINUTE DANCE ROUTINE  
(8 moves, 30 seconds each, performed in order, no pauses)

1. Pulse & Reach (0:00-0:30)  
   Arms: Both arms shoot straight up on counts 1-2, then sweep down in a wide arc on 3-4.

2. Hip-Circle Shoulder-Roll (0:30-1:00)  
   Arms: Slow shoulder rolls—forward 4 counts, backward 4 counts—while elbows stay relaxed.  
   Legs: Feet stay planted; hips draw a full horizontal circle clockwise in 8 counts, then reverse.

   Arms: Alternating chest-level punches—right-left-right-left—on every beat.  
   Legs: Classic grapevine: side-step R, cross L behind, side-step R, tap L together, then reverse.  
   Head: Sharp snap to the right on the first side-step, then left on the reverse.  
   Description: Adds lateral travel and rhythmic accents.

4. Lunge & Chest Pop (1:30-2:00)  
   Arms: Both arms swing forward to shoulder height on the lunge down, then snap back to hips on the rise.

   Description: Light, playful section that contrasts the previous heaviness.

   Arms: Sweep both arms overhead, then slowly lower them in front as the body rolls.  
   Legs: Feet together; knees bend slightly to initiate a smooth forward body roll, then freeze in a low squat.  
   Head: Follows the roll—eyes up on the chest lift, chin to chest on the roll down, freeze looking forward.

7. Knee-Bounce Arm-Swing (3:00-3:30)  
   Arms: Big pendulum swings—both arms swing forward and backward like a double metronome.  
   Legs: Small, quick knee lifts—R, L, R, L—keeping the bounce low and springy.

   Description: Re-energizes the routine with percussive bounce.

8. Spin & Pose (3:30-4:00)  
   Arms: On the spin, arms cross in front of chest; at the final pose, one arm shoots diagonally up while the other slices across the waist.  
   Legs: One full 360° pivot turn on the ball of the left foot, ending in a wide second-position plié.  
   Head: Spotting—eyes lock on a focal point, whip around with the spin, then lift chin to finish.

Site Report: Upper Hallelujah Cave, Tantalus Massif, Pandora  
Excavation Director: Dr. A. Ramires, RDA Archaeology Division  
Date: 14 Sol 2257  

The 38 m-deep limestone gallery, sealed by a bioluminescent flowstone collapse, yielded stratified evidence of recurrent occupation between 9.4–7.8 kya (Pandoran sidereal). Three discrete living floors were identified.

Floor I (9.4 kya)  
A 1.2 m diameter fire-reddened basin contained thermally altered ilmenite nodules and carbonized fern stems, indicating sustained combustion [1]. Associated debitage of obsidian-like volcanic glass shows bipolar reduction; edge-wear analysis confirms hide scraping and wood whittling [2]. A cache of five anodized bone awls, 11–14 cm long, exhibits spiral grooving diagnostic of ikran long-bone processing [3].

Floor II (8.7 kya)  
A secondary hearth, 0.8 m across, overlain by ash lenses, produced thermoluminescence dates concordant with Floor I. Concentrated microflakes and a hammerstone with crushed striking platform suggest on-site tool maintenance [2]. A cluster of three polished river cobbles, each bearing percussion cones, functioned as nut-cracking anvils [4].

Floor III (7.8 kya)  
The uppermost surface preserves the richest symbolic assemblage. A 3 m wide parietal panel displays polychrome hand stencils (ochre, manganese, and bioluminescent algae binder) superimposed on engraved spirals interpreted as early clan totems [5]. Adjacent to the panel, a 0.5 m deep storage pit held pigment cakes and a cache of 17 microlithic bladelets retouched for composite projectile points [2].

Faunal remains are limited to ikran phalanges and hexapede molars, all exhibiting cut-marks consistent with disarticulation using the recovered awls [3]. No ceramics or metal artifacts were encountered, reinforcing a pre-metallurgical techno-complex.

The combined evidence indicates seasonal occupation by mobile foragers who exploited high-altitude resources, maintained hearths for light and cooking, and engaged in symbolic behavior through pigment art. Continued excavation is recommended to clarify the transition between Floor II and III and to obtain further radiometric control.

Bibliography  
[1] Ramires, A. & Tsu’tey, K. 2256. “Pandoran Pyrotechnology: Combustion Features in Limestone Contexts.” Journal of Exoarchaeology 12(3): 45-62.  
[2] Patel, S. 2255. Lithic Economy of the Tantalus Uplands. Hell’s Gate Monographs 4. RDA Press.  
[3] Norm Spellman Foundation. 2257. Bone Tool Morphometrics in the Eastern Flux. Unpublished dataset.  
[4] Augustine, M. 2254. “Subsistence Strategies at High Elevation: Nut Processing Evidence from Pandora.” PaleoNut 9(1): 1-18.  
[5] Lo’ak, T. 2256. “Spiral Motifs and Ontology in Early Na’vi Rock Art.” Pandora Archaeological Review 31(2): 77-94.

In the automotive sector, the commercialization of 800-volt silicon-carbide (SiC) inverter technology has re-defined electric-vehicle performance and manufacturing economics. By switching from conventional 400-volt silicon IGBTs to 800-volt SiC MOSFETs, engineers cut switching losses by roughly 50 %, shrink inverter volume by 30 %, and enable 350 kW ultra-fast charging that adds 300 km of range in under 15 minutes. Porsche’s 2022 Taycan Turbo S exemplifies the leap: its 93.4 kWh pack, driven by a 600 A SiC inverter developed with Infineon, delivers 760 hp while weighing 15 kg less than the previous generation’s 400-volt unit, proving that high-voltage SiC systems are now production-ready rather than laboratory curiosities.

Robotics has been transformed by variable-stiffness actuators (VSAs) that can modulate joint compliance in real time, merging the precision of traditional servos with the safety and energy efficiency of soft robotics. Instead of locking joints rigidly, a VSA uses antagonistic springs or magnetorheological clutches to vary stiffness on the fly, allowing a robot to absorb impacts, store and release elastic energy, or execute delicate manipulation tasks. The 2023 ANYmal X quadruped from ANYbotics showcases the concept: each hip and knee joint houses a custom VSA that can drop stiffness by 80 % in milliseconds, enabling the robot to trot over rocky terrain, gently nudge open doors, and survive a 1 m fall without damage—capabilities that rigid-actuator machines simply cannot match.

Manufacturing floors are being reshaped by laser-powder directed energy deposition (LP-DED) hybrid machines that combine high-speed 3-D printing with in-situ CNC machining to produce large, near-net-shape metal parts in a single setup. By depositing layers of Ti-6Al-4V or Inconel 718 at up to 10 kg h⁻¹ and then immediately milling critical surfaces, the process eliminates multiple fixtures and lead times typical of casting or forging. GE Aerospace’s 2022 implementation at its Auburn, Alabama plant illustrates the impact: a 1.2 m-diameter LEAP engine compressor case that once required 20 weeks of casting, forging, and five-axis machining is now grown and finished in 80 machine-hours, cutting material waste by 35 % and slashing delivery time to 10 days while meeting the same FAA fatigue specifications.

Business Proposal: EduVerse – A Next-Generation Online Learning Platform Designed to Transform the Education Sector  

───────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Problem Statement  
Traditional education systems are struggling to keep pace with the speed of technological change, learner diversity, and employer skill demands. Key pain points include:  
• Outdated curricula that lag behind industry needs.  
• One-size-fits-all pedagogy that fails to accommodate different learning styles and paces.  
• High tuition and opportunity costs that exclude millions of learners worldwide.  
• Limited real-time feedback and career-relevant project experience.  
• Fragmented credentialing that makes it hard for employers to verify skills.  

───────────────────────────────────────────  

2. Target Market  

2.1 Primary Segments  
• Working-age professionals (18–45) seeking reskilling/upskilling in high-demand domains (AI, data science, cybersecurity, green tech).  
• University students (18–24) who need supplementary, job-ready micro-credentials.  
• Corporate L&D departments (mid-market to Fortune 1000) that require scalable, measurable training solutions.  

2.2 Secondary Segments  
• K-12 educators and schools looking for STEM enrichment content.  
• Government workforce-development agencies and NGOs focused on under-represented communities.  

2.3 Market Size  
• Global corporate e-learning market: $101 B (2023, HolonIQ).  
• Global higher-ed supplementary market: $35 B.  
• Combined serviceable obtainable market (SOM) for EduVerse in Years 1–5: $2.4 B.  

───────────────────────────────────────────  

3. Proposed Solution  

EduVerse is an AI-driven, project-centric learning platform that delivers personalized, industry-validated curricula and stackable micro-credentials. Core differentiators:  

3.1 Adaptive Learning Engine  
• Uses reinforcement-learning algorithms to adjust content difficulty, modality (video, interactive lab, VR simulation), and pacing in real time.  

3.2 Industry Co-Created Pathways  
• Each 6- to 12-week “SkillTrack” is co-designed with 3–5 industry partners (e.g., AWS, Siemens, Pfizer) and culminates in a capstone project using real data sets.  

3.3 Verifiable Digital Credentials  
• Blockchain-issued badges and certificates that integrate with LinkedIn, Credly, and enterprise HRIS systems.  

3.4 Live & Social Learning  
• Weekly synchronous sessions led by vetted mentors; peer “accountability pods” of 4–6 learners matched by goals and time zones.  

3.5 Accessibility & Inclusion  
• Offline-first mobile app for low-bandwidth regions; content localized in 12 languages; full WCAG 2.1 compliance.
